On the crowd’s side we see another kind of “self”: twenty thousand people shouting a slogan for two hours, most not knowing why. This is collective self-centeredness—no heart, no mind, only throat. A person whose focus is on Jesus, when the whole city is shouting, will quiet down and ask: Is this true? Then he will discover: noise scatters, the word remains. The visible storm is not the end; the unseen King is.
a: Don’t shout along
In the emotions of a crowd, first discern with the heart; do not echo with the throat.
Be willing to be stopped
God’s guidance sometimes comes to me through a brother’s “don’t”; courage also needs the ability to stop.
Ask why first
Before forwarding, echoing or taking sides, ask whether I know how things came about.
Trust God’s hand
He can use anyone to stop a storm, including unbelievers; however chaotic things are, he still reigns.
Build on the word
Noise scatters, the word remains; build my life on what remains.
q: Think of the last time you spoke, forwarded or took sides along with the emotion of a group. Did you know how things came about? If you had first asked, “Is this true?”, would you have acted differently?

Paul wanted to rush into the theater but stayed because of the disciples and friends who held him back. Is there something in your life you “had every reason to do” but were counseled against by brothers? Are you willing to stop and see what God will do?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that when the whole city of Ephesus was in uproar and two hours of slogans shook the sky, your hand never left for a moment. You protected Paul through his brothers’ restraint, and calmed the crowd through an unbelieving clerk; you do not need your servant to appear in order to reign.
Lord Jesus, we admit that we often feel we must do something in a storm to prove ourselves, and often shout along in the voice of the crowd, mostly not knowing why. Give us a quiet heart, to ask “Is this true?” when the whole city is shouting; and give us a humble heart, to stop when a brother says “no.” Keep our focus on you alone, not on circumstances; let us see that noise scatters but your word endures. May our lives not be built on noise that scatters, but on your word that never shakes. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: After the uproar had ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, took leave of them, and departed to go into Macedonia.
When he had gone through those parts, and had encouraged them with many words, he came into Greece.
When he had spent three months there, and a plot was made against him by Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he determined to return through Macedonia.
These accompanied him as far as Asia: Sopater of Beroea; Aristarchus and Secundus of the Thessalonians; Gaius of Derbe; Timothy; and Tychicus and Trophimus of Asia.
But these had gone ahead, and were waiting for us at Troas.
We sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and came to them at Troas in five days, where we stayed seven days.
On the first day of the week, when the disciples were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day, and continued his speech until midnight.
There were many lights in the upper room where we were gathered together.

A certain young man named Eutychus sat in the window, weighed down with deep sleep. As Paul spoke still longer, being weighed down by his sleep, he fell down from the third floor and was taken up dead.
Paul went down and fell upon him, and embracing him said, “Don’t be troubled, for his life is in him.”
When he had gone up, and had broken bread and eaten, and had talked with them a long while, even until break of day, he departed.
They brought the boy in alive, and were greatly comforted.
b: In the last devotion, the slogans shouted for two hours in the theater at Ephesus were finally dispersed by a few words from a clerk. The noise scattered; the word remained.

In this devotion, Luke takes Paul at great speed through a whole year of travel—Macedonia, Greece, back to Macedonia, across the sea to Troas; then suddenly the pace slows and stops on one night, one upper room, one window, one young man who fell. Paul traveled thousands of miles, but what is truly recorded is the moment he stopped for one person.
I. “After the uproar had ceased… encouraged them”—After the Storm, Comfort People First

In just two verses, “encouraged” appears twice. The word in the original means “comfort, exhort, speak alongside,” from the same root as “Comforter.” Paul had just been through a riot that nearly cost him his life and himself needed comfort; yet the first thing he did was call the disciples together and comfort them. He knew that after he left, the brothers in Ephesus would still be facing a city where Demetrius remained.

Then he went to Macedonia—Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea—“encouraging them with many words.” From 2 Corinthians we know this stretch was extremely hard for Paul: “Our flesh had no relief, but we were afflicted on every side. Fightings were outside. Fear was inside” (2 Cor. 7:5). A man with fear in his own heart went along the road comforting others “with many words.” This is the example of Jesus: on the night he was betrayed, it was the disciples he comforted.
• Comfort people first: after a storm, is my first thought my own shaken nerves, or the brothers around me?
• Encourage even in fear: there is no need to wait until I am completely well before helping others up; helping others is itself the road to healing.
II. “A plot was made against him by Jews, and he determined to return through Macedonia”—Change the Route, Not the Direction

In verse 3, Paul “came into Greece,” that is, Corinth, and “spent three months there.” It was winter, the sea lanes were closed, and he wrote Romans there. After three months he planned to sail for Syria—very likely on a ship carrying Jewish pilgrims to Jerusalem for Passover. “A plot was made against him by Jews”: on a ship crowded with enemies, it would be all too easy to strike at sea.

Paul “determined to return through Macedonia”—giving up the sea route and going north by land, a long detour. The destination had not changed, still Jerusalem; only the route changed. There is no miracle here, no vision, only a man who heard the news and adjusted his plans. The Spirit’s guidance is sometimes a voice from heaven, but more often a clear judgment: this road is dangerous, take another.
• The destination stays, the route may change: obedience is not stubbornness; when a detour is called for, take it.
• Discernment is also guidance: the Spirit’s guidance often comes through common sense and news from the brothers; there is no need to wait for a vision for everything.
III. “Accompanied him as far as Asia”—A Church in a List of Names

Verse 4 is a list: Sopater of Berea, Aristarchus and Secundus of the Thessalonians, Gaius of Derbe, Timothy (of Lystra), and Tychicus and Trophimus of Asia. Seven men from four regions—exactly the churches Paul had founded on his three journeys.

Why did they travel together? Because this trip was to carry the offering of the Gentile churches to the saints in Jerusalem (Rom. 15:25–26). When Paul wrote to the Corinthians, he said the offering would be carried together by “those whom you approve” from each church (1 Cor. 16:3–4)—he would not handle money alone; he wanted every church to have its own representative present. This list is a miniature of God’s system: not one man carrying a bag of money, but a group carrying the love of their own churches.

In verses 5 and 6 “we” appears. Luke rejoins the company from Philippi (he had stayed in Philippi in chapter 16); after the days of Unleavened Bread, they came to Troas in five days and “stayed seven days”—waiting in order to meet with the brothers on the Lord’s Day.
• Don’t handle it alone: in matters of money and testimony, letting brothers be present protects me and honors others.
• The list is the system: God’s system is not one leader and a crowd of followers, but a place and a share for people everywhere.
IV. “Talking until midnight… fell down from the third story”—Eutychus’s Windowsill

In verses 7–9 the scene slows down. “On the first day of the week”—this is the first explicit record in the New Testament of believers gathering on the Lord’s Day to break bread. Paul was leaving the next day, so he “talked with them, and continued his speech until midnight.” The meeting was on the third floor, “and there were many lights”—many lamps, many people, much smoke, the air growing ever more stuffy.

A young man named Eutychus sat in the window. His name means “fortunate.” The window was the only place in the room with fresh air, but also the most dangerous. “Weighed down with deep sleep”—Luke uses a progressive description: first drowsing, then “as Paul spoke still longer,” he fell fast asleep, and then fell down from the third story. “He was taken up dead”—Luke was a physician, and would not misjudge.

Luke does not cover for Paul: “Paul spoke still longer.” Scripture is uncomfortably honest. But Eutychus’s window is also a mirror: it is a place half inside and half outside—the body in the meeting, but the person propped up by the air outside. Many people’s faith also sits on the windowsill: they hear, but as soon as they grow drowsy, they fall outward.
• Honestly see where I am sitting: in a meeting, do I sit in the middle, or on the windowsill?
• The speaker must see people too: Paul spoke on and Eutychus fell; when I am absorbed in the matter at hand, do I see the one about to fall asleep?
V. “His life is in him”—Stopping a Whole Night for One Person

In verses 10–12, “Paul went down, and fell upon him, and embracing him.” This action is exactly the same as that of Elijah and Elisha in raising the children (1 Kings 17:21; 2 Kings 4:34)—the God of the prophets is still at work. Paul said, “Don’t be troubled, for his life is in him.”

Then comes the most moving sentence: “When he had gone up, and had broken bread, and eaten, and had talked with them a long while, even until break of day.” He did not revive the young man and rush on his way; he went back upstairs, broke bread with everyone, and “talked”—a word more intimate than the earlier “spoke,” meaning conversation with each other. From midnight until dawn, it was for this group and for the young man who had just come back from the dead. Verse 12 calls him a “lad”—he may have been a young servant, a boy of ten-odd years.
Paul had to walk many miles the next day, and could well have rested early. But people matter more than tasks, relationships more than schedule. For one boy who fell, he left the whole night open.
• Stop for one person: in my schedule, is there room to stop for someone?
• Comfort is not small: what truly stays in people’s hearts is not the message that went on until midnight, but the boy who was lifted up and embraced.
321 Principles Insight: People Matter More Than Tasks, Relationships More Than Schedule

In these twelve verses Paul does many “things”: comforting Ephesus, traveling through Macedonia, writing Romans in Corinth, escaping an assassination plot, organizing a seven-man delegation, preaching until midnight. But where does Luke’s camera finally stop? On a boy who fell from a windowsill and an apostle lying over him.

The self-centered make tasks the center, and people the tools for completing them; a young man falling asleep is his problem, and the sermon must go on. The self-denying make people the center, and tasks the way of serving people; when a young man falls, the whole meeting stops and the whole night is given up. When Paul was preaching he did not see Eutychus about to fall asleep—this is an honest record; but after Eutychus fell, everything Paul did lived out “life first, relationship second, ministry last.”

Jesus is my example: on his busiest road he stopped for a woman who touched his garment, and for a tax collector who climbed a tree. Letting Jesus be King today may look just like this—in my schedule, staying one more night for one person.
a: Comfort people first
After a storm, think first of the brothers beside me; there is no need to wait until I am fully well before helping others up.
Take the detour when needed
The destination stays, the route may change; obedience is not stubbornness.
Let brothers be present
In matters of money and testimony, do not handle things alone.
Leave the windowsill
In the meeting, move to the middle; don’t be half inside and half outside.
Stop for one person
People matter more than tasks; in my schedule, leave room to stay one more night for someone.
q: Think honestly: in the church, in your small group, in your relationship with the Lord, where are you sitting now? In the middle, or on the windowsill? What keeps you propped up by the air outside?
Paul gave up a whole night for Eutychus. In this week’s schedule, is there someone the Lord wants you to stop for and stay with a little longer? Are you willing to adjust your schedule?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that after Paul had traveled thousands of miles and done so many things, your servant Luke stopped his camera on a boy who fell from a window. Thank you for letting us see that what you care about is people, and that your servant gave up a whole night for one.
Lord Jesus, we admit that we often make tasks the center and treat people as tools for completing them; when someone in a meeting is about to fall asleep or fall away, we do not see. Give us your eyes, to see people while we speak, and to stop for one person even when we are hurrying. Search us also: if we are sitting on the windowsill of faith, half in and half out, lead us to the middle. May our lives have you first, then relationships, and only then ministry; may you reign in every one of our schedules. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: But we, going ahead to the ship, set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there; for he had so arranged, intending himself to go by land.
When he met us at Assos, we took him aboard, and came to Mitylene.
Sailing from there, we came the following day opposite Chios. The next day we touched at Samos and stayed at Trogyllium, and the day after we came to Miletus.
For Paul had determined to sail past Ephesus, that he might not have to spend time in Asia; for he was hastening, if it were possible for him, to be in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost.
From Miletus he sent to Ephesus, and called to himself the elders of the assembly.
When they had come to him, he said to them, “You yourselves know, from the first day that I set foot in Asia, how I was with you all the time,
serving the Lord with all humility, with many tears, and with trials which happened to me by the plots of the Jews;
how I didn’t shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, teaching you publicly and from house to house,
testifying both to Jews and to Greeks repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus.
Now, behold, I go bound by the Spirit to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there;
except that the Holy Spirit testifies in every city, saying that bonds and afflictions wait for me.

But these things don’t count; nor do I hold my life dear to myself, so that I may finish my race with joy, and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to fully testify to the Good News of the grace of God.
b: In the last devotion, in the upper room at Troas, Paul stopped for a whole night for a young man who had fallen from a window, and did not leave until daybreak.

In this devotion, day has broken and Paul leaves—but he does not board the ship with the others; he chooses to go on foot alone. A few days later the ship stops at Miletus, where Paul summons the elders of Ephesus and begins the only sermon in the book of Acts addressed to believers. This farewell address will be read in three devotions, and today is the first part: a man looking back on his past and then facing his future.
I. “He himself was planning to go on foot”—The Road to Assos

In verse 13, his companions “went ahead to the ship, and sailed for Assos,” while Paul “was planning to go on foot.” From Troas to Assos the ship had to go around a cape, but by land it was only about thirty kilometers, a day’s walk. Paul “had so arranged”—it was his own decision.

Luke does not say why. But think of that night: preaching until midnight, the young man falling, dying and living again, talking until dawn. Paul had not slept all night, and ahead lay Jerusalem, the chains he already sensed. He chose to walk a day’s road alone.

Some roads must be walked alone. Not to withdraw from the group, but to be alone with the Lord before entering the next stage. Jesus himself did this often—“Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there” (Mark 1:35). The order of relationships is first with God, then with oneself, then with others, then with tasks; the road to Assos was the day Paul put the order back in its right place.
In verses 14 and 15 he boarded at Assos and passed through Mitylene, Chios and Samos to reach Miletus.
• Leave a stretch of road alone: before the next important stage, do I have a stretch of road that I walk only with the Lord?
• God first: praying only after everything is busy and praying first and then being busy are two completely different lives.
II. “Had determined to sail past Ephesus”—Letting Go of the Dearest Place

In verse 16, “Paul had determined to sail past Ephesus, that he might not have to spend time in Asia.” Ephesus was where he had lived for three years, the deepest stretch of ministry in his life; the ship passed Ephesus offshore and he did not go ashore.

Why? “He was hastening, if it were possible for him, to be in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost.” He wanted to hand the Gentile churches’ offering to the saints in Jerusalem in person at the festival. And he knew that if he landed at Ephesus, the brothers and sisters would never let him go. So he stopped the ship at Miletus—about fifty kilometers south of Ephesus—and “sent to Ephesus, and called to himself the elders of the assembly.”

Self-denial is not abstract: it is not going ashore at the place you cannot bear to leave. Paul loved Ephesus, but he loved the course the Lord had given him more; for a greater purpose he let go of a dearer place.
• Discern what I cannot bear to leave: do I have an “Ephesus” the Lord wants me to sail past but I keep wanting to land at?
• Let go of the dearer for the greater purpose: not that I do not love, but that I put love in its right order.
III. “You yourselves know… how I was with you all the time”—A Life That Withstands Scrutiny
In verses 18–21, the elders arrived, and Paul’s first words were: “You yourselves know.” He did not say “I tell you,” but “you know”—for three years they had seen him every day.

What had they seen? “Serving the Lord with all humility, with many tears, and with trials which happened to me by the plots of the Jews.” The Greek word for “humility” was originally a pejorative term meaning “lowly, base”; Christians turned it into a virtue, and Paul uses it to sum up his three years of ministry. What humility looked like is in the next phrase: tears and trials—a leatherworker who preached in the school at midday, wept over people in the evening, and could be harmed by the Jews at any moment.

In verses 20 and 21, his teaching also withstood scrutiny: “I didn’t shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable,” “publicly, and from house to house”—the public platform and the private visit; “testifying both to Jews and to Greeks repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ”—the content was only one thing from beginning to end.
Jesus is my example, and in the end it comes down to one sentence: can my life say to others, “You know”?
• Can my life be watched: three years later, could the brothers and sisters say, “We know how you lived”?
• What humility looks like: not a posture, but tears in the eyes, work in the hands, words not held back.
IV. “Bound by the Spirit”—The One Bound by the Spirit Is Free

In verses 22 and 23, Paul turns from the past to the future: “Now, behold, I go bound by the Spirit to Jerusalem.” The Chinese Union Version margin notes the original: “heart bound”—literally “bound in the spirit.” He was not going on impulse but was bound by the Spirit to go forward; and at the same time the Spirit “testifies in every city, saying that bonds and afflictions wait for me.”

This is a strange situation: the Spirit urged him to go, and the Spirit also told him that going would mean chains. God did not hide the cost, and did not remove the cost; he simply said clearly: go, and it will be hard. The details were unknown, but the direction was clear.

Like a sailboat. Only when the sail is “bound” by the wind does the boat have power; a boat that refuses to be bound by the wind can only drift freely in the harbor. The person bound by the Spirit looks unfree—he cannot choose his own road; yet only such a person is truly moving forward.
• Discern the binding: am I bound by my own plans, or bound by the Holy Spirit? The former brings anxiety, the latter peace.
• Accept “go, and it will be hard”: God’s guidance does not remove affliction; it keeps the direction clear within affliction.
V. “I do not count my life of any value”—Finishing My Course

Verse 24 is the peak of this passage: “But I don’t count my life of any value to myself, so that I may finish my race with joy, and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify the Good News of the grace of God.”

“Race” is the picture of a running track—Paul regarded his whole life as a race, and the point was not how fast he ran but that he finished. And the track was not drawn by himself but was “the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus”; the content of the track was only one thing: “to testify the Good News of the grace of God.”

“I do not count my life of any value”—this is not despising life but putting life in its proper place: life is for finishing the race, not for preserving. A person who counts his life most precious cannot finish the course, because he will stop at every danger. It is no longer I but Christ—and here Paul says it in the plainest words: only that I may finish my race.
• Who drew my track: is the course I am running one the Lord gave, or a comfortable route I chose?
• What is most precious to me: if even life is not counted precious, what about the thing I am gripping hardest now?
321 Principles Insight: Self-Denial Is Walked Out One Step at a Time

In these twelve verses self-denial never appears by name, yet it is everywhere in the picture: walking the road to Assos alone is laying down one’s own weariness; sailing past Ephesus is laying down the place one can least bear to leave; “serving the Lord with all humility, with many tears” is laying down one’s own dignity; going bound by the Spirit to Jerusalem is laying down one’s own plans; “I do not count my life of any value” is laying down one’s own life.

The self-centered can also say “I offer myself for the Lord,” but when he reaches the sea off Ephesus, he will go ashore; when he hears “chains await,” he will take a detour. Self-denial is not a resolution but a series of concrete “not going ashore.”

And the power behind all this is not Paul’s will. It is “bound in the spirit”—the Holy Spirit is my guide. The one bound by the Spirit is actually the freest person: he need not plan for his own life, for his life has been handed over; he has only one thing left to do—finish the race. This is precisely the life in which Jesus is King: the King sets the course, and the servant only runs.
a: Leave a stretch of road alone
Before the next stage, walk a stretch alone with God and put the order right.
Sail past my Ephesus
Do not go ashore at the dearest place the Lord asks me to leave.
Live a life that can be watched
Three years from now, may the brothers and sisters say, “We know how you lived.”
Let the Spirit bind me
Discern whether I am bound by my own plans or by the Spirit; accept “go, and it will be hard.”
Only finish the race
Do not count precious what I grip hardest; only finish the course the Lord has given.
q: Paul chose to walk the road to Assos alone. Before your next important stage, have you left a stretch of road to walk only with the Lord? If not, where could you start this week?

“I do not count my life of any value.” Ask yourself honestly: what is the thing you are gripping hardest and are least willing to let go of right now? Does it keep you from finishing the course the Lord has given you?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for letting us see how your servant walked his course step by step: walking the road to Assos alone, sailing past Ephesus which he loved most, going bound by your Spirit to Jerusalem. Thank you also that he could say to the brothers, “You know how I lived”—a life that withstands scrutiny.
Lord Jesus, we admit that we often say we will lay ourselves down for you, but at the place we cannot bear to leave we want to go ashore, and when we hear there will be affliction we want to take a detour. Give us a heart bound by your Spirit, clear in direction even when we do not know what lies ahead; and take our lives out of our own hands, so that we no longer count them most precious but only want to finish the course you have given us. May our lives be watched, and may the tears in our eyes and the work in our hands testify to the Good News of your grace. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: “Now, behold, I know that you all, among whom I went about preaching God’s Kingdom, will see my face no more.
Therefore I testify to you today that I am clean from the blood of all men,
for I didn’t shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God.
Take heed, therefore, to yourselves, and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the assembly of the Lord and  God which he purchased with his own blood.
For I know that after my departure, vicious wolves will enter in among you, not sparing the flock.
Men will arise from among your own selves, speaking perverse things, to draw away the disciples after them.
Therefore watch, remembering that for a period of three years I didn’t cease to admonish everyone night and day with tears.
b: In the last devotion, at Miletus, Paul looked back for the Ephesian elders on his three years—“you know how I lived”—and faced his own future—“I do not count my life of any value, only that I may finish my race.”

In this devotion, he turns his eyes from himself to these elders. He begins with a heartbreaking sentence: you will see my face no more. Then he does what a father does before leaving: he hands over the household. In handing it over, he makes three things clear—whom the watchman must watch first, whose flock this is, and where danger comes from.
I. “You will see my face no more”—The Last Words

In verse 25, “I know that you all, among whom I went about preaching the Kingdom of God”—three years in Ephesus, summed up in one sentence; then: “Now behold, I know that you all… will see my face no more.”

This is a farewell. The Spirit had testified in every city that chains awaited him, and he faced the worst case as real. Such words make every sentence that follows heavy: this is the last time, and there will be no next time to add anything.

When people know “this is the last time,” they speak differently—no more pleasantries, no more going in circles, only what matters most. If I knew that today’s words to someone were the last, what would I say? That is what I truly should say.
• Speak with a last-time heart: no pleasantries, no circling, only what matters most.
• The content of the preaching is one thing: in three years at Ephesus, Paul preached “the Kingdom of God,” not his own opinions.
II. “I am clean from the blood of all men”—The Watchman’s Innocence

In verses 26 and 27, Paul says something very heavy: “I testify to you this day, that I am clean from the blood of all men.” This is the language of the watchman in Ezekiel: God says to the watchman, if you warn the wicked and he does not turn back, “he will die in his iniquity, but you have delivered your soul”; if you do not warn him, “his blood I will require at your hand” (Ezek. 33:6–9).

On what ground could Paul say he was innocent? Verse 27: “For I didn’t shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God.” “The whole counsel of God” means God’s complete plan—not choosing what is pleasant to say, not choosing what is safe, but all of it. Repentance and grace, cross and resurrection, judgment and hope, nothing left out.

The word “shrink” appeared in the last devotion as well (20:20)—in the original it means “to draw back out of fear.” Where does a preacher most easily draw back? On the truths that offend people. Paul says he never drew back once, and only such a man dares say “I am clean from the blood of all men.” I may not be a preacher, but I am certainly a watchman for some people—children, spouse, brothers and sisters in my small group. Have I swallowed what I should have said because I feared his displeasure?
• Preach the whole: do not choose the pleasant, do not choose the safe; speak all of God’s word.
• Do not draw back out of fear: think of the sentence I did not say because I feared offending—that is exactly what I owe.
III. “Take heed to yourselves, and to all the flock”—Watch Yourself First

Verse 28 puts three words on the same group of people: verse 17 calls them “elders,” here they are called “overseers,” and they are told to “shepherd”—the shepherd’s verb. Elder is identity, overseer is duty, shepherding is work. And the one who appointed them was not Paul, nor a church vote, but “the Holy Spirit has made you overseers.”

Notice Paul’s order: “take heed to yourselves” first, “to all the flock” afterward. A person watching a flock must first watch himself. How many servants fall not because they were struck down from outside, but because something first loosened within: weariness, pride, secret sin.
Life first, relationships second, ministry last. “Take heed to yourselves” is life, “to all the flock” is relationship, “shepherd” is ministry. Paul states the order perfectly clearly.
• Watch myself first: when did I last seriously examine my own life?
• The office was set by the Spirit: my service today was not won by me nor given by people but appointed by him; then do it his way.
IV. “Which he purchased with his own blood”—Whose Sheep

The second half of verse 28 is the deepest sentence of this sermon: “to feed the assembly of the Lord and God which he purchased with his own blood.” The church is “the assembly of God,” not Paul’s, not the elders’. And this ownership was paid for: “purchased with his own blood.” The blood of God—this is one of the strongest expressions in the New Testament: what bought this people was God’s own blood.

This sentence fixes the place of all shepherding. If the sheep are mine, I can treat them as I please; if the sheep were bought with God’s blood, then every person in my hands is one for whom he paid the highest price. A person entrusted with caring for someone else’s child holds that child more carefully than his own, because he knows the child is not his and the parents may return at any moment.

Pride is leaving one’s place and grasping power, wanting to replace God; in shepherding, pride looks like treating God’s sheep as one’s own—using them to build one’s own influence and satisfy one’s need to be needed. Humility is returning to one’s place: I am only the watchman; the sheep are his, and the price was paid by him.
• The sheep are not mine: every person I serve was bought by him with blood; how I treat them, he sees.
• Do not build my own sheepfold: bring people to Jesus, not to myself.
V. “Fierce wolves… and from among your own selves”—Danger from Outside and from Within

In verses 29 and 30, Paul tells what he knows of the future: “fierce wolves will enter in among you”—this comes from outside; “and from among your own selves, men will arise, speaking perverse things”—this comes from within.

“Perverse” in the original means “twisted”—not an outright lie but truth bent a little. “To draw away the disciples after them”—note, after “them,” not after the Lord. This is the mark of false teachers: they want followers. Later history confirmed Paul’s words: his letter to Timothy was to have him deal with “those who teach a different doctrine” in Ephesus (1 Tim. 1:3).

Facing such a future, Paul did not give a system of defense but one word: “watch”—stay awake, do not fall asleep. Then an example: “remembering that for the space of three years I didn’t cease to admonish everyone night and day with tears.” Three years, night and day, tears, everyone—shepherding is not talk from a platform but admonishing one by one, with tears.
• What comes from within is harder to guard against: the standard of discernment is not “is he speaking correctly” but “whom does he want people to follow.”
• Remember the admonition with tears: someone once wept over me and admonished me; I too should treat people this way.
321 Principles Insight: God’s System, Not Mine

In these seven verses Paul hands over the church in Ephesus. But he does not hand it to the elders—he makes it clear in verse 28 that this is “the assembly of God,” “which he purchased with his own blood.” The elders are only overseers, not masters.

The key to building God’s system is the two words “God’s.” A system can have elders, overseers and shepherding yet still be human—sheep revolving around the shepherd, people following “them” and not following the Lord. God’s system is exactly the opposite: the shepherd first takes heed to himself, then brings the sheep to the Lord who paid the price in blood.

What letting Jesus be King looks like here is very concrete: not one person in my hands is mine. I weep for them and admonish them night and day, but I do not own them; they are his, and I am only the one who keeps watch until he returns. Self-denying shepherding means moving oneself out of the center of the flock and letting the Lord who bought them with his blood stand in the middle.
a: Speak with a last-time heart
To those near me, no pleasantries and no circling; only what matters most.
Do not draw back out of fear
Say in love the word I swallowed because I feared offending.
Take heed to myself first
Examine my own life before managing anyone else’s.
Remember whose sheep
Everyone I serve was bought by him with blood; do not build my own sheepfold.
Watch and weep
The standard of discernment is “whom does he want people to follow”; remember those who wept over me and treat people the same way.
q: Whose watchman are you? Among those you look after, is there a word you know you should say but have not, for fear of his displeasure? When and with what heart will you say it?

“Take heed to yourselves, and to all the flock.” Ask honestly: have you been busy looking at others’ problems and not watched yourself for a long time? What is one thing you could begin with today to “take heed to yourself”?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for letting us hear Paul’s last words to the elders of Ephesus. Thank you that through him you remind us that the church is yours, bought with your own blood; every person in our hands is one for whom you paid the highest price.
Lord Jesus, we admit that we often swallow what we should say because we fear offending; we are often busy watching others and forget to watch ourselves first; and we even unknowingly treat your sheep as our own, letting people follow us and not you. Forgive us, and make us take heed to ourselves first, then to others; make us bring people to you, not to ourselves. Give us a heart that watches and discerns perverse words; and give us Paul’s tears, willing to admonish people night and day without ceasing. May your church always be yours, and may you reign in it. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: Now, brothers, I entrust you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build up, and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified.
I coveted no one’s silver, gold, or clothing.
You yourselves know that these hands served my necessities, and those who were with me.
In all things I gave you an example, that so laboring you ought to help the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’”
When he had spoken these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all.
They all wept freely, and fell on Paul’s neck and kissed him,
sorrowing most of all because of the word which he had spoken, that they should see his face no more. Then they accompanied him to the ship.
b: In the last devotion, Paul handed the church in Ephesus over—not to the elders, but to the God who “purchased it with his own blood.” He warned that wolves would come and that perverse men would rise from within, and told the elders to watch.

In this devotion, the farewell address reaches its last few sentences. A man who knows he will not return leaves his final words on two things: to whom he entrusts the people, and what kind of hands he leaves behind. Then the sermon ends on knees, in tears, at the harbor. Nowhere in the whole book of Acts do we see more clearly how the gospel turns a group of people into a family.
I. “I commend you to God and to the word of his grace”—Entrusting, Not Handing Over

In verse 32, “Now, brothers, I entrust you to God and to the word of his grace.” The word “entrust” in the original means “to deposit, to lay up for safekeeping”—to place something precious with someone reliable. Paul did not hand Ephesus over to a successor; he “deposited” them with God and with “the word of his grace.”

Why “the word”? Because Paul was leaving, the elders would grow old, and wolves would come; the only thing that does not leave, grow old, or fear wolves is the word of God. This word has two powers: “which is able to build you up”—“build” in the original is “to construct a house,” raising people brick by brick; “and to give you the inheritance”—this is the language of dividing the land among God’s people, speaking of a person’s share in God’s household. People leave, the word remains; the word remains, and the house keeps being built.

Scripture is my standard—this is the most practical entrusting a person can make at a farewell: I can no longer care for you, but this word can. If a person builds his faith on a certain pastor or a certain experience, when the pastor leaves, the house stops being built; those who build on the word keep building no matter who leaves.
• Entrusted to the word: is the foundation of my faith a certain person, or the word of God? If that person left, could I still stand?
• Let the word build me: the passage I read each day is not just knowledge, but a brick God is laying in me.
II. “I coveted no one’s silver, or gold, or clothing”—The Testimony of Two Hands

In verses 33 and 34 Paul suddenly speaks of money. These are Samuel’s words at his farewell (1 Sam. 12:3)—a departing servant laying his innocence before everyone. “Silver, gold, clothing” were the three forms of wealth in the ancient world. He probably held up his hands as he said: “these hands”—leatherworker’s hands, hands worn with calluses. Working in the morning, preaching in the school at midday, he also “ministered to my necessities, and to those who were with me”—even the living of his co-workers was earned by his labor.

Paul was not against preachers being supported—he said plainly, “those who proclaim the Good News should live from the Good News” (1 Cor. 9:14); but in a city full of religious business, he deliberately kept the gospel free of money. Ephesus had the pilgrim trade of the temple of Artemis, Demetrius’s silver shrines, and books of magic worth fifty thousand pieces of silver; Paul wanted the people of this city to know: this Way is not a business. “You yourselves know”—a person’s innocence is established not by declaration but by hands seen over three years.
• Look at my hands: are the hands I serve with giving hands, or hands stretched out to take?
• Keep the word free of money: whatever possession could make people doubt my motives for serving, I would rather not have.
III. “It is more blessed to give than to receive”—A Word of the Lord Not in the Gospels

In verse 35, Paul states his reason for working: “It is more blessed to give than to receive”—a saying not found in any of the four Gospels. It is a word the Lord Jesus spoke himself but which the Gospels did not record; the apostles passed it on by mouth, and Paul preserves it here. This sentence best sums up the Lord’s whole life: though he was rich, for our sakes he became poor (2 Cor. 8:9); he came not to be served but to serve (Mark 10:45). Paul’s example came from the Lord’s example—Jesus is my example. “Laboring, we ought to help the weak”: the aim of work is not that I have enough, but that I have more than enough to give to those who cannot work.

Like a river and a lake. A lake only receives and does not release; the water accumulates until it becomes a stagnant pool. A river receives and releases at the same time; the water keeps flowing and stays alive. The one who “receives” is a lake; the one who “gives” is a river. The blessing the Lord speaks of lies not in how much has been gathered but in how much has flowed.
• Giving is blessing, not loss: in what small matter today can I turn from one who receives into one who gives?
• For whom do I labor: is the aim of my work that I have enough, or that I have more than enough to help the weak?
IV. “He knelt down and prayed with them all”—The Sermon Ends on Its Knees

Jews usually prayed standing; kneeling was a sign of deep earnestness or grief—the Lord knelt in Gethsemane (Luke 22:41), and Stephen knelt as he was martyred (7:60). When Paul finished speaking, there was no summary, no further instructions; he knelt. And “with them all”—a whole group kneeling on the ground at the harbor.

The best ending to a sermon is not applause but a group of people kneeling together. Because the speaker knows that when the words are done, what will keep this group is not his words but the God who hears prayer. This is the final station on the road of service—after spirit, understanding, life and service, comes “God”: let Jesus receive glory, give thanks in all things, and hand everything back into his hands.
• Kneel when the words are done: does my service end by taking credit back, or by handing everything over?
• With them all: it was not Paul alone praying, but all together; a farewell is not one person’s business.
V. “Fell on Paul’s neck and kissed him”—A Parting with Tears

“Wept aloud” in the original is “wept greatly”; “falling on his neck and kissing him” is the Old Testament gesture of fathers and sons at reunion or final parting. These elders were not seeing off a speaker but a father. “Kissed him” in the original means kissed again and again—one by one they came forward, time after time unwilling to let go.

Think of who these people were. Three years earlier they were Jews and Greeks of Ephesus, worshipers of Artemis, practitioners of magic, men who had shouted slogans in the theater; three years later they were embracing a Jewish leatherworker on the dock and weeping. What did the gospel do? It turned strangers into family. People matter more than tasks, relationships more than things—here that is not a principle but tears.

What grieved them most was the word that they would “see his face no more,” and then “they accompanied him to the ship.” They did not hold him back; they knew he had to finish his course. True love weeps, and also lets go.
• Do I have this kind of relationship: in the church, are the brothers and sisters and I merely people at the same meeting, or a family who would weep at parting?
• Weep and let go: to love someone is not to hold on to him but to send him off to finish the course the Lord has given him.
321 Principles Insight: Those Who Hand Over Are the Ones Who Remain
The last three things Paul did at Miletus: he entrusted the people to God and his word, held up his working hands, and then knelt. The three say the same thing—he never regarded Ephesus as his own.

The self-centered, on leaving a place, fear above all being forgotten, so they try to leave behind influence, power, “my people.” The self-denying, on leaving, entrust people to God, return the credit to the Lord, and place themselves in the prayers of everyone. Yet strangely, the one who handed everything over is embraced around the neck and wept over; the one who would not let go of anything simply leaves and is gone.

Let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory—Paul lived out both core principles in his farewell: the one who reigns is God and the word of his grace, not Paul; the one who receives glory is the Lord who said “it is more blessed to give than to receive,” not Paul’s hands. For that very reason these elders did not lose their shepherd, but were placed in the hands of the Shepherd who never leaves. Self-denial is not loss but entering the limitless—the tears on the dock are the proof.
a: Build on the word
If my faith is built on a person, the building stops when he leaves; built on God’s word, it keeps going whoever leaves.
Look at my hands
Hands that serve give and do not reach out to take; keep the word free of money.
From lake to river
Today, in one small matter, turn from one who receives into one who gives.
End on my knees
At the end of every service, hand over the credit and entrust people to God.
Weep and let go
Live as family with brothers and sisters; to love someone is to send him to finish the Lord’s course.
q: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.” Think back over this week: in what matters were you the one who received, and in what matters the one who gave? From what small thing could you begin today to turn from lake to river?

If you had to leave the place you serve today, to whom would you entrust the people? Would they be unable to stand without you, or would they keep standing because they were already built on God’s word? What does this answer tell you?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for letting us stand at the dock of Miletus and see a group of former idol worshipers embrace a Jewish leatherworker and weep. Thank you that your gospel turns strangers into family, and that your servant entrusted them to you and the word of your grace rather than keeping them in his own hands.
Lord Jesus, we admit that when we leave a place we often want to leave behind our own influence; the hands with which we serve are often stretched out to take, not to give. Make us remember what you yourself said: it is more blessed to give than to receive. Build our faith on your word and not on any person; make our hands working hands, giving hands; make every service of ours end on our knees, handing everything back into your hands. And give us the love the elders of Ephesus had—willing to weep, and willing to let go. May you reign, and may you receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: When we had departed from them and had set sail, we came with a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.
Having found a ship crossing over to Phoenicia, we went aboard, and set sail.
When we had come in sight of Cyprus, leaving it on the left hand, we sailed to Syria and landed at Tyre, for the ship was there to unload her cargo.
Having found disciples, we stayed there seven days. These said to Paul through the Spirit that he should not go up to Jerusalem.
When those days were over, we departed and went on our journey. They all, with wives and children, brought us on our way until we were out of the city. Kneeling down on the beach, we prayed.
After saying goodbye to each other, we went on board the ship, and they returned home again.
When we had finished the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais. We greeted the brothers and stayed with them one day.
On the next day, we who were Paul’s companions departed, and came to Caesarea. We entered into the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him.
Now this man had four virgin daughters who prophesied.
As we stayed there some days, a certain prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

Coming to us and taking Paul’s belt, he bound his own feet and hands, and said, “The Holy Spirit says: ‘So the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt, and will deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles.’ ”
When we heard these things, both we and the people of that place begged him not to go up to Jerusalem.
Then Paul answered, “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.”
When he would not be persuaded, we ceased, saying, “The Lord’s will be done.”
b: In the last devotion, at Miletus, Paul entrusted the elders of Ephesus to God and the word of his grace and knelt to pray with them all. Everyone wept and fell on his neck and kissed him, and what grieved them most was the word that they would see his face no more. They accompanied him to the ship.

The ship set sail. Luke records this voyage with “we”—he himself was aboard. Port after port, and at every stop there were people who loved Paul and urged him not to go. The tension in this passage lies not with enemies but with friends: when those who love you stop you with tears, and the Holy Spirit clearly tells you to go forward, what do you do?
I. “When we had parted from them and had set sail”—Parting Is a Tearing Away

The word “parted” in verse 1 means in the original “torn away.” Luke chooses this word to let us know how painful the farewell at Miletus was: not a wave of the hand, but something stuck together being torn apart.

Next Luke writes like a ship’s log: Cos, Rhodes, Patara, one stop a day; at Patara they boarded a larger ship bound for Phoenicia, sailed straight across the Mediterranean south of Cyprus, and landed at Tyre. The smoother the sea, the heavier the heart, since every stop brought them closer to Jerusalem, where Paul already knew chains and afflictions awaited him (20:23).
• A smooth road is not a smooth heart: God’s guidance sometimes means a fair wind and a heavy heart, and the two do not conflict.
• Only by tearing away can one go: some farewells, if not torn through, mean a person never reaches the place the Lord wants him to go.
II. “They said to Paul through the Spirit that he should not go up to Jerusalem”—One Spirit, Two Messages?

Verse 4 is the hardest verse in this passage. The disciples at Tyre spoke “through the Spirit,” yet said to Paul, “Do not go up to Jerusalem.” But Paul had plainly said that he was “bound by the Spirit” to go to Jerusalem (20:22). How could the same Spirit tell him to go and tell him not to go?

The most reasonable understanding is that what the Spirit revealed was “Paul will suffer in Jerusalem,” and “do not go” was a conclusion the disciples added out of love. The Spirit gave the fact; the people gave the reaction. A weather forecast tells you it will rain heavily tomorrow, but never tells you whether to go out—whether to go depends on whether you have a reason you must. The disciples heard “it will rain” as “do not go out”; this is love, and also human weakness.

Paul did not rebuke them and did not waver. The picture in verses 5 and 6 is beautiful: all the disciples of the city, with wives and children, accompanied him out of the city, and on the beach they all knelt and prayed and bid each other farewell. Then the ship sailed and they went home.
• Distinguish revelation from reaction: when I hear what God has said, I must also separate which part is his and which part I added out of fear.
• Love may hold back but cannot decide for God: the tears of those who love me deserve respect, but they are not my standard.
III. “Entered into the house of Philip the evangelist”—Twenty Years Ago’s Persecutor Sleeps in His Guest Room
In verses 7–9 the ship reached Ptolemais, staying only one day; the next day it reached Caesarea, and they entered Philip’s house.

Luke specifically notes that this Philip was “one of the seven” (6:5). Over twenty years earlier the Jerusalem church had suffered great persecution; Philip went down to Samaria to preach, baptized the Ethiopian eunuch, and finally “came to Caesarea” (8:40). And that persecution had been launched by Saul—“Saul ravaged the assembly, entering into every house, and dragging both men and women, committed them to prison” (8:3).

Now that Saul who once dragged people to prison was staying in the house of Philip, whom he had driven out of Jerusalem. Twenty years lay between, a road to Damascus, and a Lord who died and rose again. Philip had four daughters who prophesied—what Joel said, “your sons and your daughters will prophesy” (2:17), had become ordinary in this household.

The gospel can really turn enemies into family. A life of self-denial can be seen here—Philip did not settle old scores, and Paul did not avoid him; the two lived under one roof because what lived in them was no longer themselves but Christ.
• Old accounts can be settled: a person who has met Christ can have even the deepest old account wiped to zero in him.
• A home is a testimony: a home where Jesus is King will have people used by the Spirit in it, and guests finding rest in it.
IV. “Took Paul’s belt and bound his own feet and hands”—A Prophet Acts Out the Outcome for Him

In verses 10 and 11, the prophet Agabus came down from Judea. In chapter 11 he had foretold a great famine over all the world, and it had come to pass (11:28). This time he did not just speak but acted: he took Paul’s belt, bound his own feet and hands, and declared the Spirit’s word: the owner of this belt would be bound like this in Jerusalem and handed over to the Gentiles.

This is the way of the Old Testament prophets. Jeremiah wore a yoke on his neck, and Ezekiel lay on his side for hundreds of days—the prophet acts out God’s message not only with his mouth but with his whole body, so that people cannot pretend not to have heard. And the words “delivered into the hands of the Gentiles” are the very words the Lord Jesus used to foretell his own suffering (Luke 18:32). The road Paul was to walk was the road his Master had walked.
In verse 12, “we and they of that place”—even Luke himself joined the ranks of those urging him in tears. This was the third time on the journey that people stopped him, and the most intense.
• The Spirit speaks clearly: God never lies that the road ahead is smooth; he always lets people see the cost first.
• Opposition can come from the most spiritual people: prophet, disciples, co-workers—all loved him, all urged him not to go.
V. “Breaking my heart” and “The will of the Lord be done”—The Most Painful Obedience

In verse 13, Paul finally speaks: “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart?” “Breaking” in the original is “crushing the heart.” Paul was not hard-hearted; his brothers’ tears really did crush his heart. Yet crushed as it was, he still said: “I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.”

The weight of this sentence lies in “for the name of the Lord Jesus.” Not for an ideal, not for his own stubbornness, but for the Lord who appeared to him on the road to Damascus. The focus was on Jesus—so tears could crush his heart but not his direction.

In verse 14, “we ceased, saying, ‘The Lord’s will be done.’” This is the same sentence as the Lord Jesus’ prayer in Gethsemane: “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). They finally understood that what they had been urging was in fact their own will; now they laid it down and committed Paul into the Lord’s will.

There are two kinds of self-denial here: what Paul gave up was his life, what the disciples gave up was their holding back—laying down the heart that says “I want to protect you.” The latter is often harder than the former.
• Heartbreak and obedience can coexist: true obedience is not painless, but goes on even in pain.
• Letting go is also obedience: the highest expression of love is to place a person in the Lord’s will, not to keep him by my side.
321 Principles Insight: To Let Jesus Be King, Even Love Must Yield
In these fourteen verses there is no enemy, only a group of people who love Paul. Their tears were real, and their urging well-meant. Yet Luke honestly records that Paul “would not be persuaded.”

This gives us an important point of discernment: what holds back my obedience is not always Satan; sometimes it is love. A self-centered life is most likely to give way in love—what “self” fears most is not an enemy’s attack but a family member’s tears; when opposed I can still hold firm, but when someone weeps and begs me to stay, I soften. Yet Paul’s focus was not on his brothers’ tears, nor on his own safety, but only on the name of the Lord Jesus. The focus on Jesus, not on myself, not on others, not on circumstances—this is why he could go forward even with a broken heart.

This passage says clearly what letting Jesus be King looks like: when God’s guidance is clear and those who love me most urge me not to go, I respect their love but do not make it my standard; when I am the one holding someone back, I am willing, like the disciples of Tyre, to fall silent and say “the Lord’s will be done.” Self-denial is not lack of love, but love yielding to the Lord’s will.
a: Distinguish revelation from reaction
God saying storms lie ahead does not mean God says do not go out; do not add my own fear to God’s word.
Respect tears, but do not make them the standard
The dissuasion of those who love me deserves a hearing, but cannot replace the Spirit’s guidance.
Let old accounts go to zero
As Philip received Paul, let the fact of meeting Christ cover past hurts.
Go on with a broken heart
Obedience is not painless; it goes on in pain, because the focus is on the name of the Lord Jesus.
Learn to let go
When the Lord takes someone I love to a place I am uneasy about, I am willing to say, “The Lord’s will be done.”
q: Is there something now that the Spirit has clearly guided you to do, but you have delayed because those who love you object? Where do you put their tears—as respect, or as the standard?

Think the other way: are you using “it’s for your own good” to hold someone back from the road the Lord wants him to walk? Are you willing to kneel today for that person and say, “The Lord’s will be done”?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for honestly recording this voyage of Paul’s: at every stop there were people who loved him and held him back, and his heart was truly broken, yet he still went where you wanted him to go. Thank you for letting us see that you never hide the cost ahead and never withdraw your guidance.
Lord, we admit that we most easily lay down your will before the tears of family, and often take our own fear for your word to hold others back. Give us a discerning heart, to hear which sentence is yours and which we added ourselves. Keep our focus on your name alone, not on our own safety, nor on whether circumstances are smooth or rough; and teach us to kneel when it is time to let go, like the disciples on the shore at Tyre, placing those we love into your will and saying, “The Lord’s will be done.” In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: After these days we took up our baggage and went up to Jerusalem.
Some of the disciples from Caesarea also went with us, bringing one Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we would stay.
When we had come to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly.
The day following, Paul went in with us to James; and all the elders were present.
When he had greeted them, he reported one by one the things which God had worked among the Gentiles through his ministry.
They, when they heard it, glorified God. They said to him, “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed, and they are all zealous for the law.
They have been informed about you, that you teach all the Jews who are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children and not to walk after the customs.
What then? The assembly must certainly meet, for they will hear that you have come.
Therefore do what we tell you. We have four men who have taken a vow.

Take them and purify yourself with them, and pay their expenses for them, that they may shave their heads. Then all will know that there is no truth in the things that they have been informed about you, but that you yourself also walk keeping the law.

But concerning the Gentiles who believe, we have written our decision that they should observe no such thing, except that they should keep themselves from food offered to idols, from blood, from strangled things, and from sexual immorality.”

Then Paul took the men, and the next day purified himself and went with them into the temple, declaring the fulfillment of the days of purification, until the offering was offered for every one of them.
b: In the last devotion, at Caesarea, everyone urged Paul not to go up to Jerusalem, and Paul said he was ready, for the name of the Lord Jesus, even to die at Jerusalem. They fell silent and said only, “The Lord’s will be done.”

So they set out. This devotion records Paul’s first days in Jerusalem: a warm welcome, and a thorny problem. What Paul faced was not an enemy’s attack but his brothers’ misgivings—people who believed in the same Lord yet misunderstood him. The way he handled it teaches a lesson about freedom and love.
I. “We packed up and went up to Jerusalem”—The Home of an Early Disciple

In verses 15 and 16, they “packed up”—in the original “made ready,” taking baggage and also the offering the Gentile churches had gathered for the poor in Jerusalem (Rom. 15:25–26). From Caesarea to Jerusalem is about a hundred kilometers, two or three days’ journey, and some disciples from Caesarea went with them.

Luke records one name: Mnason, a Cypriot, “an early disciple”—perhaps a believer from the Pentecost generation, having believed for over twenty years. His home, on the road or in Jerusalem, received Paul’s party. This name appears only once in Scripture; he did not preach and did no miracles, he simply opened his door. But without men like Mnason, Paul would have had nowhere to stay on this trip.

In verse 17, “the brothers received us gladly.” Paul had been urged against going all along the way, and the first thing to greet him in Jerusalem was joy. God often prepares, in the very place we fear most, a home with an open door first.
• Opening the door is also ministry: in God’s system some preach and some open doors, and neither can be lacking.
• The value of an early disciple: after believing for many years, one need not stand at the pulpit; a steady home is a blessing to the church.
II. “He reported one by one the things which God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry”—The Subject of the Report Was God

In verses 18 and 19, the next day Paul went to see James—the Lord’s brother, leader of the Jerusalem church (15:13)—and all the elders were present. Paul greeted them and “reported one by one the things which God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry.”

Notice the subject of this sentence: God. Paul did not say, “I founded a church in Corinth, I stayed three years in Ephesus, how I was stoned”; he told what God had done through him. Three journeys, countless cities, a whole account, and the main character was never himself.

In verse 20, “they glorified God when they heard it.” When God is the subject of the report, the hearers naturally give glory to God; if I am the subject of the report, the hearers can only admire me. The most concrete place for letting Jesus receive all the glory is how I tell about my own service.
• Check my subject: when I tell of what God did, how many times does “I” appear in the sentence?
• Where does the glory go: when I finish, do people think “God is so good,” or “he is so capable”?
III. “How many thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed, and they are all zealous for the law”—A Real Problem

In verses 20–22, after glorifying God, James and the elders changed the subject: “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed, and they are all zealous for the law.” “Thousands” in the original is “myriads,” an expression of great number. These believing Jews still kept the law, practiced circumcision and went up to the temple; this was their life and identity.
And they had heard a rumor: that Paul taught the Jews among the Gentiles to “forsake Moses,” telling them not to circumcise their children or follow the customs.

This was a false report. What Paul opposed was imposing circumcision on Gentiles as a condition for salvation; he never told Jews not to be Jews. He himself circumcised Timothy (16:3) and took a vow and cut his hair (18:18). But rumor does not care about this; it grabs half of the truth and enlarges it. “They will certainly hear that you have come. What then should be done?”—the elders were truly in a bind.
When misunderstood, what “self” most wants to do is defend immediately: I didn’t! Who told you that! Paul did not do this. He heard it through.
• Half the truth hurts most: rumor is often not entirely false but enlarges half into the whole.
• Hear it through before speaking: when misunderstood, the one who can hold back from instant defense is the one who has denied self.
IV. “Do therefore what we tell you”—Freedom Laid Down for Love

In verses 23–25, the elders proposed a solution: there were four men in the church who “have a vow on them,” a Nazirite vow (Num. 6)—at the end of the vow they must shave their heads and offer sacrifices, which was costly. They asked Paul to take these four, join in their purification, and pay their expenses, so that everyone would see that he “himself also walk[s] keeping the law.”

As for the Gentile believers, the elders restated the decision of chapter 15 (15:29): they need only abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from sexual immorality. This had not changed—Gentiles need not keep the law, and there was no compromise at the core of the gospel.

Paul agreed. Why was he willing? Because he himself had said: “To the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain Jews… I have become all things to all people” (1 Cor. 9:20–22). In Christ he was free, and whether he observed these rites had no bearing on his salvation; precisely because he was free, he could lay down his freedom for his brothers.

It is like taking off your shoes when entering someone’s home. Taking off shoes does not deny your shoes; it respects the home. A truly free person does not argue at the door, “Why should I take them off?” He quietly takes them off, because he cares about the people inside, not his shoes.
Humility looks very concrete here: not yielding on truth, but yielding on one’s own freedom, so that a brother’s conscience may be at rest.
• Truth does not yield, freedom may: the core does not shake, habits can bend.
• Take off my shoes for a brother: is there a freedom of mine today that I can set aside for a time for the sake of a brother’s weakness?
V. “Purifying himself with them, entered into the temple”—After Obedience, Still Storms

In verse 26, the next day Paul took the four men, purified himself with them, entered the temple, gave notice of the completion of the days, and waited for the offering to be made. He did it thoroughly, without delay, without half-hearted reluctance.

But those who have read on know that it was exactly this entry into the temple that brought on that riot. Paul did what the elders said, did it out of love, and the result was being seized, bound and imprisoned.

This reminds us: obedience does not guarantee smoothness. The outcome of obedience is in God’s hands, not mine; I am only responsible for obeying. Paul’s focus was not on “will this have a good result” but only on “is this the Lord’s will.” In the last devotion he said, the Lord’s will be done. In this one, he said the same sentence with his actions.
• Obedience is not a transaction: I obey not to exchange for a good outcome but because he is King.
• Leave the result to the Lord: after doing the right thing, whatever happens is in his hands.
321 Principles Insight: Only Self-Denial Can Bring Unity

The Jewish believers in Jerusalem were zealous for the law, while the Gentile believers lived in freedom; both groups were the Lord’s church, yet lived in two entirely different sets of habits. How can such a church be one?

The answer lies not in persuading someone to change habits but in someone being willing to lay himself down. Paul laid down his freedom to observe a rite he could have skipped, so that his brothers’ hearts could be at rest. Only self-denial can bring unity—not everyone becoming the same, but someone being willing not to be himself for the sake of others. The price of unity is always someone’s “self.”

In the church, a self-centered life says, “I am free, and you can’t tell me what to do”; a self-denying life says, “I am free, so I can lay it down for you.” People matter more than tasks, relationships more than being right. Paul did not give an inch on truth (Galatians is the proof), but on his own rights he could retreat all the way. When these two are distinguished, the church has a chance at unity; when they are not, only who overpowers whom remains.
a: Opening the door is ministry
Like Mnason, let my home be a place where God’s servants can stay.
Check my subject
When telling of my service, change “I” to “God used me.”
Hear it through before defending
When misunderstood, hold back instant rebuttal and take in my brothers’ difficulty.
Take off my shoes for a brother
Truth does not yield, freedom may; for a brother’s conscience, lay down my rights for a time.
Obey without eyeing the result
Do what the Lord asks, and leave the result in his hands.
q: Think of the last time you told about your own service: was the subject of the sentences “I” or “God”? To whom did the hearers finally give the glory?

Is there a brother or sister near you whose conscience is troubled because of one of your “freedoms”? Are you willing, as Paul paid the expenses for those four men, to set that freedom aside for him for a time?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that in Jerusalem, the place Paul feared most, you first prepared for him the home of an early disciple and a group of brothers who received him gladly. Thank you for letting us see that a report with you as its subject makes the hearers give glory to you.
Lord, we admit that we are good at fighting for our own freedom but not so good at laying freedom down for our brothers; when misunderstood, our first thought is defense, not listening. Give us Paul’s heart, to give no ground on truth and to yield all the way on our own rights; make us willing to take off our shoes for our brothers’ weakness, and to obey in your will even when the outcome is not what we wanted. May you reign among us, that through self-denial we may be one, and that your church may be not a place where some overpower others but where we lay down for each other. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: When the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia, when they saw him in the temple, stirred up all the multitude and laid hands on him,

crying out, “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches all men everywhere against the people, and the law, and this place. Moreover, he also brought Greeks into the temple, and has defiled this holy place!”
For they had seen Trophimus, the Ephesian, with him in the city, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple.
All the city was moved and the people ran together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple. Immediately the doors were shut.
As they were trying to kill him, news came up to the commanding officer of the regiment that all Jerusalem was in an uproar.
Immediately he took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. They, when they saw the chief captain and the soldiers, stopped beating Paul.
Then the commanding officer came near, arrested him, commanded him to be bound with two chains, and inquired who he was and what he had done.
Some shouted one thing, and some another, among the crowd. When he couldn’t find out the truth because of the noise, he commanded him to be brought into the barracks.
When he came to the stairs, he was carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd;
for the multitude of the people followed after, crying out, “Away with him!”
b: In the last devotion, for the sake of his brothers’ unity, Paul laid down his own freedom, took four men with vows, performed the rite of purification, and entered the temple, waiting only for the priest to offer the sacrifice. He did it thoroughly and sincerely.

Then the storm came. The seven days of purification were nearly over, and right in the temple a riot began from a single “supposed.” This devotion shows us that a person can do every single thing right and still be misunderstood, beaten and bound. And in the confusion, God used the most unexpected pair of hands.
I. “The Jews from Asia”—One “Supposed” Sets the Whole City Ablaze

In verses 27–29, the troublemakers were not people of Jerusalem but “the Jews from Asia”—the capital of the province of Asia was Ephesus, where Paul had spent three years, and they knew him. It was the time of Pentecost, with Jews from everywhere pouring into Jerusalem, and these men saw Paul in the temple and “stirred up all the multitude”—in the original, “stirred into confusion.”

They shouted three charges: against the people, against the law, against this place. These were exactly the charges against Stephen (6:13); Paul had stood there guarding the garments, and now it was his turn to be accused in the same words. Then came a deadly accusation: “Moreover, he also brought Greeks into the temple, and has polluted this holy place.”

Between the Court of the Gentiles and the inner court of the temple there was a low wall bearing a warning: any Gentile who entered would be responsible for his own death. The Romans even allowed the Jews to carry out the death penalty for this, Roman citizens included. This was the accusation most likely to stir the crowd to murder.

And verse 29 reveals the truth: they had seen Trophimus the Ephesian with Paul in the city and “supposed” that Paul had brought him into the temple. Seen in the city, supposed in the temple. One “supposed” became “this is so,” and then became the shouting of the whole city.

It is like a message forwarded in a family group chat: someone saw half of something, added their own guess, and pressed forward; by the time the next person received it, the word “guess” was gone, leaving only “fact.” Every one of us has received such messages, and every one of us has forwarded them.
• “Supposed” is not evidence: before saying “this is so,” ask myself: did I see the whole?
• Do not heat up rumors: what “self” loves most is to present half the truth as all of it, because that makes me look well informed.
II. “The doors were immediately shut”—That Door Closed
In verses 30 and 31, “All the city was moved, and the people ran together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple. Immediately the doors were shut.”

On the surface, the doors were shut because the Levite guards feared bloodshed would defile the temple; but Luke records this detail with deeper meaning. This is the last time Acts mentions Paul in the temple. Once the doors closed, they never reopened. The messenger of the gospel was dragged out and the door shut behind him—the old order centered on the temple shut the gospel outside.

But the door closed and the gospel did not stop. From this moment, Paul’s platform changed from the temple to the steps of the barracks, the Sanhedrin, the governor’s court, the presence of kings, and finally Rome. When people shut one door, God opens another road.

And “they were trying to kill him”—not a trial, but killing, beating to death on the spot. “News came up to the commanding officer of the regiment”—Luke gives no name to the “someone” in that sentence.
• A closed door is not a cut road: God never needed the door people shut.
• In the confusion there is a “someone”: in the most chaotic scene, God has always placed a nameless person.
III. “He immediately took soldiers… and ran down”—Rome’s Chains Became Chains That Saved

In verses 32–34, the commanding officer was the commander of the Roman garrison, in charge of about a thousand men, stationed in the Antonia Fortress at the northwest corner of the temple, with stairs leading straight to the outer court, overlooking the temple precisely to watch for such disturbances. He “immediately” took soldiers and “ran down.” When the crowd saw the soldiers, “they stopped beating Paul.”

Then the officer “came near, and arrested him, and commanded him to be bound with two chains”—one on each hand, chained between two soldiers. What Agabus acted out at Caesarea was now fulfilled word for word: bound by the Jews and handed to the Gentiles.

But look: the very chains that bound him saved his life. If the Romans had not chained him away in time, he would have been beaten to death outside the temple doors. God’s protection often comes in ways completely different from what we expect—not an angel opening the door (12:7), but the chains of a Gentile officer.

The officer asked who he was and what he had done, but the crowd “shouted some one thing, some another,” so confused that he “could not find out the truth.” A crowd wants to kill a man but cannot say what he did—this is the true nature of a crowd.
• Chains can also be protection: the very thing that makes me unfree today may be what the Lord is using to shield me.
• Those who shout loudest often explain least: before shouting along with the crowd, ask myself whether I know the truth.
IV. “The soldiers had to carry him”—He Walked the Road the Lord Walked

In verses 35 and 36, at the steps of the barracks, the crowd pressed so violently that the soldiers “had to carry him.” A man who had just been beaten, carried upstairs by Gentile soldiers, with the crowd behind shouting, “Away with him!”

“Away with him!”—these words Jerusalem had shouted once before, over twenty years earlier. That time, before Pilate’s court, the crowd cried “Away with this man!” (Luke 23:18). The same city, the same words, only this time it was his servant being carried away. Paul had said he “imitated Christ” (1 Cor. 11:1), and at this moment he imitated him at the most similar point: innocent, falsely accused, shouted at with “away with him,” handed over to Gentiles.

Jesus is my example—this is easy to say in good times, but only when carried on the steps with people shouting to remove you behind you do you know its weight. Paul did not struggle and did not defend himself; he let them carry him. The self-denying person in times of misunderstanding has a visible look: he is not in a hurry to prove himself, because his reputation is not his focus.
• Walk the road the Lord walked: when falsely accused, remember that he too was shouted at this way.
• Let yourself be carried: in some moments the most spiritual posture is not to struggle but to place oneself in the hands God has arranged.
321 Principles Insight: The Focus Is on Jesus, Not on Circumstances
