This passage turned the facts completely around. The truth of chapter 21 was: the crowd seized Paul, dragged him out of the temple, and was about to beat him to death; the officer ran in with soldiers and rescued him. But in Tertullus’s mouth, lynching became “arrested,” and rescue became “taking away with great violence.”

When people defend themselves, one thing they do best is rewrite the facts—not all lies, but changing the verbs: calling “beating” “discipline” and “avoiding” “waiting.” We often do this with God as well, in prayer making our own offenses sound like someone else’s fault. “By examining him yourself you may find out”—in the end the burden of proof was pushed onto the judge, because he actually had no witness in hand.
• Face the facts honestly: don’t change verbs, don’t rewrite the process; tell God things as they were.
• The burden of proof is on the other side: if those who accuse me cannot produce evidence, I need not supply it for them.
V. “That these things are so”—The Voices That Chimed In
In verse 9, “The Jews also joined in the attack, affirming that these things were so.”

When the lawyer finished, a crowd nodded along. They added no evidence, only chimed in with one voice. These elders had personally seen Paul tried before the council, knew that hearing had ended in infighting between Sadducees and Pharisees (23:7–10), and knew the Jews from Asia had not even shown up. Yet they all said: it is so.

Chiming in is participation without responsibility. I didn’t bring the charge, I only nodded; I didn’t bear false witness, I only said “it’s so.” But in God’s eyes the one who nods is as guilty as the one who accuses.

Think of a choir. If the conductor’s tuning fork is wrong, the whole choir goes off key together, and each person feels he is not wrong because everyone is the same. Unity not aligned to truth is only collective off-key. Paul stood there alone, with no lawyer, facing a chorus of “it is so.” But he did not need a lawyer—he knew the Lord stood beside him.
• Don’t be one who nods: when a crowd says “it’s so,” first ask: have I seen it myself?
• One person can stand: one standing in truth has never needed numbers.
321 Principles Insight: The Focus Is on Jesus, Not on Those Who Accuse Me

In these nine verses Paul said not one word. He stood and listened—listened to himself called a plague, to the one who rescued him described as the one who seized him, to a crowd saying in unison “it is so.”

At such a time the self-centered burn inside: I must explain, I must rebut. What “self” can least bear is being misunderstood. But Paul did not interrupt; he waited until the governor nodded for him to speak, and then he spoke.

This was not weakness but focus. His focus was not on Tertullus or Felix but on the Lord who had said to him the night before, “so you must testify also at Rome.” Since the Lord had determined he would reach Rome, however this trial went, it was only a stop on the road.

Self-denial is not having no feelings but moving oneself out of the center and putting Jesus in the center. When Jesus is in the center, accusations become small; when I am in the center, one misunderstanding is enough to ruin a whole day. The focus on Jesus, not on myself, not on others, not on circumstances—Paul lived this out in the defendant’s seat.
a: Recognize the pattern of attack
If assassination fails, he goes to court; the method changes, the goal does not; I need not be surprised, only stand firm.
Examine my mouth
When I speak to those in power, is it sincerity or “winning favor”?
Neither apply labels nor fear them
I do not judge people by “he’s that kind of person,” nor let others’ labels decide who I am.
Don’t change the verbs
Before God, tell it as it was; don’t make my offenses sound like others’ fault.
Don’t be one who nods
When everyone says “it is so,” first ask whether I have seen it.
q: Tertullus began with flattery, and a crowd began by chiming in. Looking back over what you said this week, which sentence was “winning favor” rather than sincerity? When did you nod with “it is so”?
What label have you been given? Does that label still affect how you see yourself? Are you willing today to place it before the Lord and let him tell you again “who you are”?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for recording this day of Paul’s at Caesarea in Scripture. We see that human methods can change, from assassination to courtroom, from swords to rhetoric; and we see your servant standing silent, because his focus was on you.
Lord, we admit that we often cannot bear being misunderstood. When someone says a wrong word about us, we hurry to explain and hurry to hit back; that “self” flares up and pushes you out of the center. Teach us, like Paul, to be quiet first and listen first, and to speak when you give the word. Search also our mouths, that we may not package lies in beautiful words, nor nod along with the crowd, nor casually put labels on people. May we remember in every misunderstanding what you said: Cheer up, I am with you. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: When the governor had beckoned to him to speak, Paul answered, “Because I know that you have been a judge of this nation for many years, I cheerfully make my defense,
seeing that you can verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship at Jerusalem.
In the temple they didn’t find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the synagogues, or in the city.
Nor can they prove to you the things of which they now accuse me.
But this I confess to you, that after the Way, which they call a sect, so I serve the God of our fathers, believing all things which are according to the law, and which are written in the prophets;
having hope toward God, which these also themselves look for, that there will be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust.
In this I also practice always having a conscience void of offense toward God and men.
Now after some years, I came to bring gifts for the needy to my nation, and offerings;
amid which certain Jews from Asia found me purified in the temple, not with a mob, nor with turmoil.
They ought to have been here before you, and to make accusation, if they had anything against me.
Or else let these men themselves say what injustice they found in me when I stood before the council,
unless it is for this one thing that I cried standing among them, ‘Concerning the resurrection of the dead I am being judged before you today!’ ”
b: In the last devotion, the lawyer Tertullus accused Paul as a “plague”—stirring up insurrection, a ringleader of a sect, trying to profane the temple; and the Jews chimed in with one voice: “These things are so.” Paul stood and said nothing.
Now the governor nodded. It was Paul’s turn to speak. With no lawyer and no prepared speech, he faced three charges alone. Let us see how a person who lets Jesus be King makes his defense.
I. “I cheerfully make my defense”—The Truth Needs No Flattery
In verse 10, “Because I know that you have been for many years a judge to this nation, I cheerfully make my defense.”

Compare Tertullus’s opening: “Seeing that by you we enjoy much peace… with all thankfulness.” Paul said only one fact: you have been a judge here for many years. Felix had been procurator of Judea since AD 52, and by this time had been there six or seven years, indeed familiar with Jewish affairs. Paul neither flattered him nor belittled him, only stated one true thing.

The word “cheerfully” is special. A falsely accused prisoner says he is “cheerful” in making his defense—because there is no fear in his heart. The night before he had heard the Lord say “Cheer up,” and he knew the outcome of this trial was not in Felix’s hands.
• The truth is enough: to those in power, I need not add a word of flattery, nor leave out a word of fact.
• Peace within makes one “cheerful”: the fearful hurry to argue; those at peace are glad to speak.
II. “No more than twelve days”—Answering the Charge with Facts

In verses 11–13, Paul answered the charge of “insurrection” point by point. First, time: from the day he went up to Jerusalem until now, no more than twelve days. Of the twelve days, five were in prison at Caesarea, one before the council, and several in the purification rite—where was the time to “stir up all the Jews throughout the world”? Second, place: in the temple, in the synagogues, in the city, in none of these three places had they “found” him arguing with anyone or stirring up a crowd. Third, the conclusion: “Neither can they prove to you the things of which they now accuse me.”
Paul’s defense had no emotion, only facts: time, place, witnesses. The charge said “throughout the world,” he answered “twelve days”; the charge said “insurrection,” he answered “did not find.”

A good doctor, seeing a patient, does not prescribe a pile of medicine because the patient says, “Nothing feels right in my whole body”; he asks: where does it hurt? when did it start? how long? Breaking a vague feeling into specific facts is the way to treat the real problem. What Paul did in court was exactly this—breaking the vague label “plague” into details that can be verified.
• Use facts, not emotion: when misunderstood, first state the time, place and course of events clearly, without hurrying to vent my heart.
• Let the other side provide proof: “Neither can they prove to you”—I need not prove my innocence; those who accuse me must prove my guilt.
III. “But this I confess to you”—What He Confessed Was the Way They Called a Sect
In verses 14–16, Paul turned: “But this I confess to you.”

He denied causing insurrection, yet voluntarily confessed one thing: “According to the Way which they call a sect, so I serve the God of our fathers.” “Sect” in the original is the very word Tertullus used, “faction”; “Way” in the original is “road”—the earliest name Christians used for themselves in Acts (9:2). Paul’s meaning was: you call it a faction, I call it a road; and in walking this road I am serving the God of my fathers, not setting up another god.

Then he stated three things about this road: believing “all things which are according to the law, and which are written in the prophets”; having hope that “there will be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust”; and “I also practice always having a conscience void of offense toward God and men.” “Practice” in the original is “train, work at,” and “void of offense” is “without stumbling.” A conscience is not clean by nature but trained—each day before God and men, admitting what should be admitted, returning what should be returned, leaving no stone on the road.

This is exactly what the three foundations look like: Scripture is my standard (believing all that is written), the Holy Spirit is my guide (serving God in that Way), Jesus is my example (a conscience void of offense). In court, Paul stated his whole faith in full.
• Do not deny my faith: when others call it a sect, I can call it back by its true name.
• Train the conscience: a conscience void of offense is not feeling good but clearing the account every day before God and men.
IV. “I came to bring gifts for the needy to my nation”—He Came to Give, Not to Make Trouble
In verses 17–19, Paul told the real purpose of his going up to Jerusalem: “Now after some years, I came to bring gifts for the needy to my nation, and offerings.”

This is the only time Acts mentions that offering. In his letters to Rome and Corinth Paul mentioned it several times: he collected funds in the churches of Macedonia and Achaia for the poor saints in Jerusalem (Rom. 15:25–26; 1 Cor. 16:1–4). He went up to Jerusalem at the risk of his life in order to hand the love of the Gentile churches to the Jewish brothers with his own hands. How could a man who came bringing money for the relief of his own nation be one coming to “cause insurrection”?

“While I was offering them, they found me purified in the temple”—he had not only not defiled the temple, but was one keeping the rite of purification and in the midst of offering. And the “certain Jews from Asia” who actually caused the uproar were not present today. Under Roman law, if the accuser did not appear, the accusation fell. Paul pointed this out: “They ought to have been here before you, and to make accusation, if they had anything against me.”
• One who came for others does not fear scrutiny: if what I do is for the Lord and for others, it can stand anyone’s examination.
• The real witnesses are absent: many accusations stand only because no one demands that they produce witnesses.
V. “Only for this one voice”—The Only “Crime” He Admitted Was the Resurrection

In verses 20 and 21, Paul finally said: let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found in me when I stood before the council. “Unless it is for this one thing that I cried standing among them, ‘Concerning the resurrection of the dead I am being judged before you today.’”

This was the peak of Paul’s defense. He turned the focus of the whole case from his conduct to one thing: resurrection. He was in effect saying: if I have a crime, my crime is only one—I believe Jesus rose from the dead.

This was not a defense technique but testimony. Felix sat on the bench wanting to hear a legal contest, but Paul put the gospel of resurrection before him. From today until chapter 26, every time Paul opened his mouth he stopped at the same place—Jesus is alive. Because that was the whole foundation of his life, and the one sentence he would rather sit in prison than let go.
• What is my “one sentence”: if someone asks me why I live this way, is “Jesus is alive” in my answer?
• Testimony does not depend on the setting: courtroom, hospital room, or office, the focus can return to the living Lord.
321 Principles Insight: A Conscience Void of Offense Is the Freedom of Those Who Let Jesus Be King

What is most moving about Paul’s defense is not his eloquence but his ease. He could say “cheerfully,” could say “you may find out by examining,” could say “let them themselves say”—because he had nothing to hide.

A conscience void of offense is not a conscience that never did wrong, but one that settles its account before God every day. Paul had persecuted the church and killed saints, but after the Lord seized him he never again lived a day in hiding. He “practiced”—and what that looks like today is simple: before God, admit what is owed; before people, apologize and return what is owed, not leaving it until tomorrow.

The self-centered most fear being examined, because “self” always has something to cover; the self-denying do not, because they no longer have their own face to protect. A person who lets Jesus be King lives openly, and can say “cheerfully” even in the defendant’s seat. This freedom is worth more than acquittal.
a: The truth is enough
To those in power, no extra word of flattery and no missing word of fact.
Use facts, not emotion
When misunderstood, first state the time, place and course of events clearly.
Do not deny my faith
When others call it a sect, I call it back by its name—the Way.
Train a conscience void of offense
Settle accounts with God and men every day; leave no stone until tomorrow.
Hold on to my one sentence
If someone asks why I live this way, the answer should include “Jesus is alive.”
q: Paul “practiced always having a conscience void of offense toward God and men.” Right now, is there something owed to God or to someone that you have not cleared? Are you willing to deal with it today?
If someone asked you, “Why do you live this way?” what sentence would you answer with? Does that sentence include the risen Lord?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for letting us see your servant’s ease in the courtroom. He had no lawyer, yet had peace; he was called a plague, yet cheerfully made his defense; he denied every false charge, yet loudly confessed the resurrection of your Son.
Lord, we admit that we often live in hiding, unwilling to admit what we owe to God and unwilling to return what we owe to people, so that when questioned we panic. Give us a trained conscience, void of offense, that we may settle accounts before you every day, live openly, and not fear being seen. And make us, like Paul, put the focus of our lives on the risen Lord, so that in any setting we can say plainly that one sentence: Jesus is alive. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: But Felix, having more exact knowledge concerning the Way, deferred them, saying, “When Lysias, the commanding officer, comes down, I will decide your case.”
He ordered the centurion that Paul should be kept in custody, and should have some privileges, and not to forbid any of his friends to serve him or to visit him.
But after some days, Felix came with Drusilla, his wife, who was a Jewess, and sent for Paul, and heard him concerning the faith in Christ Jesus.
As he reasoned about righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come, Felix was terrified, and answered, “Go your way for this time, and when it is convenient for me, I will summon you.”
Meanwhile, he also hoped that money would be given to him by Paul, that he might release him. Therefore also he sent for him more often and talked with him.
But when two years were fulfilled, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus, and desiring to gain favor with the Jews, Felix left Paul in bonds.
b: In the last devotion, Paul made his defense, dismantling the false charges one by one with time, place and witnesses, and finally resting the whole case on one sentence: “Concerning the resurrection of the dead I am being judged before you today.”

The accusers had finished, and the defendant had finished. Now it was the judge’s turn to pronounce. But Felix did not decide. These six verses record a man who heard the truth, was afraid in his heart, yet kept saying, “When I find it convenient”—and once he waited, it was two years.
I. “Having more exact knowledge concerning the Way, put them off”—The Clearer the Knowledge, the Less the Excuse
In verse 22, “But Felix, having more exact knowledge concerning the Way, deferred them, saying, ‘When Lysias, the commanding officer, comes down, I will decide your case.’”

“More exact knowledge” in the original is “knowing more accurately.” Felix had been governor in Judea for six or seven years, and Caesarea was the city where Philip lived (21:8); he was not ignorant of “the Way”—the Christian faith—but knew it better than many in the room. He knew this group were not insurgents, and he knew Paul was innocent.

But he “put them off.” The original is “postponed, delayed.” He found a reason: wait until Lysias comes down. In fact Lysias’s letter had long since arrived (23:26–30), stating that Paul had “nothing worthy of death or of imprisonment”; waiting for him would produce nothing new. This was a man who knew the answer and deliberately did not write it down.
• Knowing is not obeying: the more clearly I know the truth, the heavier the responsibility of delay.
• Recognize my own “putting off”: how many of the “when I’m ready” and “when circumstances improve” are really “when Lysias comes down”?
II. “And to give him some liberty”—Half a Justice
In verse 23, Felix ordered the centurion to keep Paul, “and to let him have some liberty, and not to forbid any of his friends to serve him or to visit him.”

“Liberty” in the original is “relaxation, freedom,” meaning a looser kind of custody: Paul was still guarded, but could receive visitors and be provided for. This shows Felix knew in his heart that Paul was innocent—a real rebel would not have received such treatment.

But he did only half. He did not judge Paul guilty, and did not judge him innocent; did not let him go, and did not mistreat him. This is a very common approach: neither offending the Jews nor violating conscience too much. Half a justice looks better than injustice, but in fact keeps an innocent man in prison.

We too often do “half” obedience: knowing we should forgive, we are a little polite to the person but do not truly let go; knowing we should admit fault, we say “we were both wrong” but do not truly admit. Half obedience, in God’s eyes, is not obedience.
• Don’t do half a justice: knowing what is right, do it all the way; don’t use “liberty” in place of “release.”
• Examine my “halves”: what in my life do I know I should do but have done only halfway?
III. “Heard him concerning the faith in Christ Jesus”—Curiosity Is Not Faith
In verse 24, “After some days, Felix came with Drusilla, his wife, who was a Jewess, and sent for Paul, and heard him concerning the faith in Christ Jesus.”

Drusilla was the youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I—the daughter of the Herod of chapter 12 who killed James and was eaten by worms. She had already been married to a petty king of Syria; Felix, taken with her beauty, used a scheme to draw her away from her husband, and she was now about twenty. A governor who rose by brutality and a princess who left her lawful husband sat together in the hall wanting to hear Paul on “the faith in Christ Jesus.”

Why did they want to hear? Perhaps curiosity, perhaps because Drusilla, as a Jew, was interested in the new faith. But they did listen—and Paul did speak, without changing his content because of the identity of his hearers.
• Many hear the word, few believe it: am I here to listen, or to believe?
• The speaker does not look at the audience: Paul spoke the same gospel to the governor as to the jailer in prison.
IV. “Righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come”—What Paul Spoke Was Just What They Least Wanted to Hear
In verse 25, “As he reasoned about righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come, Felix was terrified.”

Note the topics Paul chose. To a governor who rose by injustice, he spoke of “righteousness”; to a couple joined by passion, he spoke of “self-control”—in the original “self-mastery,” especially the mastery of desire; to two who thought they held power, he spoke of “the judgment to come”—you try me today, but there is One who will try you.
Paul did not give a comforting talk, did not stop at “God loves you.” He brought the gospel to Felix’s sore spot. This is true love: not being pleasing, but bringing people before the truth.

The result was “Felix was terrified.” The original is “became afraid.” This is the work of the Holy Spirit—a brutal governor trembling before a prisoner’s talk. Fear itself is not bad; it is a good beginning; the question is what he does next.

“Go your way for this time, and when I find it convenient, I will send for you.” “Convenient” in the original is “opportune time”—when I have time, leisure, convenience. In the very moment of fear he pushed the door a little farther away.

Think of answering the phone. An important call comes in, we see the caller ID, our heart jolts, and we press “reply later.” Not a refusal, only “wait a moment.” But once “wait a moment” is pressed, the call is often never returned. This is the key Felix pressed.
• Fear is a door, not a wall: when the Spirit makes a person afraid, it is to bring him in, not drive him away.
• Don’t press “reply later”: what God says to me today, respond today, not leaving it to “when convenient.”
V. “Sent for him often”—Two Years of Talks, Not One Repentance

In verses 26 and 27, “He hoped withal that money would be given him by Paul, that he might release him. Therefore also he sent for him more often, and talked with him. But when two years were fulfilled, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus; and desiring to gain favor with the Jews, Felix left Paul in bonds.”

In verse 24 the motive was “hearing the word”; by verse 26 the motive had become “hoping money would be given him.” Felix had heard that Paul had brought a large offering to Jerusalem (24:17), assumed he had money, and so sent for him often, hinting that he could buy his freedom. Roman law forbade governors to take bribes, but Felix did not care.

So for two years he “often” talked with Paul. He heard the gospel many times and was afraid many times, but never once repented. His “convenient time” never came. Two years later he was recalled to Rome to answer charges—the Jews accused his tyranny before the emperor—and on leaving, “desiring to gain favor with the Jews, left Paul in bonds.” He spent his life seeking favor, and in the end even favor-seeking could not save him.

And Paul sat two years in prison at Caesarea. Some say these two years were wasted, but what the Lord said was “you must testify also at Rome”—Rome was still ahead. During these two years Luke was quite possibly in Caesarea gathering material and writing his Gospel and the Acts. God wasted not one day.
• Motives can spoil: at first it was “hearing the word,” later “hoping for money”; has my motive for drawing near the Lord changed unnoticed?
• Two years are not wasted: the days I think I have stopped, God may be writing his book.
321 Principles Insight: Change the Concept and Change the Life; Without Change, Only Fear Remains

Felix is the person in the whole book of Acts who heard the gospel most and never responded. It was not that he did not know—he had “more exact knowledge”; it was not that he had no feeling—he was “terrified”; it was not that he had no chance—he sent for Paul “often.” What he lacked was only one thing: yielding the throne.

The self-centered, hearing truth, hear only what “I” will lose—losing the Jews’ favor, losing Drusilla, losing money. So each time, in fear, he said, “When I find it convenient.” Only by changing concepts can a life be changed; but Felix would not change his concept, and he still viewed everything from an earthly, temporary, worldly viewpoint, so after hearing for two years, his life did not move at all.

What letting Jesus be King looks like here is very concrete: at the moment when the heart trembles, not saying “wait a moment,” but saying “Lord, I respond to you today.” Fear plus delay becomes numbness; fear plus obedience becomes repentance. The difference between the two is only that one “convenient time.”
a: Knowing means obeying
The more clearly I know the truth, the heavier the responsibility of delay.
Don’t do half a justice
Do what I know should be done all the way; don’t use “liberty” in place of “release.”
Examine my motive for hearing
Am I here to listen, to believe, or hoping unnoticed for something else?
Don’t press “reply later”
What jolts my heart today from God, respond to today.
Trust that God wastes nothing
The days I think I have stopped, God may be writing his book.
q: Felix said, “When I find it convenient, I will send for you.” Is there something now that God has made clear to you, yet you keep waiting for “a convenient time”? Until when do you plan to wait?

Paul spoke to Felix about righteousness, self-control and judgment until he trembled. If the Lord spoke to you today about these three, which would jolt your heart? Are you willing to let that jolt become repentance rather than delay?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for letting us see Felix—a man who knew the truth in detail, was afraid in his heart, yet for two years kept saying, “When I find it convenient.” In him we see ourselves: not doing what we know to do, the heart having trembled yet we pressed “reply later.”
Lord, forgive us for leaving your word to “when convenient.” Make us not draw back at the moment of fear but come in; not put off at the moment of knowing but obey. Remove from us the self that fears loss, fears offending, fears losing face, and make us change our concepts and see everything from your viewpoint. And thank you that of Paul’s two years in prison you wasted not one day; make us also believe that in the days we stop, you are still writing your book. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: Festus therefore, having come into the province, after three days went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea.
Then the high priest and the principal men of the Jews informed him against Paul, and they begged him,
asking a favor against him, that he would summon him to Jerusalem; plotting to kill him on the way.
However Festus answered that Paul should be kept in custody at Caesarea, and that he himself was about to depart shortly.
“Let them therefore”, he said, “that are in power among you go down with me, and if there is anything wrong in the man, let them accuse him.”
When he had stayed among them more than ten days, he went down to Caesarea, and on the next day he sat on the judgment seat, and commanded Paul to be brought.
When he had come, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing against him many and grievous charges which they could not prove,
while he said in his defense, “Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar, have I sinned at all.”
But Festus, desiring to gain favor with the Jews, answered Paul and said, “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem, and be judged by me there concerning these things?”
But Paul said, “I am standing before Caesar’s judgment seat, where I ought to be tried. I have done no wrong to the Jews, as you also know very well.

For if I have done wrong and have committed anything worthy of death, I don’t refuse to die; but if none of those things is true that they accuse me of, no one can give me up to them. I appeal to Caesar!”
Then Festus, when he had conferred with the council, answered, “You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you shall go.”
b: In the last devotion, Felix listened to the message for two years and said “when I find it convenient” for two years. In the end, to win the favor of the Jews, he left Paul in prison and went away.

A new governor arrived. Porcius Festus was a far more upright official than Felix. But an upright man taking office did not mean Paul’s situation would improve. Two years had passed and the Jews’ hatred had not lessened by a single degree; and what a new official most wants to do is please the people he is going to govern. At this trial Paul made a decision that would shape the rest of his life.
I. “After three days, he went up to Jerusalem”—An Old Grudge Does Not Expire

Verses 1–3: Only three days after arriving in his province, Festus went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem to call on the leaders of the nation he governed. The chief priests and the leaders of the Jews seized the opportunity. They “informed him against Paul, and they begged him, asking a favor against him, that he would summon him to Jerusalem, plotting to kill him on the way.”

Two years had gone by. The high priest had changed, the governor had changed, but the plan to kill Paul had not changed—it was still the trick of chapter 23, an ambush on the road. Last time it was more than forty men under an oath; this time it was the highest leaders of the Jews themselves, “asking a favor,” wrapping a murder in the form of a courtesy request.

We often assume that time softens everything. Some things it does, but sin it does not. If a person has not repented, what he hated two years ago he hates just the same two years later; the evil he wanted to do two years ago he will do again in a more respectable way. Time does not heal a heart that has not repented.
• Do not wait for time to deal with sin: is that bitterness or scheme in my heart still there after all this time? If it is, what I need is not more time but repentance.
• Recognize the wrapping: dressing malice up as a favor and revenge as justice is what the old self does best.
II. “Paul was kept in custody at Caesarea”—God Protects His Servant Through a New Official’s Firmness

Verses 4–6: Festus answered that “Paul should be kept in custody at Caesarea, and that he himself was about to depart shortly.” He said, “Let them therefore, who among you are able, go down with me, and if there is anything wrong in the man, let them accuse him.”

Festus knew nothing of the ambush. He refused simply because of Roman procedure: the prisoner was in Caesarea, so the trial would be in Caesarea. He did not realize that this procedural decision of his had just wrecked a murder plot.

God does not always protect His servant by sending an angel to open the prison doors (12:7); sometimes He uses nothing more than the working principles of a Gentile official. Last time it was a commander’s four hundred seventy soldiers; this time it was a new governor’s sentence, “kept at Caesarea.” “When he had stayed among them not more than eight or ten days… the next day he sat on the judgment seat”—Festus acted promptly, unlike Felix who dragged on for two years.
• See God’s hidden protection: how many “coincidences” in my life are really God protecting me through people who do not know Him?
• Give thanks for those in authority: an official who goes by the rules is a grace God gives to the people.
III. “Many and grievous charges… which they could not prove”—The Same Accusations, the Same Lack of Evidence
Verses 7–8: When Paul came, “the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing against him many and grievous charges which they could not prove.”

“Stood around him” paints a picture: a crowd closing in on Paul like hunters surrounding their prey. “Many and grievous charges”—two years earlier there had been three, now there were more and heavier; but Luke adds one line: “which they could not prove.” The accusations had increased, and the evidence was still zero.

Paul’s defense is just one sentence, yet it covers three areas: “Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar, have I committed any offense at all.” The law (religion), the temple (worship), Caesar (politics)—three realms, three “nots.” He needed no long speech, because for two years his conscience had been clear and the answer had not changed.
• Accusations swell; the truth does not: after two years the charges are more numerous, but if I have walked uprightly, my answer is still the same sentence.
• A short defense comes from a settled heart: a person who can say it in one sentence is a person with nothing to hide.
IV. “Festus, wishing to gain favor with the Jews”—Even Decent People Compromise
Verse 9: “But Festus, desiring to gain favor with the Jews, answered Paul and said, ‘Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem, and be judged by me there concerning these things?’”

This is almost word for word what is said of Felix in 24:27: “desiring to gain favor with the Jews.” Festus was more decent than Felix, yet on this point the two walked the same road. He had just taken office and needed the cooperation of the Jewish leaders, so he offered a “middle way”: change the location, but I will still judge. It sounds reasonable, but he knew what it meant to bring a man the Jews hated to the bone into Jerusalem.

Even a decent person will compromise in order to be liked. He will not do evil; he will only “meet halfway.” He will not pronounce an innocent man guilty; he will only send him into danger. Once the desire to please people is enthroned, even decency cannot protect justice.
• Examine my own compromises: my most recent “middle way”—was it for the sake of justice, or so as not to offend someone?
• People-pleasing is a chronic disease: Felix had it, Festus had it; if I am not watchful, I will have it too.
V. “I appeal to Caesar”—Placing the Road in the Lord’s Hands, and Using the Rights God Gave
Verses 10–12: Paul answered, “I am standing before Caesar’s judgment seat, where I ought to be tried… I appeal to Caesar!”

“Appealing to Caesar” was a privilege of Roman citizens: a citizen dissatisfied with a trial in a provincial court could demand that his case be handed directly to the emperor. The emperor then was Nero, and in AD 59 the first years of his reign, guided by capable advisers, were still relatively sound. The moment Paul said this, Festus could no longer judge the case—it passed automatically to Rome.

Why did Paul do this? Not out of fear of death—he said it plainly: “If I am a wrongdoer, and have committed anything worthy of death, I don’t refuse to die.” He was not fleeing judgment; he was refusing an unjust trial. He knew Festus was wavering, he knew there was an ambush on the road to Jerusalem, and he knew what the Lord had said to him two years earlier: “You must testify also at Rome.”

So he used a legal right God had given him to walk the road God had pointed out. He did not wait for a miracle to open the prison, nor did he force his way by his own strength; with the citizenship in his hand he walked toward the city the Lord had already named. Trusting God does not mean doing nothing; one who lets Jesus be King puts every legitimate resource in his hand toward His direction. “You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you shall go.” The door opened. That road would pass through storm, shipwreck, and a viper, but its end was Rome.
• Use the rights God gave: what legitimate, proper resources do I hold that I could use in God’s direction?
• Walk the road the Lord has spoken of: do I clearly know the direction the Lord has pointed, yet keep waiting for Him to push me there with a miracle?
321 Principle Light: Letting Jesus Be King Is Not Passive; It Is Aiming Everything at Him

In these twelve verses, three parties are moving: the Jews move, to kill Paul; Festus moves, to please the Jews; Paul also moves, appealing to Caesar. The difference is that the first two move around themselves—their own hatred, their own career; Paul moves around a single sentence the Lord spoke two years earlier.

Letting Jesus be King is often misunderstood as “doing nothing and waiting for God to arrange things.” But Paul was not like that. He argued his case, invoked his citizenship, and made a decision with no way back. He did a great deal, yet every bit of it was aimed at the place the Lord had named. This is following the Holy Spirit with the heart, not leaning on self with the head: not that he did not use his head, but that every calculation in his head was submitted to what the Lord had already said.

A person emptied of self looks like this today: he does not compromise to protect himself (like Festus), and does not plot to vent his hatred (like the Jews); he asks, “Where is the direction the Lord has pointed?” and then uses everything proper that he holds to walk that way.
a: Do not wait for time to deal with sin
Two years do not soften hatred that has not repented; the bitterness in my heart needs repentance.
See the hidden protection
God protected His servant through a Gentile official’s working principles; every “coincidence” in my life is His hand.
Examine my compromises
My most recent “middle way”—was it for justice, or so as not to offend?
Use the rights God gave
Put every legitimate resource in my hand toward the direction the Lord has pointed.
Walk the road the Lord has spoken of
Not waiting for a miracle to push me, nor forcing my own way, but aiming at the sentence He has already spoken.
q: The Jews’ plan had not changed in two years, and Festus’s compromise was the same as Felix’s. Is there something in your life that, with a change of time and circumstances, has not truly changed? What does it need?

Paul used his rights as a Roman citizen to walk toward the Rome the Lord had spoken of. What proper resource, identity, or opportunity do you hold that the Lord may want you to use in His direction, while you have been “waiting for Him to arrange things”?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that after two years the Jews’ hatred has not changed, and neither has your word. You used a new governor who followed the rules, though he did not know you, to wreck a murder plot; and you used the citizenship in your servant’s hand to send him on the road to Rome.
Lord, we confess that we are often like Festus: decent, yet compromising to be liked; and often like those Jews, giving an old hatred a respectable wrapping. Search the unrepentant bitterness in our hearts, and remove from us the self that fears offending people. Give us also Paul’s wisdom and courage: when we know the direction you have pointed, to walk that way with every proper resource in our hands, neither waiting for a miracle to push us nor forcing our own way. May the center of everything we do be the word you have spoken. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: Now when some days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea, and greeted Festus.
As he stayed there many days, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying, “There is a certain man left a prisoner by Felix;
about whom, when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews informed me, asking for a sentence against him.

I answered them that it is not the custom of the Romans to give up any man to destruction before the accused has met the accusers face to face and has had opportunity to make his defense concerning the matter laid against him.
When therefore they had come together here, I didn’t delay, but on the next day sat on the judgment seat and commanded the man to be brought.
When the accusers stood up, they brought no charges against him of such things as I supposed;
but had certain questions against him about their own religion, and about one Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive.
Being perplexed how to inquire concerning these things, I asked whether he was willing to go to Jerusalem and there be judged concerning these matters.
But when Paul had appealed to be kept for the decision of the emperor, I commanded him to be kept until I could send him to Caesar.”
Agrippa said to Festus, “I also would like to hear the man myself.” “Tomorrow,” he said, “you shall hear him.”

So on the next day, when Agrippa and Bernice had come with great pomp, and they had entered into the place of hearing with the commanding officers and the principal men of the city, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in.

Festus said, “King Agrippa, and all men who are here present with us, you see this man about whom all the multitude of the Jews petitioned me, both at Jerusalem and here, crying that he ought not to live any longer.
But when I found that he had committed nothing worthy of death, and as he himself appealed to the emperor I determined to send him,
of whom I have no certain thing to write to my lord. Therefore I have brought him out before you, and especially before you, King Agrippa, that, after examination, I may have something to write.
For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to also specify the charges against him.”
b: In the last devotion, Paul said before Festus’s tribunal, “I appeal to Caesar.” The door opened, and the case passed automatically to Rome.

But Festus now faced a difficulty: he was to send a prisoner to the emperor, yet could not write down what the man had done wrong. Just then a king who understood Jewish affairs came to visit. In today’s passage Paul does not say a word; it is Festus who does all the talking. Yet we will see a Gentile governor, without realizing it, state the very core of the gospel.
I. “King Agrippa and Bernice arrived”—The Last Generation of the Herod Family
Verse 13: “Now when some days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and greeted Festus.”

This was Herod Agrippa II, son of the Herod Agrippa I of chapter 12 who killed James and was later struck down and eaten by worms, and brother of Drusilla from the last devotion. Rome had not let him inherit all of Judea, giving him only some northern territories; but the emperor entrusted him with a privilege: oversight of the temple in Jerusalem and the appointment of the high priest. So he was the highest authority in Jewish religious affairs, and Festus consulted the right man.

Bernice was his sister, who after being widowed lived in her brother’s palace, and their relationship was a public scandal at the time. This brother and sister were one more meeting of the Herod family with Jesus Christ: the great Herod tried to kill the infant Jesus, Antipas killed John the Baptist and tried Jesus, Agrippa I killed James, and now Agrippa II was about to hear Paul speak of Jesus. One family, four generations, and each generation came across the gospel, but none truly received it.
• A family’s track record is not destiny: four generations refused, which does not mean a fifth cannot turn; I need not be determined by my family’s history.
• Recognize the difference between “encountering” and “receiving”: being near the gospel is not the same as being in it.
II. “It is not the custom of the Romans”—A Gentile’s Sense of Justice Becomes God’s Instrument

Verses 14–17: Festus laid Paul’s case before the king. He especially mentioned what he had told the Jewish leaders: “It is not the custom of the Romans to give up any man to destruction before the accused has met the accusers face to face, and has had opportunity to make his defense concerning the matter laid against him.”

This is a basic principle of Roman law: confrontation, defense, and only then a verdict. Festus did not know God, but he held to this principle, and Paul’s life was preserved. God’s justice is sometimes displayed through laws set up by people who do not know Him.

It also reminds us: when we condemn someone, have we given them a chance to defend themselves? Many times we have already judged a person guilty in our hearts, and that person has no idea what he has been charged with. Even the Romans knew that this was against their custom.
• Listen before judging: before I condemn someone in my heart, have I heard his own account?
• Give thanks for the rule of law: an official who keeps procedure is God’s protection for the innocent.
III. “A certain Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive”—A Gentile Hits the Gospel in One Sentence

Verses 18–19: Festus said that the accusers “brought no charges of such things as I supposed; but had certain questions against him about their own religion, and about one Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive.”

“Their own religion” can also be rendered “superstition,” and in Festus’s mouth it carried a trace of contempt: just their own religious quarrel. But the next sentence is the finest in the whole passage. A Roman official with no interest in the gospel summed up the entire dispute in the simplest way: a man named Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul said was alive.

This is exactly the gospel. Every argument comes back to this one point: is Jesus dead, or alive? Festus thought this was one of “certain questions”; he did not know that what he had said was the sentence that split human history in two.

Imagine a person who knows nothing of music walking into a concert hall and afterward saying, “It was just a group of people arguing on stage—one said he had left, another said he was still there.” His description is quite accurate; he just does not know what it was. Festus was like that: he stated the core of the gospel accurately, yet was not touched by that sentence.
• Not only to say it right but to be touched: I can say accurately that “Jesus is alive,” but has this sentence touched my life?
• The gospel is simple: dead, or alive—everything is here.
IV. “I also would like to hear the man myself”—Many Want to Hear, Few Take It In

Verses 20–23: Festus said he was “perplexed,” so he asked Paul whether he would go up to Jerusalem; but Paul appealed to be kept for the emperor’s decision. When Agrippa heard it, he said, “I also would like to hear the man myself.”

The next day, “Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp, and they had entered into the place of hearing with the commanding officers and the principal men of the city.” “Great pomp” means show and display. Caesarea garrisoned five cohorts, so the “commanding officers” were five battalion commanders; add the city’s notables—the king in purple, Bernice in jewels, officers in rank. Then, “at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in”—a prisoner in chains.

Agrippa “wanted to hear.” His ancestor Antipas also “wanted”—Herod had “long wished to see” Jesus, because he had heard about Him and hoped to see Him do a miracle (Luke 23:8). The people of the Herod family were always willing to “hear a bit” and “see a bit,” treating the gospel as a performance. Many want to hear, but few give up the throne.
• Do not treat the gospel as a performance: when I come to a meeting or to hear the word, am I coming to take a look, or to let the Lord be King?
• Pomp cannot hide emptiness: a whole hall full of purple robes and jewels, all gathered around one man in chains to hear him speak of Jesus.
V. “I have nothing definite to write to my lord”—A Trial That Could Find No Charge

Verses 24–27: Festus explained to everyone that the Jews had cried out that “he ought not to live any longer,” “but I found that he had committed nothing worthy of death”; and now that he was sending Paul, “I have nothing definite to write to my lord about him.” “My lord” is literally “the Lord”—Nero had by now begun to accept this title. Festus had to write an official letter to “the Lord,” and could not write a single charge.

“It seems to me unreasonable, when sending a prisoner, not to also specify the charges against him.” This was Festus’s most honest sentence. The whole trial, from Felix to Festus, over two years, two governors, one conclusion: no crime.

Yet Paul was still bound. Festus set him before the king, hoping Agrippa would help him find a charge he could write. He did not know that what Paul would say was not a defense of himself but a testimony that would almost make Agrippa a Christian.

The Lord Jesus was the same: Pilate said three times, “I find no basis for a charge against him” (Luke 23:4, 14, 22), yet still handed Him over to be crucified. To be bound though innocent is the road the Lord walked; Paul was walking the same one.
• To be bound though innocent is the Lord’s road: if I walk uprightly and am still wronged, I need not be surprised; the Lord has walked it.
• Who writes my “charge”: people may find no charge against me, but in God’s eyes, is my account cleared?
321 Principle Light: When Jesus Is Glorified, Even Unbelievers Testify for Him
In these fifteen verses Paul did not say a word, yet the gospel was spoken—by an unbelieving governor: “a certain Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive.”

This is what it looks like when Jesus receives all the glory. Paul did not need to open his mouth; the Lord’s name had already reached the king of the Herod family, five battalion commanders, and all the notables of the city. When a person is truly emptied of self, his very existence becomes a testimony: people talk about him, and end up talking about Jesus.

A person full of self in such a setting would think: so many distinguished people have come to hear me, I must perform well. A person emptied of self thinks: so many people have come, and the Lord is about to speak to them. When Paul stands up tomorrow, he will not tell how he was wronged; he will tell how the living Lord took hold of him. The focus is on Jesus, and even the chains become a pulpit.
a: Not determined by family history
Four generations of Herods refused, yet a fifth still has a chance; I need not repeat my family’s track record either.
Listen before judging
Before condemning someone in my heart, give him the chance to confront and defend.
Let the gospel touch me
Not only to say rightly that “Jesus is alive,” but to let that sentence touch my life.
Do not treat the gospel as a performance
I come to hear the word not to look around but to let the Lord be King.
Let my very existence be a testimony
Even when I do not open my mouth, may people talk about me and end up talking about Jesus.
q: Festus could accurately say, “Jesus was dead, but Paul says He is alive,” and yet was not touched. How much of your knowledge of the gospel is “saying it right,” and how much is “being touched”?

Agrippa “wanted to hear,” and so did his ancestor. Think of your most recent gathering or time in the word: did you come to take a look, or to let the Lord be King? What is the difference between the two in you?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that even when your servant said not a word, you still caused the gospel to be spoken from the mouth of an unbelieving governor: Jesus was dead, but Paul says He is alive. Your name does not need our eloquence; you yourself cause people to talk about you.
Lord, we confess that we are often like Agrippa, willing to hear a bit and see a bit, treating your word as a performance while refusing to give up the throne; and often like Festus, able to state your resurrection accurately while our lives are not touched by that sentence. Let the words “Jesus is alive” touch us today, so that we are no longer spectators but witnesses taken hold of by you. And make us so emptied of self that even our chains, our grievances, and our silences may lead people to speak your name. May all the glory be to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: Agrippa said to Paul, “You may speak for yourself.” Then Paul stretched out his hand, and made his defense.
“I think myself happy, King Agrippa, that I am to make my defense before you today concerning all the things that I am accused by the Jews,
especially because you are expert in all customs and questions which are among the Jews. Therefore I beg you to hear me patiently.
“Indeed, all the Jews know my way of life from my youth up, which was from the beginning among my own nation and at Jerusalem;
having known me from the first, if they are willing to testify, that after the strictest sect of our religion I lived a Pharisee.
Now I stand here to be judged for the hope of the promise made by God to our fathers,
which our twelve tribes, earnestly serving night and day, hope to attain. Concerning this hope I am accused by the Jews, King Agrippa!
Why is it judged incredible with you, if God does raise the dead?
“I myself most certainly thought that I ought to do many things contrary to the name of Jesus of Nazareth.
I also did this in Jerusalem. I both shut up many of the saints in prisons, having received authority from the chief priests, and when they were put to death I gave my vote against them.
Punishing them often in all the synagogues, I tried to make them blaspheme. Being exceedingly enraged against them, I persecuted them even to foreign cities.
b: In the last devotion, Agrippa and Bernice entered the hall with great pomp, officers in ranks and notables gathered; Festus publicly admitted, “I have nothing definite to write to my lord.” Then a man in chains was brought in.

Now the king spoke: “You may speak for yourself.” This is Paul’s last and longest speech in Acts. Before him sat a king of the Herod family, yet what he would speak of was not law but his own story—how a persecutor was taken hold of by the living Lord. Today we look at the first half: who he was, and what he had done in the past.
I. “Paul stretched out his hand and made his defense”—He Turned the Courtroom into a Pulpit

Verses 1–3: “Then Paul stretched out his hand, and made his defense.” “Stretching out the hand” was the opening gesture of an orator in those days, not the posture of a prisoner. Paul had chains on, but the moment he stretched out his hand, the whole hall changed from a courtroom into a pulpit.

His opening was: “I think myself happy, King Agrippa, that I am to make my defense before you this day… especially because you are expert in all customs and questions which are among the Jews.” “Happy” can also be rendered “blessed.” A man locked up for over two years, standing before the king who would decide his fate, calls himself “blessed.” This was not courtesy; he truly saw it that way: Agrippa oversaw the temple and appointed the high priest, the Gentile in the whole empire who best understood Jewish religion, and to tell the gospel of the resurrection to such a man was a tremendous opportunity.
What he saw was not “I am on trial” but “I get to speak.” In the same scene, a person full of self sees humiliation, and a person emptied of self sees opportunity.
• See my situation with new eyes: could the place I least want to be be the very place where the Lord wants me to open my mouth?
• Posture is decided from within: the chains are on the hands, but how the hands are stretched out is decided by who is King in the heart.
II. “After the strictest sect of our religion I lived a Pharisee”—His Former Righteousness

Verses 4–5: Paul spoke of his background: “So then all the Jews know my way of life from my youth up, which was from the beginning among my own nation and at Jerusalem. They knew me from the first, if they were willing to testify, that after the strictest sect of our religion I lived a Pharisee.”

“Strictest” means most exact, most rigorous. Paul was born in Tarsus but raised from childhood in Jerusalem and taught at the feet of Gamaliel (22:3), walking the most rigorous road within Judaism. His point: I am no outsider; I know the law better than those who accuse me. “If they were willing to testify”—this has a little sting: they know, they just will not say.

Paul did not say this to boast. Later in Philippians he listed all of it and then said, “However, what things were gain to me, those I have counted as loss for Christ’s sake” (Philippians 3:7). He had once thought that strictness was righteousness, until he met true righteousness.
• Strictness is not knowing God: however precisely I keep the rules, if the center is myself, it is still the old self’s righteousness.
• Do not prop up today with past credentials: Paul had more credentials than anyone, yet he stood not by these.
III. “For the hope of the promise made by God to our fathers”—The Real Reason He Was on Trial

Verses 6–8: Paul stated the real reason he was accused: “Now I stand here to be judged for the hope of the promise made by God to our fathers; to which promise our twelve tribes, earnestly serving night and day, hope to attain.”

He turned his own case upside down. The Jews accused him of betraying Judaism; he said, I am accused precisely because I believe what Judaism promised. “Twelve tribes”—not ten tribes long scattered with only Judah and Benjamin left, but all Israel; “earnestly serving night and day” describes the hope of the whole nation through the generations. What were they hoping for? The Messiah God promised to Abraham and David, and the resurrection He would bring.

Then he asked one question: “Why is it judged incredible with you, if God does raise the dead?” This was said to “you”—everyone in the hall. You all believe in God, so what is so hard to believe about God raising the dead? Your difficulty is not in the intellect but in the heart.
• What is my hope: what I earnestly long for day and night, is it what God promised, or what I myself want?
• The difficulty of the resurrection is in the heart, not the head: those things I do not believe, are they truly “incredible,” or am I unwilling to believe?
IV. “I myself thought that I ought to”—The Persecutor’s Confession

Verses 9–11: Paul began on the most inglorious part of his story: “I myself most certainly thought that I ought to do many things contrary to the name of Jesus of Nazareth. I also did this in Jerusalem.”

Notice the words “I myself thought that I ought to.” He was not doing evil at the time; he was doing what he thought he “ought” to do—he sincerely believed that persecuting Christians was zeal for God. This is the most frightening kind of sin: sin dressed in the clothes of righteousness, carrying God’s name. A person can “serve God” with one hand and throw God’s children into prison with the other, and not feel the least uneasy in conscience.

Think of a person driving in the wrong direction yet driving with great earnestness: pedal to the floor, hands gripping the wheel, never stopping. The harder he tries, the farther he gets from the destination. Paul was just like that—his zeal was real, his direction was wrong; and wrong direction plus real zeal does the most damage.
• Examine my “oughts”: the “ought” I am insisting on right now, did God say it, or do I only think so?
• Zeal cannot replace direction: make sure the direction is right first, then press the accelerator.
V. “When they were put to death, I gave my vote against them”—He Did Not Save Face for Himself

Verses 10–11: Paul spelled out the details: “I both shut up many of the saints in prisons, having received authority from the chief priests, and when they were put to death I gave my vote against them. Punishing them often in all the synagogues, I tried to make them blaspheme. Being exceedingly enraged against them, I persecuted them even to foreign cities.”

“Gave my vote” is literally “cast my pebble”—he had voted in favor of condemning Christians to death; “tried to make them blaspheme”—he used torture to force believers to curse Jesus; “exceedingly enraged” is literally “raging mad”; “even to foreign cities”—he pursued them beyond Judea, and Damascus was one stop.

Paul could have left this out. A man defending himself before a king usually touches up his past a little. But he did not omit a word. He applied the word “saints” to the very people he had jailed and killed—the very community he now belonged to. He publicly confessed: those I persecuted were God’s people.

This is not self-flagellation; it paves the way for the next part. The more honestly a person speaks of his darkness, the brighter the light that follows. The measure of grace is taken from the size of the sin a person is willing to admit.
• Do not touch up the past: before God and before people, tell my past as it was, unadorned.
• Honesty is the entrance to grace: the more truly I confess, the brighter the Lord’s light shines on me.
321 Principle Light: Change Begins with Me—First Admit Who I Once Was

Half of Paul’s testimony is about who he used to be. He was in no hurry to speak of the light on the Damascus road; first he made the darkness clear: I was the strictest Pharisee, I thought I ought to attack the name of Jesus, I voted for the saints’ death sentences, I used torture to make people blaspheme.

Change your concepts and you change your life; change your life and you change your living; change begins with me. The first step of that is to honestly admit what “I” originally was. This is the very thing a person full of self least wants to do—the self finds excuses for the past: back then I was zealous for God, back then I did not know, back then everyone did it. A person emptied of self needs no excuse, because he no longer stands on his own past; today he looks like this: when he tells of his failures, he does not add a “but.”

Paul stood before the most distinguished people in the hall and spoke of the most shameful things in his life, without the least panic. Because his righteousness was not in his own record but in the living Lord. When a person truly lets Jesus be King, his past no longer needs protecting; it becomes the material for his testimony.
a: See my situation with new eyes
The place I least want to be may be the very pulpit where the Lord wants me to speak.
Do not stand on credentials
My strictness and my credentials are not why I stand today.
Examine my hope
What I earnestly long for day and night, is it what God promised, or what I myself want?
Check the direction before pressing the accelerator
Zeal plus the wrong direction does the most damage.
Do not touch up the past
When I tell of my failures, I do not add a “but.”
q: Paul said, “I myself thought that I ought to.” Is the one thing you are insisting on right now something God said, or an “ought” you only think? How do you tell?
Paul told his past without touching up a word. The part of your past you least want to mention before others—if told just as it was, might it become a testimony to the Lord’s grace instead?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for letting us see your servant stretch out his hand in chains and turn a courtroom into a pulpit; and for letting us see him stand before a king and tell his most shameful past just as it was, without a word of adornment.
Lord, we confess that we often find excuses for our past, saying back then we were zealous for you, back then we did not know. We also often drive with great earnestness in the wrong direction, replacing your word with our own “ought.” Make us honest, first admitting who I originally was, so that your light may shine brighter on us. And place what you have promised in our hearts, so that what we long for day and night is you, not the things we want for ourselves. May every time we speak of our weakness become a testimony to your grace. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: “Whereupon as I traveled to Damascus with the authority and commission from the chief priests,
at noon, O king, I saw on the way a light from the sky, brighter than the sun, shining around me and those who traveled with me.
When we had all fallen to the earth, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’
“I said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ “He said, ‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.

But arise, and stand on your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose: to appoint you a servant and a witness both of the things which you have seen, and of the things which I will reveal to you;
delivering you from the people, and from the Gentiles, to whom I send you,

to open their eyes, that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive remission of sins and an inheritance among those who are sanctified by faith in me.’
b: In the last devotion, Paul stood before King Agrippa and told his most shameful past just as it was: the strictest Pharisee, voting for the saints’ death sentences, forcing people by torture to blaspheme, raging against them, pursuing them to foreign cities.

The darkness was made clear, and now the light comes. This is the third time Acts records the Damascus road (in chapter 9 Luke narrates it, in chapter 22 Paul tells it to the Jewish crowd, and now to a king). The same event told three times shows that it is the hinge of the whole book: how a man who set out to destroy the church became the man who built it up.
I. “At midday I saw a light from heaven, brighter than the sun”—The Light Found Him

Verses 12–13: “Whereupon as I traveled to Damascus with the authority and commission from the chief priests, at midday, O king, I saw on the way a light from the sky, brighter than the shining of the sun, shining around me and those who traveled with me.”

“Midday” is noon, the brightest hour of the day, yet this light was “brighter than the sun.” Paul stressed to the king that it was no twilight illusion and no dream in the night, but noon, brighter than the sun, shining even on those who traveled with him. It was not a feeling inside him but something that happened outside.

He went “with the authority and commission from the chief priests”—documents in his hand, certainty in his heart. He was not seeking God; he thought he was doing God’s business. But God found him. This is the order of grace: not that I find God first, but that God finds me first. “We love, because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). The light of Damascus was not something Saul sought; it was the Lord who took the initiative to shine down.
• God found me first: that I can believe is not because I am clever or seeking, but because the Lord stopped me when I was heading the wrong way.
• The light comes from outside: true change is not that I figured it out, but that the Lord shone in.
II. “It is hard for you to kick against the goads”—He Had Been Fighting a Thorn All Along
Verse 14: “When we had all fallen to the earth, I heard a voice speaking to me and saying in the Hebrew language, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’”

“In the Hebrew language”—the Lord called him by name in Saul’s mother tongue, twice. This is how God called people in the Old Testament: “Abraham! Abraham!” “Moses! Moses!” The Lord was not rebuking a criminal; He was calling a person He knew.
“Why do you persecute me?”—Saul was persecuting believers, yet the Lord said “persecute me.” The church is the body of Christ, and every blow on a member is felt by the Head.

“It is hard for you to kick against the goads”—this was a Greek proverb. A goad was a pointed stick for driving oxen; when the ox would not move, the farmer poked it, and if the ox kicked back, the goad pierced deeper. The Lord meant: Saul, you have been kicking, fighting the goad inside you all along. What goad? Stephen’s face at his death, “as if it were the face of an angel” (6:15), his prayer, “Don’t hold this sin against them” (7:60); those he tortured who would rather die than blaspheme Jesus. These scenes kept pricking him, and the more he kicked, the more enraged he became. Being exceedingly enraged was precisely because the goad had already gone in.

We often do the same: when God’s word pricks us, we do not obey but resist—and the more we resist, the more restless we become. One who uses the head and leans on self keeps kicking; one who uses the heart and follows the Holy Spirit stops and asks, Lord, is this thorn you?
• Recognize my own goad: the thing that has angered me most lately, could it be the Lord pricking me?
• Stop kicking: the more you kick the deeper it goes; the more you obey the lighter it becomes.
III. “Who are you, Lord?” “I am Jesus whom you persecute”—His Lifelong Question Was Answered
Verse 15: “I said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ He said, ‘I am Jesus whom you persecute.’”

Saul lay on the ground and asked just one thing: “Who are you, Lord?” He knew this was “Lord,” but did not know who this Lord was. He had served God strictly all his life, yet only at this moment would he learn God’s name.

The answer: “I am Jesus whom you persecute.” This one sentence turned Saul’s whole world over. He had thought Jesus was a crucified impostor; now this name was spoken out of the light from heaven. Jesus is alive—not a doctrine, but the One speaking to him at this very moment. And this living Lord was the very one he had been persecuting. All his life’s zeal had been striking God.

Every true transformation begins with this question: not “What should I do?” but “Who are you?” The order cannot be reversed—first know Him, then talk about serving. First with God, then with self, then with people, then with things.
• Ask first “Who are you?”: in my daily prayer, do I first ask for things, or first get to know Him?
• Whom am I persecuting: every harsh word and every cold shoulder toward my brothers and sisters, the Lord feels.
IV. “Rise, and stand on your feet”—The One Struck Down Was Raised Up and Became a Servant

Verses 16–17: The Lord said, “But arise, and stand on your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose, to appoint you a servant and a witness both of the things which you have seen, and of the things which I will reveal to you; delivering you from the people, and from the Gentiles, to whom I send you.”

“Stand on your feet”—a moment ago it was the Lord who struck him down; now it is the Lord who tells him to stand up. God never strikes a person down to leave him on the ground, but so that he may stand up in a new posture.

“Servant” is literally an “under-rower,” one who rows on the lowest deck of a large ship—the lowest position, unable to see the direction, only hearing the command to row. “Witness” is the very word that later became “martyr.” From a persecutor with documents in hand to a servant rowing below deck—this was a complete humbling, yet Paul took pride in it all his life.

“Delivering you from the people and from the Gentiles”—in the very act of calling, the Lord foretold persecution and also foretold deliverance. Paul experienced this sentence again and again at Lystra, at Philippi, at Jerusalem, at Caesarea.
• Stand up after being struck down: the Lord strikes me down so that I may stand up in a new posture, not stay on the ground in self-pity.
• From one in power to a servant: one who lets Jesus be King is glad to be the one rowing below deck.
V. “To open their eyes”—The Whole Gospel in One Sentence

Verse 18: The Lord explained the purpose of the sending: “I send you, to open their eyes, that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive remission of sins and an inheritance among those who are sanctified by faith in me.”

This is one of the most complete summaries of the gospel in the whole Bible, in five steps: eyes opened—first to see; from darkness to light—a change of realm; from the power of Satan to God—a change of king; receiving forgiveness—the past cleared away; an inheritance among the sanctified—a share in the future. The first three are turning around; the last two are received freely.

“From the power of Satan to God”—this puts it most clearly: man’s problem is not only doing wrong but being under the wrong king. The gospel is not telling people to be a little better but to change who reigns. And this is exactly what Saul himself had just experienced: his eyes had just been opened (though his physical eyes were blind for a time), he had just turned from darkness to light, he had just changed kings. What the Lord sent him to do was what had just been done to him.
• Under whose power am I: today’s choices, are they under God’s power, or still in the old master’s hands?
• Share what I have experienced: all I can give people is what the Lord has done in me.
321 Principle Light: From Self to Self-Denial Is a Change of King

What happened on the Damascus road was not a bad man becoming a good man but a man full of self becoming a man emptied of self. Saul had been his own king: his righteousness, his zeal, his documents all centered on “I thought I ought to.” When the Lord’s light shone, he fell down, he asked “Who are you?”, and then he stood up—no longer Saul on the throne but Jesus as King.

Pride is leaving one’s place and seizing power, wanting to take God’s place; the documents in Saul’s hand were the power he seized. Humility is putting down power and returning to one’s place—at the moment he fell to the ground, the documents dropped from his hand and he returned to a human’s place. From that day his position was a servant rowing below deck, and his words were “It is no longer I, but Christ” (Galatians 2:20).

Self-denial is not having nothing but entering the limitless. Saul lost his own direction but gained the Lord’s sending; lost the chief priests’ authority but gained the authority to open people’s eyes. Today it looks very simple: when I hear the Lord’s prick, I do not kick; I fall down, ask “Who are you?”, and then stand up as He says.
a: God found me first
That I can believe is because the Lord stopped me when I was heading the wrong way, not because I found Him myself.
Stop kicking the goads
What has angered me most lately may be the Lord pricking me; the more I obey, the lighter it gets.
Ask first, “Who are you?”
In prayer, first know Him, then talk about things.
From one in power to a servant
Be glad to be the one rowing below deck.
Share what I have experienced
Eyes opened, a king changed, sins forgiven—this is all I have to give.
q: “It is hard for you to kick against the goads.” Is there something lately that the more you resist, the more restless you are, and the harder you push, the heavier it gets? Could it be the Lord pricking you? Are you willing to stop today and ask, “Who are you, Lord?”

The Lord turned Saul from a man with documents in hand into a servant rowing below deck. In your present position, what is the “document” you are holding on to? If the Lord wanted you to put it down and go row, what would your first reaction be?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that when Saul had documents in hand and was heading the wrong way, your light shone down. Thank you for finding him first, and for finding us first; while we were still kicking at the goads and still thought we were doing your business, you called us by name.
Lord Jesus, we bow before you and ask you that question: Who are you? Reveal yourself to us, and let us recognize that the One we often persecute by coldness and harshness is you. Strike down the self in us that makes itself king, and then raise us up in a new posture to be your servants rowing below deck. Open our eyes, truly turn us from the power of Satan to you, and let us carry this gospel to those you send us to. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: “Therefore, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision,
but declared first to them of Damascus, at Jerusalem, and throughout all the country of Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, doing works worthy of repentance.
For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me.
Having therefore obtained the help that is from God, I stand to this day testifying both to small and great, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would happen,
how the Christ must suffer, and how, by the resurrection of the dead, he would be first to proclaim light both to these people and to the Gentiles.”
b: In the last devotion, Paul spoke of the light on the Damascus road: he fell down and asked “Who are you, Lord?”, then was told to rise, to be a servant and a witness, to go open people’s eyes, that they might turn from the power of Satan to God.

That was about twenty-five years earlier. From that day to standing before Agrippa today, there lay between three journeys, countless beatings, stonings, and prisons. Paul accounted for these twenty-five years in five verses, and then stopped his whole testimony at one place: Christ must suffer, and rise from the dead.
I. “I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision”—Twenty-Five Years, Doing One Thing
Verse 19: “Therefore, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision.”

“Disobedient” means unpersuaded, not yielding. Paul did not say “I fulfilled the vision,” nor “look how much I did for the vision”; he only said: I was not disobedient. This is a very low way to put it, and also a very high one. Low, because he claims no credit; high, because for twenty-five years there was truly not a day he walked outside the vision.

A vision can move a person in one evening, but for a person not to disobey it for twenty-five years is no longer being moved; it is life. We have all had moments of being moved by the Lord—a meeting, a prayer, a passage. The question is not how real that moment was, but whether after it I have kept walking in it. Feelings fade; obedience is what remains.
• Not being disobedient is enough: I need not achieve anything astonishing, only keep walking today in the direction the Lord has given me.
• Examine my own vision: what did the Lord once say to me? Is that word still in my life today?
II. “Doing works worthy of repentance”—Repentance Is Visible

Verse 20: Paul summarized what he preached: “but declared first to those who were at Damascus, at Jerusalem, and throughout all the country of Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, doing works worthy of repentance.”

Damascus, Jerusalem, all Judea, the Gentiles—this is exactly the order the Lord gave in chapter one (1:8), and Paul’s footsteps followed that line. And what he preached was just one sentence: repent and turn to God, doing works worthy of repentance.

“Repent” is literally “a change of mind”; “turn” is “to turn around”; “doing works worthy of repentance” means to do deeds fitting for repentance. Three levels: the mind turns, the direction turns, and then the steps must follow. Repentance is not shedding tears but turning around; turning around is not just saying so but walking out.
