John the Baptist said the same thing: “Bring forth therefore fruit worthy of repentance” (Matthew 3:8).

Imagine a person on a highway who finds he is going the wrong way. He can regret, he can blame himself, he can sigh over the map—but as long as the car keeps going forward, he is still on the wrong road. Repentance is taking the next exit and turning around. Only after the U-turn, every mile the car travels is what is called “worthy of repentance.”
• Repentance must be visible: the sin I confessed, has even one thing in my behavior truly changed?
• Do not stay in regret: regret is a feeling, turning around is an action; what matters is the latter.
III. “The Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me”—The Preacher of Repentance Is Hated
Verse 21: “For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple, and tried to kill me.”

“For this reason”—because he preached repentance, and especially because he preached repentance to the Gentiles too, the Jews seized him in the temple. Paul made the whole case as clear as it could be: he was not arrested for stirring up disorder but for preaching the gospel.

Those who preach repentance are always hated, because repentance touches a person’s “self” directly—it asks people to admit they have gone wrong, to turn around, to change. People can accept a religion that comforts them; it is hard to accept a message that makes them turn back. John the Baptist was killed for it, the Lord Jesus was crucified for it, Paul was seized for it. Yet Paul said this with no bitterness. He was not accusing the Jews; he was explaining: this is the normal cost of preaching repentance.
• Do not fear being hated: if I speak the truth faithfully, there will always be those who dislike it; that is not my doing wrong, but the cost of the message itself.
• Without bitterness: when hated, still state the facts and do not accuse.
IV. “Having obtained the help that is from God, I stand to this day”—The Reason He Stood Was Not in Himself
Verse 22a: “Having therefore obtained the help that is from God, I stand to this day testifying both to small and great.”

“Help” is a military term meaning “the aid of allied forces”—when an army is about to be unable to hold, another army rushes to it. Paul said he could stand to this day not by holding himself up but because there was a God who kept rushing to his aid. In twenty-five years, how many times he nearly fell—stoned at Lystra until they thought him dead, dragged out of the temple by the mob at Jerusalem—and each time there was God’s help.

“Both to small and great”—he spoke to the king and also to the jailer; to the notable and also to the prisoner. The gospel makes no distinction of audience, because everyone needs the same repentance.

I am still standing because God helps. Not because I am strong, not because I have gifts, but because of Him. A person full of self, giving a testimony, will unconsciously turn it into how he pulled through; a person emptied of self tells how God rushed to his aid again and again.
• Standing is grace: that I still stand in the faith today is not because I held on well, but because He has come to my aid again and again.
• The same to small and great: in preaching the gospel and caring for people, do I pick my audience?
V. “That the Christ must suffer, and rise from the dead”—The Endpoint of Testimony Is Christ

Verse 22b–23: Paul said that what he spoke was “nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would happen, how the Christ must suffer, and how, by the resurrection of the dead, he would be first to proclaim light to the people and to the Gentiles.”

Paul put his message back into the Scriptures. He was not preaching a new religion; he preached exactly what Moses and the prophets had spoken—the suffering servant of Isaiah 53, the Holy One who sees no decay of Psalm 16. The Bible is my standard—standing before a king, Paul aimed all his words at the word of God.

Then he stated the core of the whole testimony: “the Christ must suffer, and… by the resurrection of the dead, he would be first to proclaim light to the people and to the Gentiles.” “Must”—not an accident but God’s decree; “first”—He is the first to rise from the dead, the firstfruits (1 Corinthians 15:20); “light”—the very light that struck him down on the Damascus road, which now would be proclaimed through him to all.

Notice the structure of this testimony. He spoke of his past, his change, his service, but the last word is not “I,” it is “Christ.” This is the standard for all testimony: I speak of myself in order to speak of Him; my story is only a small section in His story.
• The endpoint of testimony is Christ: when I tell my experience, is my last word “I” or “He”?
• Put the message back in Scripture: is what I say “nothing but” the word of God?
321 Principle Light: Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry—One Thing for a Lifetime

These five verses are Paul’s twenty-five years condensed. He first said he was not disobedient to the vision (life), then spoke of his exhortation to people and the hatred he endured (relationships), and finally of what he preached all his life (ministry). The order is not confused: first he himself was taken hold of by the Lord, and only then did he go to take hold of others; first he himself repented and turned, and only then did he preach repentance.

Letting Jesus receive all the glory looks like this here: he told a whole speech of his own story, and the last sentence was “the Christ must suffer, and rise from the dead.” His standing, he said, was God’s help; the message he preached, he said, was what Moses and the prophets had long spoken; his vision, he said, was from heaven. From beginning to end, not one thing was his own.

A person emptied of self is not one without a story but one whose story has only one main character. Today it looks very simple: when someone asks how I have come through these years, do I say “I pulled through,” or “He came to help me again and again”? When I finish telling my experience, on whom does the last sentence fall?
a: Not being disobedient is enough
No astonishing achievement needed, only to keep walking today in the direction the Lord has given me.
Repentance must be visible
For the sin I confessed, at least one thing in my behavior must truly change.
Do not fear being hated; no bitterness
Truth has its cost; when hated, I still state the facts, not accusations.
Standing is grace
I still stand in the faith because He has rushed to my aid again and again, not because I held on well.
Let testimony stop on Christ
When telling my experience, let the last sentence fall on Him.
q: Is the word the Lord once spoke to you, the stirring He once gave you, still in your life today? Are you still walking in it, or have you unknowingly become “disobedient”?
For the sin you most recently confessed, has even one thing in your behavior truly changed? If not, what is one concrete action this week that you could take “worthy of repentance”?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for letting us see your servant who for twenty-five years was not disobedient to the heavenly vision. He claimed no credit, saying only “I was not disobedient”; he did not boast of being strong, saying only, “having obtained the help that is from God, I stand to this day.”
Lord, we confess that we are often moved by you but do not keep walking in it; often regretful but do not really turn around; often tell our own testimony and let the last sentence fall on ourselves. Make our repentance visible, our works worthy of repentance; come to our aid when we are about to be unable to hold, so that we still stand today; and let every time we open our mouths end on Christ—He must suffer and rise from the dead, proclaiming light to everyone. May all glory be to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: As he thus made his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, “Paul, you are crazy! Your great learning is driving you insane!”
But he said, “I am not crazy, most excellent Festus, but boldly declare words of truth and reasonableness.
For the king knows of these things, to whom also I speak freely. For I am persuaded that none of these things is hidden from him, for this has not been done in a corner.
King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.”
Agrippa said to Paul, “With a little persuasion are you trying to make me a Christian?”
Paul said, “I pray to God, that whether with little or with much, not only you, but also all that hear me today, might become such as I am, except for these bonds.”
The king rose up with the governor, and Bernice, and those who sat with them.
When they had withdrawn, they spoke to one another, saying, “This man does nothing worthy of death or of bonds.”
Agrippa said to Festus, “This man might have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.”
b: In the last devotion, Paul’s testimony stopped at this point: “the Christ must suffer, and… by the resurrection of the dead, would proclaim light to the people and to the Gentiles.”

He had not finished speaking when someone interrupted. Today’s nine verses are the close of this great hearing at Caesarea: a governor shouts that he is out of his mind, a king says he is trying to persuade him “in a short time,” and then all the dignitaries withdraw and reach one conclusion—this man has done nothing worthy of death. It was also the last time the house of Herod brushed past the gospel.
I. “Paul, you are crazy!”—Speak of the Resurrection and the World Says You Are Mad
Verse 24: “As he thus made his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, ‘Paul, you are crazy! Your great learning is turning you crazy!’”

Festus could take no more. While Paul spoke of the Pharisees and of the vision, he could still treat it as a Jewish religious debate; but when Paul came to “Christ rose from the dead,” this Roman could not listen any longer. “Crazy” in the original is simply “mad”; “great learning” in the original is “many books”—you have read too much and it has driven you mad.

This is the world’s most typical response to the resurrection: not an argument but a sneer. The philosophers in Athens did the same—the moment they heard of a dead man rising, they mocked (17:32). The world can put up with religion, morality and charity, but it cannot put up with a man who has walked out of a grave—because that means there is a real Lord.
• Being called mad is no surprise: if I truly speak of the risen Lord, someone will always think I am not right in the head; it is not that I have said it wrong, it is the message itself.
• Not carried away by mockery: Festus was loud; Paul was not.
II. “I speak the words of truth and reason”—Calm Is Given by the Holy Spirit
Verses 25 and 26: Paul said, “I am not crazy, most excellent Festus, but boldly declare words of truth and reason.”

“Truth” means the content is true; “reason” in the original is “sober, self-controlled”—exactly the opposite of “crazy.” Paul did not lose his temper; he still addressed him as “most excellent.” A person truly led by the Holy Spirit, told to his face that he is mad, can still say calmly: I am perfectly sober.

Then he turned to the king: “For the king knows about these things… for this has not been done in a corner.” The death of Jesus, his resurrection, the rise of the church—for thirty years these had been public matters in the land of the Jews. “Not done in a corner”—the gospel has never been a secret religion; it can stand investigation.

Think of a man standing on a ship in a storm. The ship is rocking, the wind is howling, the people beside him are shouting; but if his anchor has truly reached the seabed, he can say calmly: the ship will not capsize. Paul’s calm was not temperament; it was an anchor—an anchor dropped into the living Lord.
• Calm is proof of the anchor: how I react when I am misunderstood or mocked shows where my anchor is.
• Not in a corner: can what I believe and how I live stand up to public examination?
III. “King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe”—The Gospel Speaks Straight to the Heart
Verse 27: Paul suddenly turned to Agrippa and asked a piercing question: “King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.”

It was a question that backs a man into a corner. Agrippa was the overseer of Jewish religious affairs; of course he “believed the prophets”—to say no would set all the Jews against him; to say yes meant facing what the prophets said of a Messiah who would suffer and rise. Paul gave him no middle road.

At this moment Paul was no longer the defendant; he had become the one preaching the gospel to the king. He did not care that all the great people in the hall were watching, nor that he had chains on his hands. He saw only one person who needed to repent. People matter more than events—in Paul’s eyes Agrippa was not a king who held his fate, but a soul who needed Jesus.
• The gospel is aimed at a person: when I share the gospel or care for someone, do I see an occasion, or a soul?
• Dare to ask the sharp question: to love someone is sometimes to bring him before the question he can no longer dodge.
IV. “With a little persuasion you would make me a Christian”—Almost, Always Only Almost
Verses 28 and 29: Agrippa answered, “With a little persuasion, you would make me a Christian!”

“A little” in the original is “in a little”—it can mean “in a little time” or “with a little effort.” Agrippa probably meant: you think a few sentences like these can turn me into a Christian? There is a trace of a smile in it, and a trace of evasion. He neither denied nor admitted; with one clever remark he slipped out from under Paul’s question.
The word “Christian” appears only three times in the whole Bible (11:26; 26:28; 1 Peter 4:16), and this time it came from the mouth of a king of the house of Herod, with a touch of contempt.

Paul’s reply is the most moving line in the whole passage: “I would to God that whether in a little or in much, not only you, but also all that hear me today, might become such as I am, except for these bonds.” He lifted the chains on his hands and said, to a hall of purple robes and jewels: what I ask is that every one of you become like me—only without these chains. A prisoner said to a king: I wish you were like me. Because he knew he was freer than anyone seated there.
Agrippa did not accept. “Almost” is the track record of this family: Antipas almost listened to John, and Agrippa II almost became a Christian. Almost, always only almost.
• Not slipping away with a clever remark: when the Lord’s question comes to me, do I answer, or sidestep with a polished phrase?
• See who is truly free: Paul in chains was freer than the king; is my way of looking at people deceived by outward show?
V. “This man does nothing worthy of death or of bonds”—Innocent, Yet Still Bound for Rome

Verses 30 to 32: “The king rose up, and the governor, and Bernice, and those who sat with them. When they had withdrawn, they spoke one to another, saying, ‘This man does nothing worthy of death or of bonds.’ Agrippa said to Festus, ‘This man might have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.’”

This was the third declaration of innocence: Lysias had said it (23:29), Festus had said it (25:25), and now the king said it too. The Lord Jesus was also declared innocent three times by Pilate and then handed over. Paul was walking the road his Lord had walked.

“Might have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar”—it sounds like regret. But remember what the Lord said in chapter 23: “As you have testified about me at Jerusalem, so you must testify also at Rome.” Paul’s appeal to Caesar was not a miscalculation; it was walking the road the Lord had shown. If he had been released that day, he would not have gone to Rome; without Rome there would be no Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or Philemon. God did not let him go free because the road God had for him was bigger than release.
We often think God’s good will means “release”—the problem solved, the chains off. But sometimes God’s good will is “going to Rome”—the chains remain, yet the road leads further.
• Innocent yet not released is the Lord’s road: when I do right and am still wronged, I remember the Lord walked this way too.
• God’s good will is not always release: sometimes he leaves the chains because a bigger Rome lies ahead.
321 Principles Insight: The Self-Emptied Are the Freest; the Kings Full of Self Are the Most Bound

In this trial, who was the prisoner? Paul had chains on his hands, yet he was calm, bold and straightforward, put a question to the king, and prayed for the whole hall; Agrippa wore a purple robe, yet dodged with one clever remark and in the end could only say, “might have been set free if he had not appealed”—he could not even release an innocent man.

Self-denial is not having nothing; it is entering the limitless. Paul had nothing left—freedom, position, future—but he had Christ, so he could say to a king, “I wish you were like me.” The one full of self had everything—throne, pomp, power—yet did not dare face the one question, “Do you believe the prophets?” because to answer would mean giving up the throne. Pride is leaving one’s place and grasping power; what Agrippa gripped was that self that would not answer.

Letting Jesus be King looks like this today: when the Lord’s question comes to me, I do not slip away with a clever remark, I answer; when I am called mad, I do not raise my voice, I speak words of truth and reason; when I am left in chains, I believe there is a Rome ahead. A person like that, in chains, is still the freest one in the hall.
a: Being called mad is no surprise
Speak of the risen Lord and someone will think I am odd; that is the price of the message.
Calm is proof of the anchor
How I react when misunderstood shows where my anchor is.
See a soul
When I share the gospel, I see not an occasion but a person who needs Jesus.
Don’t slip away with clever words
When the Lord’s question comes, I answer and do not dodge.
Believe there is a Rome ahead
God may leave the chains because the road he gives is bigger than release.
q: “Do you believe the prophets?”—Paul brought Agrippa before a question he could not dodge. Has the Lord lately asked you a question that you keep slipping away from with clever words? What is that question?

Paul was innocent yet was not released, because Rome lay ahead. Is there a chain in your life that has still not fallen off? Are you willing to believe that God left it there perhaps because the road he gives you is bigger than release?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for letting us see your servant standing before a king in chains, calm though called mad, bold as he questioned the king, and in the end lifting his chains and saying, “I wish you all were like me.” We see that a self-emptied person is the freest one in the hall.
Lord, we confess that we are often like Agrippa, slipping out from under your question with a clever remark; and we often think your good will is only release, and doubt you whenever the chains do not fall. Make us speak words of truth and reason when we are mocked, not dodge when you ask, and believe there is a Rome ahead while the chains remain. Remove from us the self that clings to the throne and will not answer, and make us like Paul, able to have nothing as long as we have you. May all who hear become like him—only without these chains; and if we have chains, may we still be free to witness for you. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: When it was determined that we should sail for Italy, they delivered Paul and certain other prisoners to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan band.
Embarking in a ship of Adramyttium, which was about to sail to places on the coast of Asia, we put to sea, Aristarchus, a Macedonian of Thessalonica, being with us.
The next day, we touched at Sidon. Julius treated Paul kindly, and gave him permission to go to his friends and refresh himself.
Putting to sea from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were contrary.
When we had sailed across the sea which is off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra, a city of Lycia.
There the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy, and he put us on board.
When we had sailed slowly many days, and had come with difficulty opposite Cnidus, the wind not allowing us further, we sailed under the lee of Crete, opposite Salmone.
With difficulty sailing along it we came to a certain place called Fair Havens, near the city of Lasea.
When much time had passed and the voyage was now dangerous, because the Fast had now already gone by, Paul admonished them
and said to them, “Sirs, I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives.”
But the centurion gave more heed to the master and to the owner of the ship than to those things which were spoken by Paul.

Because the haven was not suitable to winter in, the majority advised going to sea from there, if by any means they could reach Phoenix, and winter there, which is a port of Crete, looking southwest and northwest.
b: In the last devotion, after King Agrippa heard Paul’s defense, he said, “With a little persuasion, you would make me a Christian!” Then the king and the governor withdrew to confer: “This man might have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.”

And so the door closed before Paul’s eyes. But more than two years earlier, in the barracks at Jerusalem, the Lord had stood beside him and said, “As you have testified about me at Jerusalem, so you must testify also at Rome” (23:11). What people saw was a closed door; what the Lord saw was a sea route to Rome. Chapter 27 is the first leg of that route.
I. “They delivered Paul and certain other prisoners to a centurion”—A Prisoner’s Identity, a King’s Route

Verse 1: “When it was determined that we should sail for Italy…” Notice that “we”—the “we” that had vanished for more than two years since Paul’s arrest is back. Luke has stepped onto the stage again and travels with him in person, so every place name and every change of course in this chapter is an eyewitness account.

Paul was handed over to “a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan Cohort.” The Augustan Cohort was a unit charged with escort and communications. In the Roman records Paul was only one of “certain other prisoners”—not an apostle, a number.

Yet two others were on board: Luke, and “Aristarchus, a Macedonian of Thessalonica.” Aristarchus had once been dragged into the theater in the riot at Ephesus (19:29), and later, when Paul wrote from Rome, he called him “my fellow prisoner” (Colossians 4:10). Two free men voluntarily stepped into a prisoner’s itinerary. People matter more than things, relationships more than possessions—here that is not a doctrine; it is two boat tickets.
• Identity is in men’s hands, the route is in God’s hands: who I am on the record cannot change where the Lord will take me.
• Someone is willing to walk the prisoner’s road with you: such a relationship is grace the Lord prepares in a tight place.
II. “Julius treated Paul kindly”—Kindness on the Chain

Verse 3: When the ship reached Sidon, “Julius treated Paul kindly, and gave him liberty to go to his friends and refresh himself.” “Treated kindly” in the original is “treated humanely”; “refresh himself” is a medical term—the same root the Good Samaritan’s “took care of him” uses (Luke 10:34). Luke the physician is hinting that after two years in custody Paul’s body needed care, and the brothers in Sidon cared for him.
An escorting officer actually let his prisoner go ashore to see friends—before the angel (27:23) had spoken a word, God’s favor was already at work.

Verses 4 to 6: Because “the winds were contrary,” the ship could only creep along under the lee of Cyprus, and slowly made its way to Myra in Lycia—a regular stopover for the Egyptian grain fleet. There the centurion “found” a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy. A third of Rome’s grain came from Egyptian wheat, and these grain ships were among the largest merchant vessels of the day. To men it looked like chance; to God it was a connection: God arranged for his prisoner a ship bound straight for Rome.
• Favor often comes before the promise: before the angel spoke, God had already used a Gentile officer to treat Paul kindly.
• Behind every “finding” is a hand: it is not that I am lucky, it is that the Lord was already waiting for me at the next port.
III. “The wind did not permit us”—Headwinds Are Also Within His Permission

Verses 7 and 8: From Myra to Cnidus is only a little over two hundred kilometers, yet it took “many days.” At Cnidus the northwest wind blocked the westward course, so the ship turned south, rounded the eastern end of Crete at Cape Salmone, sheltered on the island’s southern lee, and inch by inch “coasted along,” until it “with difficulty” came to Fair Havens—a name meaning “good harbor,” though really a small bay with only the little town of Lasea nearby. Luke uses “with difficulty” twice; the mood of these verses is slow, blocked, barely getting by.

Paul had longed for years to go to Rome (Romans 1:13). Now the Lord had personally promised he would reach Rome, and he was at last on a ship bound for Rome—and the ship could barely move. We often think that if it is the Lord’s road, the wind should be behind us all the way; yet Acts records that on the road the Lord promised there were also “contrary winds,” and delays. A headwind is not proof the Lord is absent; a headwind is weather the Lord allows. He wanted Paul to reach Rome, but he did not promise Paul would arrive quickly.
• Slow is also the Lord’s guidance: the Holy Spirit leads me, not only in direction but in speed.
• Not suspecting the Lord in the headwind: on the days the wind is contrary, the first thing tested is my faith in his promise.
IV. “Paul admonished them”—The Prisoner Speaks Up

Verse 9: “The fast was already gone by”—that is the Day of Atonement, which falls in early October. The sailing common sense of the time was that after mid-September sea travel was already dangerous, and after mid-November the Mediterranean was closed completely. The safe season had passed.

So Paul spoke: “Sirs, I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss… also of our lives.” Notice “I perceive.” This time Paul was not speaking of a vision (that would not come until verse 23), but of the judgment of a seasoned traveler. By the time he wrote 2 Corinthians he had already “suffered shipwreck three times, a night and a day I have been in the deep” (2 Corinthians 11:25); when it came to the dangers of the sea, his experience was perhaps no less than the sailors’. The guidance God gives people is sometimes a supernatural vision, sometimes common sense governed by the Holy Spirit; both are guidance.

Verse 11: “But the centurion gave more heed to the master and to the owner of the ship than to those things which were spoken by Paul.” The “master” was the pilot, the “owner” the shipowner; one was expertise, the other the boss. How could a prisoner’s judgment compare with expertise and the boss? Julius’s choice looked entirely reasonable to men.

What most easily drowns out the Lord’s voice in life is often not an obvious sin but “reasonable”—the expert says so, the boss decided so, the data shows so. Expertise is not wrong, but above expertise there is still the Lord. When that quiet, out-of-place reminder sounds, am I willing to listen a little longer?
• Discern the source of guidance: a vision is guidance, and so is common sense governed by the Holy Spirit.
• Above the reasonable stands the Lord: what most often crowds out his voice is not sin but “everyone thinks it makes sense.”
V. “The majority advised”—The Majority Is Not Necessarily Right

Verse 12: The reason for the decision is written plainly: “because the harbor was not suitable to winter in.” Fair Havens was too small; for more than two hundred people to hole up there three or four months would be too uncomfortable. Phoenix was a decent harbor, only a few dozen kilometers to the west. So “the majority” favored taking the risk.

We often hold meetings like this at home. A typhoon is coming—do we go out for the dinner that was booked long ago? One person says it is dangerous; the rest say, “We won’t be that unlucky,” “The deposit is already paid.” The majority carries the vote, and the car pulls out. Majority rule is a way of handling opinions, not a way of discerning truth; truth is not put to a vote.

The sharpest thing is that reason: not for greater safety, but for “convenience.” What the self fears most is often not danger but discomfort; to avoid a little inconvenience it will risk a great deal. Let me ask honestly: inside that “majority,” could there be a vote of mine too? My self loves to follow the majority, because following the majority means I do not have to take responsibility myself.
• See the reason behind the decision: am I doing it because it is right, or because it is convenient?
• Not handing responsibility to the majority: one who lets Jesus be King is willing to hold quietly, before the majority, to what he has seen from the Lord, even if he loses the vote.
321 Principles Insight: Use the Heart to Rely on the Holy Spirit, Not the Head to Rely on Yourself

In these twelve verses there are three voices: expertise, the majority, and one prisoner’s “I perceive.” The first two were both reasonable and both used the head; the third was seen in the Holy Spirit by a man who had put his whole life in the Lord’s hands.

Using the head and relying on yourself does not mean people should not think—Paul was thinking too. The difference lies in “relying.” One who relies on himself treats expertise and the majority as the final authority, so when the Lord speaks through an unremarkable person, he cannot hear; one who relies on the Holy Spirit still uses his head and still respects expertise, but leaves the final decision to the Lord.

Use the head and you worry; use the heart and you are glad. The group that chose “convenient for the winter” went on to fourteen days of panic without seeing the sky; the overruled prisoner became the only person on the ship with peace. Peace does not come from “things going as I wish,” but from “I know who is at the helm.”
a: Hand over my identity to God
How others classify me cannot change where the Lord will take me.
Treasure those in the same boat
Be thankful for those who walk with me, and be willing to walk a stretch of the prisoner’s road with others.
No suspicion in the headwind
On the road the Lord promised there are also contrary-wind days; slow is also his guidance.
Listen to the Lord above the reasonable
Hear the experts, the boss and the data, but leave the last word to the Lord.
Don’t follow the majority to dodge inconvenience
Honestly look at my reason for deciding: is it to be right, or to be comfortable?
q: Think of an important decision you made recently: was your reason “this is right,” or “this is more convenient”? If Paul had been present, how would he have seen that decision?

Is there something right now in which you are plainly walking on the road the Lord promised, yet “for many days the ship moves slowly”? In the headwind, is the first thing you say to the Lord a complaint, a suspicion, or “You are still at the helm”?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that when men closed the door of release before Paul, you had already opened for him a sea route to Rome. Thank you for using a Gentile centurion to treat him kindly, the friends at Sidon to care for him, and Luke and Aristarchus to go aboard with him. Your favor always walks ahead of what we can see.
Lord, we confess that we often follow expertise and the majority and fail to hear what you say through unremarkable people; and often, to avoid a little inconvenience, we hand ourselves over to “the majority advised.” Forgive us that self that fears discomfort and will not take responsibility. Let the Holy Spirit be our guide, so that we still use our heads but do not rely on ourselves; still respect people, but leave the final decision to you. On the days the wind is contrary, keep us from suspecting your promise. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: When the south wind blew softly, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close to shore.
But before long, a stormy wind beat down from shore, which is called Euroclydon.
When the ship was caught and couldn’t face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along.
Running under the lee of a small island called Clauda, we were able, with difficulty, to secure the boat.
After they had hoisted it up, they used cables to help reinforce the ship. Fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis sand bars, they lowered the sea anchor, and so were driven along.
As we labored exceedingly with the storm, the next day they began to throw things overboard.
On the third day, they threw out the ship’s tackle with their own hands.
When neither sun nor stars shone on us for many days, and no small storm pressed on us, all hope that we would be saved was now taken away.
b: In the last devotion, a meeting was held in the harbor of Fair Havens. The experts said we could sail, the majority said wintering there was inconvenient, and one prisoner said lives would be lost; when the votes were counted, the prisoner lost.
With the decision made, all that remained was to wait for good weather. And good weather did come.
I. “When the south wind blew softly, supposing that they had obtained their purpose”—The Most Dangerous Wind Is the Tailwind That Confirms What I Wanted
Verse 13: “When the south wind blew softly, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close to the shore.”

From Fair Havens to Phoenix the course runs west and a little north, and a south wind is the ideal wind. The word “softly” is superbly chosen—neither strong nor weak, like a sentence of “you were right” sent by the weather itself for this decision. “Supposing that they had obtained their purpose” in the original is “thinking they had already reached their goal”; once the anchor was up, the ship hugged the coast and in a few hours would be there.

This is the most sobering verse in the whole chapter. When the mind has already made its decision and a small bit of smooth sailing appears, we read it as confirmation. But that breeze never said a word, from beginning to end; it was our self that spoke for it. The old self full of self is best at dubbing the circumstances: smooth sailing means God is with me, obstruction means Satan is attacking—there is only one standard, whether it fits what I want.

True guidance is not “whether things go smoothly” but “what his word says.” The Bible is my standard; this sentence matters more in a calm harbor than in a storm—a storm forces people to ask, but a gentle breeze lets them think there is no need.
• A tailwind is not confirmation: the soft south wind said nothing; it was my self that spoke for it.
• Ask when things are smooth: the decision I least want to pray about is often the one that most needs prayer.
II. “A tempestuous wind beat down from the island”—Euroclydon

Verses 14 and 15: “But not long after, a tempestuous wind beat down from it, which is called Euroclydon. When the ship was caught, and couldn’t face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along.”

“Not long after”—the south wind’s honeymoon was very short. In the middle of Crete stands Mount Ida, some twenty-four hundred meters high, and in autumn a northeast wind crossing the ridge can “beat down” from the mountain like a waterfall; sailors gave it a name, “Euroclydon”—a word combining east wind and north wind, meaning “northeaster”; “tempestuous wind” in the original is literally “typhoon.” The ship had been relying on the island for shelter, and now the wind came down from the island; the very protection had become the direction of the blow.

“The ship was caught”—“caught” is a word of seizing by force; “couldn’t face the wind” in the original is “could not look into the wind”—ancient ships had a pair of eyes painted on either side of the bow, and had to “look at” the wind to hold against it; now they could not even look. So they “gave way to it and were driven along.”

These three verbs are the three stages the proud sooner or later go through: thinking they can control things, discovering they cannot stand against them, and at last being at their mercy. Pride is leaving one’s place and trying to replace God; but people are not God, and one wind down from a mountain can turn “supposing they had obtained their purpose” into “driven along.”
• Protection can become the blow: if the island I lean on is not the Lord, it can at any moment become the place the wind comes from.
• “Could not face it” is the start of honesty: admitting I cannot hold out is not weakness; it is returning to my place.
III. “Using cables to undergird the ship”—They Did Everything People Could Do

Verses 16 and 17: The ship was driven under the lee of a small island called Cauda, a little piece of land about forty kilometers southwest of Crete, which gave a few hours of shelter. The sailors seized the pause to do three things.

First they “secured the boat”—the lifeboat towed behind the stern was already full of water, and hauling it aboard was managed only “with difficulty.” Then they “used cables to undergird the ship”—an emergency technique of ancient seafaring, passing heavy cables under the hull and binding them tight to keep the hull from splitting in the huge waves. Then they “lowered the gear,” so the ship would not be driven onto “the Syrtis”—the notorious quicksand off the coast of Libya in North Africa, where countless ships had vanished.

Notice Luke’s fairness: he does not write the sailors as incompetents. Every step they took was skilled, desperate and correct. God has never told people to throw up their hands in a storm; Paul himself later directed things all the way, telling people to eat and telling them not to flee. The difference lies in one thing only: whether these actions were doing one’s best, or proving one did not need God. The cables that undergird the hull can save the hull, but they cannot decide where the ship goes; the direction, from beginning to end, was not in human hands.
• Do your best but do not rely on your strength: leave nothing undone that should be done, but do not place the hope of salvation on my own methods.
• Tell what I can from what I cannot: what I can bind is the hull; what I cannot set is the direction.
IV. “They threw the cargo overboard”—The Storm Forces Out the True Order
Verses 18 and 19: “As we labored exceedingly with the storm, the next day they began to throw things overboard. On the third day, they threw out the ship’s tackle with their own hands.”

This was an Egyptian grain ship, its cargo wheat, the whole profit of the trip. On the second day they threw out the cargo first—to save their lives, money could go. The third day was harsher: with “their own hands” they threw out the ship’s tackle—probably the main yard and rigging, the very things that make a ship a ship. Luke specially writes “with their own hands”: this time it was not throwing out someone else’s cargo; it was dismantling their own ship.

A storm has a way of forcing, day by day, an order that people cannot make clear in ordinary times. A family wants everything in ordinary times—house, car, face, the child’s ranking; when real trouble comes, what is thrown out on the first day is what “was never necessary,” on the second day what “was thought necessary,” and what is left at last is what this family truly cannot do without.

Relationships matter more than things, people matter more than events—we all agree, yet in ordinary times our ordering is often exactly the reverse. Sometimes God allows a Euroclydon, not to destroy us, but to throw out what should be thrown out before the ship sinks.
• What can be thrown out was never the foundation: what can be tossed into the sea should never have been what I lean on.
• Set the order early: no need to wait for the storm to know what matters most; put it in its right place today.
V. “All hope that we would be saved was at last taken away”—The End of Despair
Verse 20: “Now when neither sun nor stars shone on us for many days, and no small storm pressed on us, all hope that we would be saved was at last taken away.”

The ancients had no compass; by day they fixed their position by the sun, by night by the stars; “for many days” without them meant they no longer knew where they were. “Was taken away” in the original is “was being removed”—even hope was being taken from them.
Notice that this verse has “we.” Luke counts himself in, and Paul was on this ship too. The Lord’s servant was not watching others despair from a distance; he was in the despair together with them.

Yet it is precisely this verse that brings the whole chapter to its turning point. In the next devotion Paul will “stand up in the midst of them” and say, “there will be no loss of life among you.” God’s word always shows itself as God’s word after human hope is gone; before that, people think they still have ways, and God’s promise is only one of many ways.

The last line of defense of the life full of self is “I still have a way.” Euroclydon pulled down even that. And this is exactly the entrance to self-denial—not that nothing is left, but that at last one can enter the hands of the Limitless One.
• Despair is not the end: when human ways are exhausted is when God’s word speaks.
• Not leaving those in the same boat: Luke says “we,” and Paul was on board; the Lord’s servant is not outside the storm.
321 Principles Insight: Humility Is Returning to Your Place
These eight verses record a failure, and also the whole course of pride and humility.

Pride is leaving one’s place—“supposing they had obtained their purpose,” thinking one has read the weather, seized the decision, and dubbed God’s voice. Humility is returning to one’s place—“couldn’t face the wind,” “driven along,” “hope was taken away,” step by step confessing: I am not God, I cannot set the direction, I do not even know where I am.

God gives grace to the humble and opposes the proud. It is not that God likes to see people despair, but that as long as a person’s hand still grips a cable of his own, he has no hand free to receive God’s word. The storm pries those hands open, one finger at a time; and after they are pried open, in the next devotion God’s angel stands on the ship. Let God be God, and let man be man.
a: Don’t dub the tailwind
Smooth sailing is not confirmation; his word is the standard.
Admit I cannot hold out
When I cannot stand, saying so honestly is the first step back to my place.
Do my best, not rely on my strength
Do all that should be done, yet know the direction is not in my hands.
Throw out what should go first
Don’t wait for the storm; put the order right today—life first, then relationship, then ministry.
Wait for him to speak in despair
Where hope ends is where he will speak.
q: Recall your most recent moment of “supposing you had obtained your purpose”: did the Lord truly speak in that soft south wind, or did your self speak for it? How do you tell the difference?
If a storm came to your home or your ministry today, what would you throw out on the first day? What on the third day? Is the one thing left at the end what you should put first today?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for writing this storm so honestly in the Bible, so that we see how a soft south wind confirmed the self of man, and how one wind down from a mountain tore that self down to nothing. We confess that we are often those who “supposed they had obtained their purpose,” taking smooth sailing as your presence and obstruction as the enemy’s doing, and seldom quieting ourselves to ask what your word says.
Lord, we too have a few cables of our own, binding the hull, thinking we can pull through by them. Teach us to do our best without relying on our strength, to do what should be done while placing the direction in your hands. If you allow a storm to come, let us throw out what should be thrown out on the first day, and in the moment hope is gone, still believe you will speak. Make us humble, returning to our place, letting you be God and us be human. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: When they had been long without food, Paul stood up in the middle of them, and said, “Sirs, you should have listened to me, and not have set sail from Crete and have gotten this injury and loss.
Now I exhort you to cheer up, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship.
For there stood by me this night an angel, belonging to the God whose I am and whom I serve,
saying, ‘Don’t be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar. Behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you.’
Therefore, sirs, cheer up! For I believe God, that it will be just as it has been spoken to me.
But we must run aground on a certain island.”
b: The last line of the previous devotion was the darkest in the whole chapter: “All hope that we would be saved was at last taken away.” Sun and stars had not shone for many days, the cargo was gone, the tackle was gone, and the ship was drifting toward the Syrtis.
With hope gone, human words had run out too. At that very moment, one man “stood up in the midst of them.”
I. “Paul stood up in the midst of them”—The Storm Brings the True Leader to the Surface

Verse 21: “When they had been long without food, Paul stood up in the midst of them.” “Long without food” was not a deliberate fast; it was seasickness, fear, no fire in a flooded galley, and food soaked ruined; everyone on the ship had hit bottom, in body and in mind.

The one who stood up was not the centurion, not the pilot, not the shipowner—but the prisoner who had been overruled at the council at Fair Havens. From verse 11, “gave more heed… than to those things which were spoken by Paul,” to verse 21, Paul “stood up in the midst of them,” ten days of storm had moved authority from expertise and the majority to a man who had a word before God.

When a plane hits severe turbulence, passengers do one thing: watch the flight attendants’ faces. If they are still calmly clearing the trays, everyone is reassured. People in a storm do not look at who has the higher rank; they look at whose face has peace. Paul’s was the only such face on the ship.

His first words were: “Sirs, you should have listened to me.” This was not the pleasure of settling old scores, but setting a proof in their hearts—what I said last time came true, so you can trust what I am about to say. A person’s past faithfulness becomes the weight of what he says today.
• Peace is the greatest authority: in a storm people do not look at rank; they look at whose face has the steadiness that comes from God.
• Faithfulness accumulates weight: speak and act by the Lord’s word in small things today, and tomorrow someone will be willing to listen.
II. “No life among you will be lost, but only the ship”—A Promise Has Boundaries
Verse 22: “Now I exhort you to cheer up, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship.”

“Cheer up” in the original is “take heart, have courage in the heart”—the same word the Lord Jesus used to the disciples on the sea: “Cheer up! It is I. Don’t be afraid” (Matthew 14:27). But Paul did not say “everything will be fine.” He spoke precisely: not one person lost, the ship gone.

This is how God’s promises always look—clear, solid, with boundaries. Of what he promises, not one word falls to the ground; what he has not promised, he does not pretend. What our self most wants to hear is “nothing will be lost,” but what God gives is “what should be kept is kept, what should be lost is lost.” Only one who learns to tell the two apart will not, when the ship sinks, think God’s word has sunk too.
• Know what God has said: don’t add my own expectations to his promise.
• The ship may be lost, but not the people: the order the Lord values should be my order too.
III. “The God whose I am and whom I serve”—He Knew Whose He Was
Verse 23: “For there stood by me this night an angel of the God whose I am and whom I serve.”

Paul introduced God in a special way: not “the God who made heaven and earth,” nor “the God of Israel,” but “the God whose I am and whom I serve.” “Whose I am”—I am his; “whom I serve”—I live for him. First belonging, then service; first relationship, then work.

Among the people on board were Roman soldiers, Egyptian sailors, prisoners from many places, each worshiping his own gods. Standing among them, Paul made his identity clear in one sentence: on the Roman record I belong to Caesar, on this ship I belong to Julius, but I, the man himself, belong to God.

This is exactly what letting Jesus be King means—not doing a bit more ministry, but first being clear whose I am. If a person has not first settled whom he belongs to, service turns into performance; once it is settled, service is a natural overflow. And the angel of God “stood by”—by one who knew whom he belonged to.
• First belonging, then service: relationship first, work after; life first, then ministry.
• Able to say it among people: can I naturally say “the God whose I am” in front of colleagues and people in the same boat?
IV. “Don’t be afraid… God has granted you”—One Person’s Self-Denial, Two Hundred Seventy-Six Saved
Verse 24 is the angel’s word: “Don’t be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar. Behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you.”

“Don’t be afraid”—this reveals that Paul was afraid too. The man standing on the ship saying “cheer up” had himself needed comfort the night before. The truly strong in the Bible are not those who do not fear, but those who, having feared, still commit themselves to God.
“You must stand before Caesar”—“must” is the “must” that recurs throughout Acts, God’s plan, not Paul’s luck. Since he must reach Rome, this ship cannot go down halfway.

“God has granted you all those who sail with you”—“granted” in the original is “freely given, bestowed as grace.” Two hundred seventy-six lives became God’s gift to Paul. This hints that in those dark nights Paul was not praying only for his own rescue; he prayed for everyone on the ship. And God’s answer was: because of you, I have kept them.

This is the seed form of God’s system: not an organizational chart, but a person who lets Jesus be King forming, wherever he is, a realm in which all in it are blessed. What a self-emptied person looks like is very concrete—in the storm, his prayer list has more than his own name.
• Afraid, yet still entrusting: being strong is not having no fear, but, having feared, still placing myself in his hands.
• Pray for those in the same boat: my family, my company, my group—that is the ship God wants to “grant” me today.
V. “I believe God… However we must run aground on a certain island”—Faith and Truth Together
Verses 25 and 26: “Therefore, sirs, cheer up! For I believe God, that it will be just as it has been spoken to me. But we must run aground on a certain island.”

This is one of the plainest definitions of “faith” in the Bible: as God has said, so I believe it will be. Not believing I have strength, not believing the circumstances will improve, but believing God’s word. The object of faith is not “things will be fine,” but “he has spoken.”

Yet Paul at once added a plain truth: “But we must run aground on a certain island.” He did not dress the promise up as smooth sailing, nor did he make light of the shipwreck. Those who trust God need not lie or call black white; faith is not denying the storm, but believing in the storm that his word is bigger than the storm.
The faith of the self chooses—picks the half of God’s word it likes; the faith of the self-emptied takes the whole sentence, including “run aground on a certain island.”
• Believe what he said, not what I think: faith’s foundation is his word, not my expectation.
• Faith need not lie: I can honestly admit the ship will hit the island while being sure not one person will be lost.
321 Principles Insight: The Bible Is My Standard—“As He Has Said, So I Believe”
The center of these six verses is verse 25: “I believe God, that it will be just as it has been spoken to me.”

“The Bible is my standard” is easy to say in ordinary days; only when the ship is about to sink do we know whether we have it. A standard means I measure circumstances by his word, not his word by circumstances. When sun and stars did not appear, Paul had no compass in his hand, only a sentence from the night before—and he stood up on that sentence.

And that sentence could hold because the speaker first stood in the right place: “the God whose I am and whom I serve.” Only one who lets Jesus be King can hear his word; having heard and believed, he becomes, among the despairing, a realm—a ship, a home, an office—where, because of him, God says, “I have granted them to you.” Self-denial is not shrinking; it is entering the limitless; to one who hands himself over, God hands two hundred seventy-six people.
a: Let my face have peace
In a storm people look not at my rank but at whether I have steadiness from God.
Know the promise’s boundaries
What God says he will keep, he keeps; don’t mix in my own expectations.
Settle first whose I am
I am his, and only then do I talk about service.
Pray for those in the same boat
Bring the names of family, colleagues and group into the prayer in the storm.
Believe the whole sentence
Receive also the half that says “run aground on a certain island.”
q: “The God whose I am and whom I serve”—if someone in your workplace or family asked you today, “Whose are you?”, how would you answer? Can your life show this belonging?

Paul prayed for everyone on the ship in the storm, and God said, “I have granted them to you.” In your prayers now, is there a list of “those in the same boat”? Write down three names and pray for them today.
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that on the night when all human hope was gone, your angel stood by Paul. Thank you for letting us see that your servant also feels fear, and that you said to him in his fear, “Don’t be afraid.” And thank you that your promises are always clear, solid and bounded—not one word you speak falls to the ground, and what you have not said, you do not pretend.
Lord, we confess that we often measure your word by circumstances instead of measuring circumstances by your word; we also often pick only the half of your word we like. Make us, like Paul, settle first whose we are—the God whom we belong to and serve is you. Let our faces have peace in the storm and our prayers carry the names of those in the same boat; grant us the ship we are in, that our homes, our work and our groups may be blessed because of one person who lets you be King. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: But when the fourteenth night had come, as we were driven back and forth in the Adriatic Sea, about midnight the sailors surmised that they were drawing near to some land.
They took soundings, and found twenty fathoms. After a little while, they took soundings again, and found fifteen fathoms.
Fearing that we would run aground on rocky ground, they let go four anchors from the stern, and wished for daylight.
As the sailors were trying to flee out of the ship, and had lowered the boat into the sea, pretending that they would lay out anchors from the bow,
Paul said to the centurion and to the soldiers, “Unless these stay in the ship, you can’t be saved.”
Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the boat, and let it fall off.
While the day was coming on, Paul begged them all to take some food, saying, “Today is the fourteenth day that you wait and continue fasting, having taken nothing.
Therefore I beg you to take some food; for this is for your safety; for not a hair will perish from any of your heads.”
When he had said this, and had taken bread, he gave thanks to God in the presence of all, then he broke it and began to eat.
Then they all cheered up, and they also took food.
In all, we were two hundred seventy-six souls on the ship.
When they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea.
b: In the last devotion, Paul stood among the despairing and told them what the angel had said the night before: not one life would be lost, but they must run aground on a certain island.

The word was spoken, yet the wind did not stop. From that night until the ship actually struck the island there were still several days. The stretch between promise and fulfillment is often the hardest road for faith.
I. “Hoping for daylight”—The Fourteenth Night, Four Anchors

Verse 27: “But when the fourteenth night had come, as we were driven back and forth in the Adriatic Sea…” In ancient times “the Adriatic” meant not only today’s Adriatic Sea but the whole stretch of the central Mediterranean between Crete, Sicily and North Africa. Counting from Cauda, it was the fourteenth day.

In the nineteenth century a navigator calculated from this chapter: a ship of this type drifting before a northeast gale makes about a knot and a half an hour, and from Cauda to Malta that takes just over thirteen days. What Luke wrote is not legend but a ship’s log.

At midnight, “the sailors surmised that they were drawing near to some land”—probably hearing the sound of waves on the shore. They cast the sounding lead: twenty fathoms, and again, fifteen fathoms. The water was getting shallower; ahead lay a rocky shore. So “they cast four anchors out of the stern, and wished for daylight.” Anchoring from the stern is highly unusual; it was the judgment of old sailors—with the anchors at the stern the bow keeps pointing at the shore, and at first light they could run straight onto the beach. “Wished for daylight” in the original is “prayed for daylight”; that night a crowd who worshiped all kinds of gods were praying for the same thing.

We have all lived through such nights: a hospital corridor, a sleepless hour before dawn, the hours waiting for a phone call. In such nights a person can do nothing but cast anchor and wait for day. Hebrews says we have hope “as an anchor of the soul, a hope both sure and steadfast” (Hebrews 6:19). An anchor does not make the ship go forward; it keeps the ship from being swept away in the darkest hour. Four anchors, one night of dark, one promise of “must.”
• Cast anchor, then wait: some nights you can do nothing but fix yourself on his word.
• Daylight is his business: I ask for daylight, but it is he who decides when it comes.
II. “Unless these stay in the ship, you cannot be saved”—A Promise Does Not Remove Responsibility

Verses 30 to 32: The sailors acted from selfish motives. They lowered the boat into the sea, “pretending that they would lay out anchors from the bow”—saying they were going to secure the anchors, when really they meant to escape in the boat. Once a ship has no sailors, two hundred some soldiers and prisoners who cannot handle a ship could not possibly run her onto the beach at daylight.
Paul saw through it: “Unless these stay in the ship, you cannot be saved.”

The angel had plainly said “God has granted you all those who sail with you”—so why could they not be saved if the sailors escaped? Because God’s promise was never meant to have people lie down and wait; the fulfillment of a promise usually passes through human obedience. God said “not one lost,” and so people must “stay in the ship”; the promise is his, the responsibility is mine, and the two do not conflict.

The faith of the self treats God’s promise as an exemption clause: “He promised anyway, so it makes no difference what I do.” The faith of the self-emptied is the opposite: precisely because he has promised, I must the more hold my place by his word. And this time the centurion listened to Paul—the soldiers “cut away the ropes of the boat, and let it fall off.” The retreat was gone, and for everyone on the ship only one road remained: be saved together, or sink together.
• A promise is not an exemption: he has said it will come to pass, and I must still “stay in the ship” and do what I should.
• Cut off the retreat: some decisions of faith are just letting go the little boat I had secretly kept.
III. “This is for your safety”—Eating Is Also Faith
Verses 33 and 34: As day was about to dawn, Paul did something very ordinary: he urged everyone to eat.

“Today is the fourteenth day that you wait and continue fasting, having taken nothing.” “Wait” in the original is “waiting in suspense”—this was not a religious fast; they were too frightened to eat. Paul said, “Therefore I encourage you to take some food, for this is for your safety.” “Safety” uses the very word for “saved”—eating bore on being saved. Because after daylight they would have to run aground, swim, and climb ashore, and a person who had not eaten for fourteen days could not do it.
Then he repeated the angel’s word, using an Old Testament saying: “For not a hair will perish from the head of any of you” (compare 1 Samuel 14:45; Luke 21:18).

When something big happens at home, there is often an elder who says, “Eat first, we’ll talk after.” When young, that sentence seems neither here nor there; when older, we understand it is the most practical faith—believing there is a tomorrow to live, so we must eat today. Being spiritual is not hanging in midair; it is eating a good meal inside the promise.
• Faith lands on the body: believe his word, then sleep well and eat well, and prepare for the road tomorrow.
• Don’t let anxiety replace prayer: waiting and fasting in suspense is not piety, it is fear; hand the fear over, and then you can eat.
IV. “He gave thanks to God in the presence of all, and he broke it and began to eat”—Giving Thanks in the Storm

Verses 35 to 37: “When he had said this, and had taken bread, he gave thanks to God in the presence of all; and he broke it and began to eat. Then they were all encouraged, and they also took food. In all we were two hundred seventy-six souls on the ship.”

“Took bread, gave thanks, broke”—these three verbs Luke used at the Last Supper (Luke 22:19) and at Emmaus (Luke 24:30). It does not say Paul was holding the Lord’s Supper on the ship, but that before a crowd of Gentiles he did what the Lord Jesus had done: took ordinary bread and gave thanks to God.

“In the presence of all”—he did not hide in a corner to pray silently. A shipload of people watched this prisoner give thanks, while the waves had not yet stopped, to the God he belonged to. And then “they were all encouraged, and they also took food.” One person’s thanks at a meal steadied two hundred seventy-six people.

The last stop on the road of service is “God—let Jesus be glorified, and give thanks in everything.” Giving thanks in everything looks most real not at a Thanksgiving gathering, but on the morning of the fourteenth day, with the ship breaking up and the shore not yet reached, and I still take the bread and say, “Lord, thank you.” Thanksgiving is not a reaction after things get better; it is a declaration that believes his word is already settled.
• Give thanks before others: let those around me see that the God I belong to is worth thanking in a storm.
• One person steadies many: when I eat a meal in peace, someone at home puts their heart at rest because of it.
V. “They threw out the wheat into the sea”—Faith Enough to Throw Away the Last Store
Verse 38: “When they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea.”

The wheat was the last cargo of this grain ship and also the last food on board. Fourteen days earlier they had thrown cargo overboard once; now even the wheat that served as ballast was all thrown out—the lighter the ship, the closer to the shore it could run.

This is an act of someone who truly believes “tomorrow we reach land.” If they still feared drifting a few more days at sea, no one would throw away the last food. They ate their fill, and then threw away all that was left.

Faith, when it goes far enough, often takes this step—throwing away the last bit of security so the ship will be a little lighter. Each person has a “bag of wheat” in hand: a sum of savings one dares not touch, a way of retreat kept in reserve, a relationship one will not let go. God does not necessarily ask us to throw it out, but when his word is clear and that bag of wheat is what makes the ship too heavy, throwing it out is faith.
• A lighter ship: do I have a bag of wheat in my hand that keeps me from reaching the shore?
• The mood of the last meal: eat your fill, give thanks, and then let go.
321 Principles Insight: Giving Thanks in Everything Is the Evidence of Letting Jesus Be King

In these twelve verses Paul did four things: saw through the sailors, urged people to eat, gave thanks in public, and led them in throwing away the grain. Not one was a miracle; each was the daily life of someone who lets Jesus be King, in a storm.

One who lets Jesus be King is not one who does nothing, but one who does everything by his word: he said not one would be lost, so the sailors could not leave; he said we will reach Rome, so today we eat; his word is already settled, so we give thanks now; his promise comes first, so the last wheat can be thrown away.

And at the center of all this is that meal of thanks in the presence of all. Giving thanks in everything is not an optimistic temperament; it is an acknowledgment of sovereignty: I give thanks because I know who is at the helm. A person who can take bread and give thanks in a storm—who sits on the throne of his heart, the whole ship has seen.
a: Cast anchor and wait for daylight
When there is nothing I can do in the dark, fix myself on his word.
Stay in the ship
The promise is his, the responsibility is mine; don’t treat his promise as an exemption clause.
Eat well
Faith lands on the body; hand over anxiety and prepare for the road tomorrow.
Give thanks in public
Let family and colleagues see whom I thank in the storm.
Throw away that bag of wheat
When his word is clear, let go of the security that makes the ship too heavy.
q: Is there something in your life now that you are “waiting and fasting” over—too frightened to eat or sleep, yet not truly entrusting it? What is one concrete thing you can do today: eat a good meal, or get a good night’s sleep?

What is the “bag of wheat” in your hand—a way of retreat kept in reserve, security you dare not touch, a relationship you will not let go? If the Lord’s word is already clear, are you willing to make the ship a little lighter?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that on the fourteenth night you let even a crowd who did not know you cast anchor and wait for daylight; thank you that your word, like an anchor of the soul, is sure and steadfast and holds us in the darkest hour. We thank you that your promise is not for us to lie down and wait, but for us to hold our place in your word.
Lord Jesus, teach us like Paul to take bread in the storm and give you thanks in the presence of all. We confess that we often wait and fast in suspense, replacing prayer with anxiety and your promise with the bag of wheat in our hands. Forgive us the heart that secretly keeps the little boat, and give us courage to cut the ropes; and let our families and colleagues put their hearts at rest because they see us eat a meal in peace. May you reign as King in our storm and receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: When it was day, they didn’t recognize the land, but they noticed a certain bay with a beach, and they decided to try to drive the ship onto it.
Casting off the anchors, they left them in the sea, at the same time untying the rudder ropes. Hoisting up the foresail to the wind, they made for the beach.
But coming to a place where two seas met, they ran the vessel aground. The bow struck and remained immovable, but the stern began to break up by the violence of the waves.
The soldiers’ counsel was to kill the prisoners, so that none of them would swim out and escape.
But the centurion, desiring to save Paul, stopped them from their purpose, and commanded that those who could swim should throw themselves overboard first to go toward the land;
and the rest should follow, some on planks, and some on other things from the ship. So they all escaped safely to the land.
b: In the last devotion, at dawn on the fourteenth night, Paul took bread in front of everyone and gave thanks to God. The two hundred seventy-six on board ate, and then threw the last of the wheat into the sea to lighten the ship.

The daylight they had prayed for came. But daylight is not the same as landfall. From seeing the shore to standing on it, there was still one stretch left, the shortest and most undignified of the whole chapter.
I. “Cast off the anchors and left them in the sea”—Last Night’s Lifesaver Must Be Let Go This Morning

Verses 39–40: “When it was day, they didn’t recognize the land, but they noticed a certain bay with a beach, and they took counsel whether they could drive the ship onto it.” Today the place is called St. Paul’s Bay, on the northeast of Malta. The sailors had crossed the whole Mediterranean, yet did not recognize this little bay, because grain ships did not normally come this way. What they saw was a beach, and “they took counsel whether they could drive the ship onto it.” Running aground was the last resort.

Once decided, they did three things. “Casting off the anchors, they left them in the sea”: the four anchors thrown from the stern the night before had held them steady all night, and now one cut severed them, to be left on the seabed. “Loosing the ropes of the rudders”: the two steering oars, tied up while at anchor, were dropped into the water to restore control. “Hoisting up the foresail to the wind”: the small sail at the bow went up, and “they made for the beach.”

Notice those four anchors. Last night they were a lifesaver; this morning they were an obstruction. If the anchors are not released, the ship will never reach the shore. What God gives us at one stage is often not meant to be held for a lifetime: an elder who led us, a way of serving that once worked well, a season of stability. A cast on a broken bone is a grace; but if the bone has healed and we refuse to take the cast off, the cast becomes the cause of the disability.
• Discern the season: last night’s anchor and this morning’s anchor are the same anchor; the difference is what his word says to do “now.”
• Letting go takes courage: the one who cuts the ropes trusts that the shore is more reliable than the anchor.
II. “A place where two seas met”—The Surprise on the Last Mile
Verse 41: “But lighting on a bay where two seas met, they ran the vessel aground. The bow struck and remained immovable, but the stern began to break up by the violence of the waves.”

“Where two seas met” in the original is literally “a place between two seas.” At the mouth of the bay lay a sandbar or reef where two currents collided, and the bottom was packed with thick clay. The moment the bow rammed in, it “remained immovable,” while the stern, exposed, was pulled apart by the waves one blow at a time. From the night the angel said, “only the ship will be lost,” this ship’s end had been settled; it simply broke up a few dozen yards from shore rather than in deep water.

This is the most discouraging kind of failure: not dying in the storm, but dying at the shore. The beach was already in sight, the sail already raised, and we were already thinking it was over, and then we hit a sandbar we could not see.

Yet it is exactly here that God’s promise is proved accurate. He never said the ship would come safely to shore; he said the ship would be lost and the people saved. The place where two seas met did not overturn the promise; it fulfilled it. We are often disappointed on the last mile because we read our own imagined “happy ending” into God’s word; when the real ending arrives, we find that he had only ever said that one sentence.
• Don’t write the ending for God: what he promised was the people, not the ship; the completeness I expect may not be what he ever said.
• Failure at the shore is still in his hands: a grounding a few dozen yards from land is still a step in his plan.
III. “The soldiers’ counsel was to kill the prisoners”—One Man Kept, a Whole Company Saved
Verses 42–43: “The soldiers’ counsel was to kill the prisoners, so that none of them should swim out and escape. But the centurion, desiring to save Paul, stopped them from their purpose.”

Under Roman military law, a guard who let a prisoner escape bore the prisoner’s penalty. Acts has already shown this fear twice: Herod put to death the guards who watched Peter (12:19), and the jailer at Philippi drew his sword to kill himself (16:27). So the soldiers’ proposal was perfectly “reasonable” in their world: the ship was breaking up, the prisoners would scatter the moment they hit the water, so better to kill them first and be done.

The moment Paul came closest to death was not the storm but this sentence. Fourteen days of storm could not take his life, yet a single decision by the soldiers on the same ship could have. But “the centurion, desiring to save Paul.” From Julius’s kindness at Sidon, through his unbelief at Fair Havens, to his obeying when the lifeboat was cut away, he had come all this way, and the one he wanted to save was Paul. And in order to save Paul he “stopped them from their purpose,” so not one prisoner on the ship died.

When one person is kept by God, those around him live. This is what the Lord meant by “You are the salt of the earth”: salt does not exist for itself. What a self-denied person looks like among a crowd is very concrete: it is not that he receives the most, but that because he is there, the fate of the whole company is rewritten. The angel’s words, “God has granted you all those who sail with you,” are now fulfilled through the hand of a Gentile officer.
• Be that person: don’t ask for special treatment; ask that the place where I am be preserved because of me.
• God also uses unbelievers: Julius did not know God, yet God fulfilled his promise through his hand.
IV. “On planks, and some on other things from the ship”—A Promise Fulfilled in Pieces

Verses 43–44: the centurion “commanded that those who could swim should throw themselves overboard first to go toward the land, and the rest should follow, some on planks, and some on other things from the ship. So it happened that they all escaped safely to the land.”

When we read “they all escaped safely,” we may imagine a glorious scene. The actual scene: those who could swim jumped first, and those who could not clung to a plank, a broken mast, a piece of hatch cover, and thrashed ashore through the surf. Two hundred seventy-six people, soaked, shaking, empty-handed, sprawled on the beach of an island whose name they did not know.

This is how God fulfills his promise. “Not one of you will be lost”: not one word was wrong. But the way it was fulfilled was in pieces. Nobody stepped off a whole ship onto the shore with dignity; everyone held on to a fragment.

What we expect from God is often “a whole ship”: if he is going to save me, he should settle things beautifully. But the end of Acts shows us that God’s faithfulness can be fulfilled with a plank of wood, and his promise does not need a whole ship. The plank you are holding right now, that imperfect job, that relationship barely hanging on, that body that has not been healed but can still live, may be exactly the way God is bringing you ashore.
• You can reach shore holding fragments: don’t wait for a whole ship; the plank he gives is enough.
• Count heads once you are ashore: all were saved, not one missing; his word came true.
321 Principle Light: The Holy Spirit’s Leading Includes Letting Go and Holding Fragments

In these six verses people did several things they had never been willing to do before: cut away the anchors that saved them last night, let the ship break up on the shore, an officer stopped his own soldiers for the sake of one prisoner, and a whole shipload reached land clinging to fragments. Each was undignified, and each was a step toward being saved.

The most practical meaning of “the Holy Spirit is my guide” is that he says different things at different stages: last night, “Drop anchor and wait for daylight”; this morning, “Cut the ropes.” The person full of self hears only the sentence he is used to and clings to last night’s anchor. The self-denied person listens for what he is saying now, so he waits when it is time to wait and lets go when it is time to let go.

And letting Jesus have the glory, in this passage, is not a miracle but an accurate word coming true: “There will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship.” He did not give a whole ship; he gave two hundred seventy-six whole lives. Only when we see this can we give thanks to him over our own fragments.
a: Cut last night’s anchor
If what he once used to hold me up has become an obstruction, let go according to his word now.
Don’t write his ending
The completeness I imagine may not be what he promised.
Be the one who is kept
Not asking for special treatment, but that where I am be blessed because of me.
Accept unbelievers as vessels
God used Julius’s hand to save Paul; he may use people I don’t know to help me.
Hold the fragments and come ashore
Not waiting for a whole ship; the plank he gives is enough.
q: Is there a “last night’s anchor” in your life, something God once used to steady you, which now keeps you from reaching the shore? Is he telling you today to “wait,” or to “cut it loose”?
Which “plank” are you holding right now? Are you complaining that it is not a whole ship, or can you see that it is exactly how God is bringing you ashore?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that not one word of yours has fallen to the ground: the ship was lost, and not one person was missing. Thank you for letting us see that the way you fulfill your promises is not always dignified: a cut anchor, a shattered ship, plank after plank. Yet all were brought safely to land.
Lord, we confess that we often cling to last night’s anchor and will not let go, that we often read our own imagined completeness into your promises, and that we often complain to you because we received only a fragment. Holy Spirit, lead us to discern the season, to wait when it is time to wait and to let go when it is time to let go. Make us the one who is kept, so that our homes, our workplaces and our groups are preserved because we are there. Teach us to hold on to the plank you have given and to come ashore with thanksgiving. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: When we had escaped, then they learned that the island was called Malta.
The natives showed us uncommon kindness; for they kindled a fire and received us all, because of the present rain and because of the cold.
But when Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and laid them on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat, and fastened on his hand.
When the natives saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, “No doubt this man is a murderer, whom, though he has escaped from the sea, yet Justice has not allowed to live.”
However he shook off the creature into the fire, and wasn’t harmed.

But they expected that he would have swollen or fallen down dead suddenly, but when they watched for a long time and saw nothing bad happen to him, they changed their minds, and said that he was a god.
