Now in the neighborhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius, who received us, and courteously entertained us for three days.
The father of Publius lay sick of fever and dysentery. Paul entered in to him, prayed, and laying his hands on him, healed him.
Then when this was done, the rest also who had diseases in the island came and were cured.
They also honored us with many honors, and when we sailed, they put on board the things that we needed.
b: In the last devotion, the ship broke up where two seas met, and two hundred seventy-six people reached land on planks and bits of wreckage, not one missing.
Soaked, shaking and empty-handed, sprawled on the sand, they finally thought to ask one question: where are we?
I. “The natives showed us uncommon kindness”—The First Gift on Shore Was a Stranger’s Kindness

Verses 1–2: “When we had escaped, then we learned that the island was called Malta.” Malta lies south of Sicily; the name given by the ancient Phoenicians means “refuge.” A company that had drifted fourteen days was blown onto an island called “Refuge”: God’s humor, and God’s precision.

“Natives” in the original is “speakers of a foreign tongue,” meaning islanders who did not speak Greek but a Phoenician-family dialect. Luke says they showed “uncommon kindness,” using the same root as the “kindly” with which Julius treated Paul in chapter 27, verse 3, meaning “love for people.” It was November, rainy and cold, and the islanders lit a fire for over two hundred strangers in distress.

The first experience after being saved was not a sermon or a miracle, but being treated kindly by people who did not know God. God’s grace does not come only from within the church. He also uses people who have never heard his name to build a fire on a rainy day for his servants. A person who has learned thankfulness will recognize this as the Lord’s hand too.
• Recognize a stranger’s kindness as the Lord’s hand: it is not only brothers and sisters who can be God’s provision.
• Be willing to be helped in distress: even an apostle needed a fire; those who refuse help are often proud.
II. “Paul gathered a bundle of sticks”—Even an Apostle Gathers Firewood
The first half of verse 3: “But when Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and laid them on the fire.”

This line is easily skipped, but it should not be. This man was the apostle to the Gentiles, who had just taken command of the whole ship, given thanks before everyone, and been visited by an angel. Yet the first thing he did when he came ashore was gather sticks. No one told him to, and no one knew who he was. The fire needed wood, so he went and got it.

Humility is not an attitude; it is an action. Here it looks like this: hands that had just held bread and given thanks to God went to gather wet, cold branches. What shows a person’s life in the church is often not on the platform but in who stacks the chairs, washes the cups and turns off the lights after the meeting. A person who gathers sticks when no one is watching gives weight to what he says on the platform.
• Do it without being told: the fire needs wood, so when I see it I go and gather it; this is what self-denial looks like in daily life.
• A calling does not exempt me from small things: if an apostle gathers sticks, I have even less reason to feel that some things are “not for me.”
III. “Fastened on his hand”—The Storm Passed, and the Snake Came

The second half of verse 3 through verse 5: “a viper came out because of the heat, and fastened on his hand.” A dormant snake was hidden in that bundle; the heat woke it, and it “hung from his hand,” not a mere touch but a bite that held on. “However he shook off the creature into the fire, and wasn’t harmed.”

This is a very real spiritual pattern: after the big storm passes, the small attacks come. Fourteen days of Euroclydon did not take his life, the soldiers’ swords at the shore did not take his life, and what nearly took his life was a snake in a bundle of sticks. The person who stayed alert through the big events is often bitten by a small one in the moment after being saved, when he lets out a sigh of relief.

Paul’s reaction was to shake it off. He did not panic, did not analyze where the snake came from, did not ask “why me?” He shook it into the fire and went on with what was in his hands. The Lord Jesus promised, “Behold, I give you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions” (Luke 10:19). This authority is not for going out looking for snakes, but for not being pinned down when a snake bites.
• Stay alert after being saved: when the big storm has passed, don’t be bitten by a small thing.
• Learn to “shake it off”: not every attack deserves analysis; some should simply be flung into the fire so you can keep gathering sticks.
IV. “A murderer” and “a god”—Others’ Verdicts Can Flip Twice in One Day

Verses 4 and 6 record two verdicts from the same crowd within a few hours. First: “No doubt this man is a murderer, whom, escaping from the sea, Justice has not allowed to live.” “Justice” in the original is Dike, the goddess of justice in Greek mythology; in their thinking, whoever the sea spared, the goddess of justice would not. Then, “after they watched him for a long time, and saw nothing bad happen to him, they changed their minds, and said that he was a god.”

From murderer to god: the same hands, the same snake, with only “a long time of watching” in between. The people of Lystra did the same: first they wanted to sacrifice to Paul, then they stoned him (14:11–19). Here the order is simply reversed.

Our world today moves faster. An online comment is scolded in the morning, praised in the afternoon and scolded again in the evening. A person who stakes his worth on others’ opinions dies several times a day. Focus on Jesus, not on myself, not on others, not on circumstances: on the beach at Malta this means, they say I am a murderer, and I keep gathering sticks; they say I am a god, and I keep gathering sticks. Because who I am is settled by the God I belong to and serve, not by the onlookers.
• Not crushed by blame, not lifted up by praise: neither verdict is the source of my identity.
• Throw the glory back: when people say “he is a god,” the one who lets Jesus have the glory knows it is not his.
V. “Paul entered in to him, prayed, and laying his hands on him”—A Prisoner Became a Blessing to the Whole Island

Verses 7–10: “Near that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius.” “Chief man” in the original is “first man of the island,” a title that inscriptions found by archaeologists on Malta use exactly, confirming Luke’s precision. Publius “entertained us courteously for three days,” while his father “lay sick of fever and dysentery.” Luke uses the language of a physician for the illness; Malta fever was a well-known contagious disease on the island.

Paul “entered in to him, prayed, and laying his hands on him, healed him.” The order of the three actions is worth noting: first prayer, then laying on of hands, then healing. Prayer comes first, placing the matter in the Lord’s hands and settling who will receive the glory, and only then does he stretch out his hands. “The rest also who had diseases in the island came, and were cured.” A prisoner in distress became a blessing to the whole island within three months.

In the last devotion we said that when one person is kept, a whole company lives. Here we go one step further: where one person lets Jesus be King, a whole island is blessed. This is the building of God’s system. It is not that Paul built an organization on Malta; the place where he was became a realm where God reigned. The islanders “honored us with many honors,” and when they sailed, “put on board the things that we needed.” They came ashore empty-handed and left fully loaded. God never owes his servants anything.
• Pray first, then stretch out your hand: settle who gets the glory, and only then act.
• Let the place where I am become a realm: not to build an organization, but to let Jesus be King on the island where I am.
321 Principle Light: Focus on Jesus, Not on Others’ Opinions

The ten verses at Malta draw a complete picture of a self-denied person in a strange place: when treated kindly, he accepts it; when the fire needs wood, he gathers it; when the snake bites, he shakes it off; when people call him a murderer, he does not defend himself; when they call him a god, he does not accept it; when someone is ill, he prays first and then lays on hands; and when he leaves, his hands are full.

From beginning to end, not for a moment did he put the focus on himself: he did not ask “how did I end up here?” and did not ask “what do they think of me?” When the focus is on Jesus, a person is free: free to gather sticks and free to lay hands and heal the sick. The two are the same to him, because neither is done for himself.

A proud person is bound by evaluation: scolded, he is hurt; praised, he swells. A self-denied person, like Paul shaking off that snake, shakes off “murderer” and shakes off “he is a god,” and leaves the glory with the One who deserves it. To such a person God can safely entrust an island.
a: Accept the stranger’s fire
Be willing to be helped in distress, and recognize it as the Lord’s hand.
Go gather firewood
The small things nobody assigns: do them when I see them.
Shake off the snake
Stay alert after being saved; don’t analyze small attacks, but fling them into the fire and keep going.
Don’t live by evaluation
Not crushed by blame, not lifted by praise; who I am is settled by him.
Pray first, then stretch out my hand
Settle to whom the glory belongs, and then act.
q: The last time someone praised you, and the last time someone misunderstood you, how long did it take your heart to settle each time? What does that say about where your focus is right now?
On the “island” where you are today, at home, at work, in your group, is there a bundle of sticks no one has gathered? Are you willing to gather it without being told and without anyone seeing?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for blowing a company of drifting people onto an island called “Refuge,” and for using islanders who did not know you to light a fire on a rainy day for your servants. Your grace comes from every direction; give us eyes that can recognize it.
Lord, we confess that we often relax after a big storm and get bitten by a small snake, and that we often place our worth in others’ words, falling down when scolded and floating up when praised. Give us Paul’s hands: hands that gather sticks, hands that shake off the snake, hands that lay themselves on others only after prayer. Keep our focus only on you, so that on the island where each of us is, we may be people who let you be King, and let all the glory go to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: After three months, we set sail in a ship of Alexandria which had wintered in the island, whose sign was “The Twin Brothers.”
Touching at Syracuse, we stayed there three days.
From there we circled around and arrived at Rhegium. After one day, a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli,
where we found brothers, and were entreated to stay with them for seven days. So we came to Rome.
From there the brothers, when they heard of us, came to meet us as far as The Market of Appius and The Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage.
When we entered into Rome, the centurion delivered the prisoners to the captain of the guard, but Paul was allowed to stay by himself with the soldier who guarded him.
b: In the last devotion, the islanders of Malta lit a fire for people in distress, and Paul gathered sticks, shook off the snake and laid hands on the chief’s father to heal him. A prisoner became a blessing to the whole island. A winter of three months passed in this way.
Spring came and the sea opened. In this devotion, Luke takes six verses to bring Paul into the city of Rome.
I. “Whose figurehead was ‘The Twin Brothers’”—God Also Uses a Ship Flying an Idol’s Banner
Verse 11: “After three months, we set sail in a ship of Alexandria which had wintered at the island, whose figurehead was ‘The Twin Brothers.’”

It was another Alexandrian grain ship, which had put in to winter one step ahead of them and so was undamaged. “The Twin Brothers” are Castor and Pollux, the twin sons of Zeus in Greek mythology and patron gods of sailors; their images were carved on the bow, and it was said that when the twin stars appeared in a storm it was a good omen.

Luke took care to record this mark. The ship that carried the apostle to the Gentiles to Rome bore an idol. Paul did not refuse to board, and did not demand that the figures on the bow be sawn off first. He knew those two wooden images could save no one, but God could use this ship.

We often refuse to use methods that are “not spiritual enough.” But God used an unbelieving centurion, idol-worshiping islanders and a ship with twin gods on its bow to carry his servant to Rome. He does not need everything to be clean before he works; he is Lord, and even an idol’s ship is under his command.
• Don’t despise God’s instruments: what carries me to my destination may not be the one that looks right to me.
• Be clear who is saving me: board the ship, but know in my heart that the figure on the bow is not what I rely on.
II. “There we found brothers”—Every Port Has Family

Verses 12–14a: the ship sailed north from Malta and put in at Syracuse in Sicily for three days; then they “circled around,” probably tacking against the wind, to Rhegium at the toe of the Italian peninsula; and when the south wind rose, they reached Puteoli on the Bay of Naples the next day. Puteoli was then the largest port in Italy, where Egyptian grain ships unloaded, and Rome was still over a hundred miles away by land.

“There we found brothers.” There was already a church in Puteoli. No apostle had founded it; probably merchants and sailors had brought the gospel. Paul had never been to Italy in his life, yet at the first port he found family, who “begged us to stay with them for seven days.” Julius was kind once more, letting the prisoner spend a Lord’s Day with the brothers.

This is a quiet but enormous fact in Acts: the gospel travels faster than the apostles. Everywhere Paul went, he often found that the Lord had already been there. God’s system is not an organization Paul built; it is the realm formed by people the Lord raises up everywhere who let Jesus be King. People in this realm have a home wherever they go.
• The Lord goes ahead of me: in a new city or a new stage, he has already prepared people there.
• Be a port for others: in the place where I am, can a passing brother stay seven days?
III. “And so we came to Rome”—The Letter Written Three Years Ago, and the Man Finally Arrives
The second half of verse 14: Luke writes the high point of the whole book in the plainest words: “So we came to Rome.”

The word “so” gathers in an entire chapter of storm, shipwreck, snakebite and a three-month winter. Three years earlier, in Corinth, Paul had written the letter to the Romans: “I often planned to come to you” (Romans 1:13) and “I hope to see you in my journey” (Romans 15:24). What he planned was to pass through Rome on the way to Spain. What he had not planned was to arrive as a prisoner, on a grain ship, clinging to a plank, after a winter in Malta. The letter arrived three years before the man, and when the man arrived, he looked nothing like what the letter described.

The Lord’s promise in the barracks (23:11) was right in every word: Paul reached Rome. But the route, the status and the timing were none of his own arranging. The destination God promises will be reached, but the way is almost never the kind we designed. The person full of self is still angry about the route after arriving; the self-denied person has only thanks left.
• The destination is his, and the route is his: what he promised was “Rome,” not “Rome by my plan.”
• Don’t complain about the route: once arrived, give thanks, and stop going over old accounts.
IV. “Paul thanked God and took courage”—Even an Apostle Needs Someone to Meet Him
Verse 15: “From there, the brothers, when they heard of us, came to meet us as far as The Market of Appius and The Three Taverns.”

The Market of Appius was about forty-three miles from Rome, and The Three Taverns about thirty-three, both on the Appian Way. When the brothers in Rome heard Paul had come, they went out of the city in two groups to meet him, walking more than a day to meet a prisoner. “To meet” is the word used when the people of a city went out to receive a king or a distinguished guest (compare 1 Thessalonians 4:17). The church in Rome received an apostle in chains the way one receives a king.
Then Luke writes: “When Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage.”

“Took courage” in the original is “received courage,” which means that before this, Paul had needed courage. On the ship he had calmed two hundred seventy-six people, and on the island he had healed the island’s sick; yet walking the road to Rome in chains, about to face Caesar, even this man had a sinking heart. And the way God gave him courage was not a vision or an angel, but a group of brothers who walked forty miles to meet him.

Anyone who has come home from abroad and seen someone at the airport exit holding a sign knows how that moment feels. People matter more than things: what God most often uses to strengthen people is people.
• Even an apostle needs to be met: don’t think spiritual people don’t need others; even Paul took courage when he saw the brothers.
• Walk forty miles to meet someone: is there anyone today waiting for me to go out and meet him?
V. “With the soldier who guarded him”—Freedom Within Chains
Verse 16: “When we entered into Rome, Paul was allowed to stay by himself with the soldier who guarded him.”

This was Rome’s “light custody”: the prisoner rented lodgings and lived there, guarded day and night by one soldier, chained to him at the wrist. Paul later called himself “an ambassador in chains” (Ephesians 6:20), and this is that chain. The guards changed every few hours, so soldiers of the Praetorian Guard were chained one after another beside this apostle, hearing him pray, preach and dictate letters. Later Paul said, “My bonds in Christ became evident to the whole praetorian guard” (Philippians 1:13).

One chain, a man at each end. From Rome’s point of view, the soldier was guarding Paul; from heaven’s point of view, Paul was shepherding the soldier. Freedom has never meant “no chains,” but “whether or not there are chains, I am doing what the Lord wants me to do.” A person who lets Jesus be King may have his hands bound by the chain, but the chain cannot bind the One he belongs to and serves.
• Chains limit the range, not the mission: what the Lord wants me to do can be done within any range.
• The people chained beside me: those whom circumstances force to be with me day and night are the harvest field God has given.
321 Principle Light: Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry

There is no sermon and no miracle in these six verses, yet Luke records that the brothers in Puteoli kept them for seven days and the brothers in Rome walked forty miles to meet them. On the page before the high point of the whole book, Luke shows us not ministry but relationships.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry: this is exactly the order in which Paul entered Rome. His life had been made plain in the storm and on the island; before entering Rome, the Lord first strengthened his heart through the brothers; and then, in the next devotion, he began to preach in Rome. Had the order been reversed, rushing into ministry first, a person would collapse on the road to Rome.

And the unexpected road between the letter of three years ago and the man three years later is exactly a lesson in the three foundations: Jesus is the example, since he did not enter Jerusalem by people’s script either; the Bible is the standard, since “you must bear witness at Rome” was right in every word; the Holy Spirit is the guide, since the route is his to arrange. The self-denied person accepts this route, so on arrival he has only thanksgiving and courage.
a: Board that ship
Not refusing God’s arrangement because the instrument is not spiritual enough, but being clear who is saving me.
Believe the Lord goes ahead
In a new place, he has already prepared brothers.
Don’t complain about the route
Give thanks on arrival; what he promised was the destination, not my itinerary.
Go meet someone
Today go out and strengthen a brother who is walking a hard road.
Shepherd the one chained beside me
I can’t choose my circumstances, but the person chained beside me is a harvest field.
q: Look back over the road you have walked. Is there a “Rome” God promised that you reached in a way you never imagined? Now that you have arrived, are you thankful, or still complaining about the route?

“When Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage.” Is there a brother or sister beside you right now walking a hard road who needs you to walk some distance to meet them? What is one thing you can do today?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that what you said in the barracks came true: Paul reached Rome. Thank you for using a ship with an idol on its bow, a Gentile centurion and the Appian Way to bring your servant to his destination, and thank you for strengthening his heart with the faces of the brothers before he had spoken a word of preaching.
Lord, we confess that we are often angry with you over the route: we have reached the place you promised, yet we still quarrel over why you did not follow our plan. Remove from us the self that insists on arranging its own itinerary, so that on arrival we have only thanks left. Make us brothers who walk forty miles to meet someone, and ports where a passing traveler can stay seven days; and within each of our own chains, let us shepherd those chained beside us. May you reign in Rome, and may you reign in our cities. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: After three days Paul called together those who were the leaders of the Jews. When they had come together, he said to them, “I, brothers, though I had done nothing against the people or the customs of our fathers, still was delivered prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans,
who, when they had examined me, desired to set me free, because there was no cause of death in me.
But when the Jews spoke against it, I was constrained to appeal to Caesar, not that I had anything about which to accuse my nation.
For this cause therefore I asked to see you and to speak with you. For because of the hope of Israel I am bound with this chain.”
They said to him, “We neither received letters from Judea concerning you, nor did any of the brothers come here and report or speak any evil of you.
But we desire to hear from you what you think. For, as concerning this sect, it is known to us that everywhere it is spoken against.”
b: In the last devotion, the brothers walked forty miles to the Market of Appius and The Three Taverns to meet Paul. He thanked God and took courage, entered Rome, and stayed by himself with the soldier who guarded him.
Arrived at last. It was nearly half a year since Caesarea, and almost five years since his arrest in Jerusalem. What is the first thing a person does on reaching his destination?
I. “After three days, Paul called together those who were the leaders of the Jews”—The First Thing Was Still to Go to the Jews First
The first part of verse 17: “After three days, Paul called together those who were the leaders of the Jews.”

Only three days. Settling into his lodging, handling the chain arrangements and letting his body recover from half a year adrift took three days, no more. Paul could not go to the synagogue, for the chain did not allow it; so he invited people to come. Rome’s Jewish community was large, with a dozen or more synagogues in the city. Ten years earlier Claudius had expelled all the Jews from Rome (18:2); now they were back, and the synagogue leaders were the people Paul invited.

Why did he invite the Jews first? For thirty years it had been the same in every city: first the synagogue, and only after being rejected did he turn to the Gentiles. In the letter he wrote to this city he also said the gospel was “to the Jew first, and also to the Greek” (Romans 1:16). The Jews had taken him to court before Caesar; yet when he reached Caesar’s city, the first thing he did was still to invite the Jews to hear the gospel.

This is an order that does not change. The self changes its order when it has been hurt: “Since they treated me this way, I need not bother with them anymore.” For the self-denied person, the order is decided not by the injury but by the Lord.
• Begin on arrival: no need to wait until everything is settled; three days is enough.
• Don’t change the order because of a wound: do what the Lord set, even if the other person once hurt me.
II. “Not that I had anything about which to accuse my nation”—Five Years of Injustice, and Not One Complaint
From the second half of verse 17 through verse 19, Paul told the whole five-year story. Notice how he told it.

“Brothers”: the very first word, he called a group who might be hostile to him brothers. “Though I had done nothing against the people, or the customs of our fathers”: this was fact, for in five years no court had convicted him. “Yet I was delivered prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans”: the passive voice, naming no one. “When they had examined me, they wanted to release me”: Felix, Festus and Agrippa, three judges in turn, all said he was innocent. “But when the Jews spoke against it, I was constrained to appeal to Caesar”: “constrained,” he presented the appeal as forced on him, not as a move against anyone.
Then comes that sentence: “Not that I had anything about which to accuse my nation.”

He had so much he could have accused them of: more than forty men had sworn to kill him (23:12), the high priest had come to Caesarea with a lawyer to slander him (24:1), he had been held two years for no reason, and now he had been brought in chains to the capital of the empire. Anyone telling these five years would have reason to tell them as a history of victimhood. Paul said, I am not accusing anyone.

How a person talks about his own experience shows who is king inside him. The self-full person says “how they harmed me,” and by the end even he can hear that he is pleading his own case. The self-denied person states the facts and then lays down the right to accuse. This is not Paul’s generosity; he knew that the God he belongs to and serves would examine, and he need not do it himself.
• Tell what happened without accusing: state the facts, but return the right to “accuse” to God.
• Call those who hurt me brothers: the first word decides the direction of the whole speech.
III. “For the sake of the hope of Israel I am bound with this chain”—The Chain Is the Sign of the Hope
Verse 20: “For this cause therefore I asked to see you and to speak with you, for because of the hope of Israel I am bound with this chain.”

“The hope of Israel”: this phrase appears three times in Paul’s defense. Before the Council it was “the hope and resurrection of the dead” (23:6); before Felix it was the hope that “there will be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust” (24:15); before Agrippa it was “the promise made by God to our fathers” (26:6–7). Israel’s thousand-year hope was that the Messiah would come, the dead would rise and God’s kingdom would arrive. And Paul said this hope had been fulfilled: Jesus is the one, and he has risen from the dead. It was for this that he was bound.

“This chain”: we can imagine him lifting his hand as he spoke, and the chain joined to the soldier’s wrist clinking with it. He did not hide the chain, and did not treat it as shameful; the chain became his calling card: why am I here? For the hope you too are waiting for.

Each of us has some “chain” too: a situation that cannot change, a weakness we have carried a long time, a relationship we did not choose. The self sees that chain and sees shame and limitation. The one who lets Jesus be King looks at the chain and asks: can this chain become an entry point for speaking of the hope?
• Lift up the chain: don’t cover my situation, but let it become the starting point of my testimony.
• Speak the hope aloud: I am here not because of bad luck but because of the One I hope in.
IV. “This sect is spoken against everywhere”—Slandered, Yet Heard
Verses 21–22: the Jewish leaders’ answer was honest: “We neither received letters from Judea concerning you, nor did any of the brothers come here and report or speak any evil of you.”

This is rather intriguing. Perhaps because the sea was closed in winter, the letters from Jerusalem had not yet arrived; or perhaps the Sanhedrin knew the case could not be won in Rome and gave up. Either way, the result was that before the Jews of Rome, Paul was a blank page. Five years of accusations, and not one letter had followed him to the center of the empire.

Then they said: “But we desire to hear from you what you think; for as concerning this sect, it is known to us that everywhere it is spoken against.” “Sect” in the original is “party,” and “spoken against everywhere” describes the ordinary impression of the Christian faith in the AD 60s: a small sect that provoked opposition wherever it went. All they had heard was bad, yet they were willing to listen.

This gives us a two-sided reminder. On one side, the gospel has been “spoken against everywhere” from the first day; being misunderstood and smeared is not evidence that we have done wrong, for the Lord himself said, “Blessed are you when people reproach you” (Matthew 5:11). On the other side, precisely because of the slander, my life becomes the only sample the other person can examine. The Jews of Rome had heard only rumors, and this man in chains was the first they saw with their own eyes.
• Don’t fear slander: it has been so from the first day, and it is not proof that I did wrong.
• Be the sample that can be examined: what they have heard is rumor; what they see with their own eyes is me.
321 Principle Light: The Self-Denied Person Does Not Speak of His Own Experience for His Own Sake
There is no miracle in these six verses, only a conversation. Yet that conversation shines a bright light on the inside of a person who lets Jesus be King.

Five years of injustice, told, and he accused no one; the chain, lifted, not to win sympathy but to point to Israel’s hope. He spoke of his own experience, yet the focus was not on himself but on Jesus. This is what self-denial means: not never speaking of yourself, but, when you speak of yourself, the main character is still him.

The proud person pleads his own case because he has left his place and seized the right of judgment into his own hands; the humble person returns to his place, hands the right of accusation back to God, and takes care only to make the hope clear. Today this is very concrete. When I talk at the dinner table about the person who wronged me, am I telling how he harmed me, or how the Lord led me? When I finish, do the listeners remember my wound, or my Lord?
a: Begin within three days
On reaching a new situation, don’t wait until settled; first do the one thing the Lord wants me to do.
Don’t change the order because of a wound
The order the Lord set is not decided by who has hurt me.
Tell what happened without accusing
State the facts and return the right to “accuse” to God.
Lift up my chain
Don’t hide my situation; let it become an entry point for speaking of hope.
Be a sample that can be examined
What people have heard is rumor; my life is the part they see with their own eyes.
q: Think of something that still feels unjust to you. If you told it at the dinner table today, would the listeners remember your wound or your Lord? Are you willing to practice telling it again in Paul’s way?
What “chain” do you have, a situation or weakness that cannot be changed, that you have kept hidden? Could it become an entry point for you to speak of hope to others?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that Paul reached Rome and, three days later, began doing what you wanted him to do. Thank you for letting us see that a person can tell five years of injustice without accusing anyone, only lifting up his chain and pointing to you.
Lord, we confess that when we speak of our own experience, the main character is often ourselves; we seize the right of judgment into our own hands and plead our own case in our hearts again and again. Remove from us the self that insists on vindicating itself, bring us back to our place, and let us return the right to “accuse” to you. Keep us from fearing slander, and make our lives samples that others can examine; make every chain on us an entry point for speaking of hope. May you reign in our grievances, and may you receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

v: When they had appointed him a day, many people came to him at his lodging. He explained to them, testifying about God’s Kingdom, and persuading them concerning Jesus, both from the law of Moses and from the prophets, from morning until evening.
Some believed the things which were spoken, and some disbelieved.
When they didn’t agree among themselves, they departed after Paul had spoken one word, “The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through Isaiah the prophet to our fathers,
saying, ‘Go to this people and say, in hearing, you will hear, but will in no way understand. In seeing, you will see, but will in no way perceive.

For this people’s heart has grown callous. Their ears are dull of hearing. Their eyes they have closed. Lest they should see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and would turn again, then I would heal them.’
“Be it known therefore to you, that the salvation of God is sent to the nations, and they will listen.”
When he had said these words, the Jews departed, having a great dispute among themselves.
Paul stayed two whole years in his own rented house and received all who were coming to him,
preaching God’s Kingdom, and teaching the things concerning the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness, without hindrance.
b: In the last devotion, the Jewish leaders said to Paul, “This sect is spoken against everywhere,” yet they were willing to listen. In this devotion, they came and listened for a whole day; when they finished, they dispersed, and as they dispersed the book ended, with no verdict, no account of Paul’s end, not even a proper full stop, only a rented house with its door open for two years and no one forbidding.
I. “From morning until evening… testifying about the Kingdom of God”—The Last Time, Still the Same Thing

Verse 23: the Jewish leaders appointed a day, and many came. Paul spoke for a whole day, “testifying about the Kingdom of God, and persuading them concerning Jesus, both from the law of Moses and from the prophets.”

This is the last sermon recorded in the whole book, and we can almost set it beside the first. In chapter 2, Peter at Pentecost quoted Joel and David to prove that “God has made him both Lord and Christ”; in chapter 28, Paul in Rome quotes Moses and the prophets, still saying the same thing: who Jesus is and what the Kingdom of God is. From the upper room in Jerusalem to the rented house in Rome lie nearly thirty years, thousands of miles, countless imprisonments and shipwrecks, yet not one word of the message changed. This is not running out of ideas; from beginning to end they had only one thing to say.

“The Kingdom of God” and “the things concerning Jesus” are in fact two sides of one thing: God’s kingdom is where Jesus is King. Paul spoke all day, and what he spoke was always the same question: this One, will you let him be King?
II. “Some believed… and some disbelieved”—One Message, Two Outcomes, All the Way Through

Verse 24 has only a handful of words, yet it is a picture that recurs throughout the book. When Peter finished speaking, three thousand were baptized, and some mocked. When Paul finished in Pisidian Antioch, the whole city was stirred, and some drove him out of the region. On the Areopagus in Athens, some mocked and some believed. Before Agrippa, Festus said he was out of his mind, while Agrippa was almost persuaded. Through all twenty-eight chapters, this forking road is one the disciples walked every day.

The same message, the same speaker, the same Holy Spirit at work, and the result split in two. This reminds us that a witness’s responsibility has never been to guarantee results, but to make the message clear, complete and carried through to the end. The seed has been scattered; what the soil is like is not for the sower to decide.
III. “The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through Isaiah the prophet to your fathers”—Ending the Book with an Old Testament Word Is Its Most Fitting Close

Before the meeting broke up, Paul quoted that very heavy passage from Isaiah 6: hearing, you will hear but never understand; seeing, you will see but never perceive, because the people’s heart has grown callous, their ears dull and their eyes closed. This passage was what God said to Isaiah when he was called, and the Lord Jesus himself quoted it (Matthew 13:14–15); now Paul quotes it again at the end of his ministry.

Three generations, the same passage, the same phenomenon: God’s word is set before them, yet people can look and not see, listen and not hear. This does not mean God’s word is weak. It means a human heart can harden to the point where even light cannot get in. Paul quoted this not to curse but to be honest: every synagogue he had walked into in his life confirmed what Isaiah had seen through long before. And this is also the deepest warning of the whole book: the position closest to God does not guarantee a soft heart. Judas on the list of the twelve, and the Council members who read the books of Moses every day, are the clearest examples.
IV. “This salvation of God is sent to the Gentiles. They will also listen”—The Key Verse Reaches Its End, and Enters Every Age

“This salvation of God is sent to the Gentiles. They will also listen.” This sentence takes us back to the beginning of the book: “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth” (1:8). After chapter 28, the gospel had truly reached the heart of the empire; but “the uttermost parts of the earth” was never a place where geography draws a full stop. It is the next step that every generation must set out on afresh. When Paul said in Rome, “They will also listen,” those words are still being fulfilled today, including us, and including every person we are serving who has not yet heard.
Paul’s personal story fades out here, yet the camera does not close; it only opens wider, wide enough to take in everyone who reads this book.
V. “No one forbidding him”—The Most Open Full Stop in All of Scripture

The last two verses, 30 and 31, are the most unexpected ending in the whole book of Acts. We expected to read the outcome of Paul’s trial before Caesar, to learn whether he lived or died. Luke wrote only that he stayed two whole years in his own rented house, received all who came to him, preached the Kingdom of God with all boldness and taught the things concerning the Lord Jesus Christ, “no one forbidding him.”

The last word in the original is an adverb meaning “unhindered.” Twenty-eight chapters of nothing but hindrances: the Council’s threats, prison chains, the storm at sea, the snake’s bite. Luke chose to close with “no one forbidding him” not because the hindrances had stopped, but because the hindrances had never truly stopped anything. This book is not about how one man broke through every obstacle to reach Rome; it is about one fact: from the first day, God’s word was never truly bound by anyone, and even the man in chains himself could not hold back his mouth.
This is why no book in all of Scripture ends like Acts: it simply does not end.
321 Principle Light: This Book Was Never Finished, Because It Records How God’s System Grows

Looking back over these twenty-eight chapters, what we see is a clear road. It begins with the waiting in the upper room: one hundred twenty people, each different yet of one accord, first loosened their hands and then were filled with the Holy Spirit. It passes through persecution in Jerusalem, Stephen’s martyrdom, Saul’s falling to the ground, the wall torn down at Cornelius’s house, one strange city after another on three missionary journeys, the arrest in Jerusalem and the storm on the Mediterranean, and finally stops at a rented house in Rome, with the door open and no one forbidding.

What this road walks is exactly the three foundations. Jesus was their example: as he obeyed and gave himself up, the disciples walked the same narrow way. The Bible was their standard: from Peter quoting Joel and Stephen recounting Israel’s history to Paul quoting Moses and the prophets, every action was checked against God’s word. The Holy Spirit was their guide: the wind at Pentecost, Philip carried away, Cornelius’s vision, the call from Macedonia; sovereignty never rested in human hands for a moment. This road also lived out the two cores. Letting Jesus be King is not a slogan: it is Peter saying before the Council, “We must obey God rather than men,” and Paul, even in chains, still calling the one who harmed him a brother. Letting Jesus have all the glory is Barnabas laying the money from his field at the apostles’ feet, and Luke writing after every healing that “the people praised God,” not the one who did the miracle.

And all of this accomplishes one purpose: to build God’s system. Not a temple, not an organization, not the biography of a hero, but group after group of self-denied people willing to let Jesus be King in them, carrying God’s kingdom circle by circle from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth. This is exactly why Luke does not write Paul’s end: the main character of this book was never Paul, but the risen Lord still at work through the Holy Spirit. Paul exits, and the Lord’s work does not stop.
a: Speak it through, without changing the message
From Peter to Paul, for thirty years there was only one thing to say: who Jesus is. May what I speak in my life also stand up to such repetition.
Accept both outcomes
The same message, some believe and some don’t; my responsibility is to make it clear, not to guarantee results.
Face a hard heart honestly
The position closest to God does not guarantee a soft heart; may I ask the Lord daily to search myself, not only others.
Bring the ends of the earth to today
“They will also listen” is still being fulfilled today; may I not draw the border of the gospel at the range I can reach.
Believe no one can truly forbid
A chain can bind hands but cannot bind the word; may the hindrance I suffer today become the starting point of what God does next.
q: From the first devotion (675, Acts 1:1) to today, on this journey through twenty-eight chapters, is there a scene that has stayed with you most deeply? Which of your ideas did it change?

“No one forbidding him” is the ending of this book and also an invitation. Right now, in your own life, which page of chapter 29 is waiting to be written? Are you willing to let Jesus be King on that page?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, we have walked with you to the end of these twenty-eight chapters of Acts. From the ten days of waiting in the upper room to the door in Rome that no one forbade, what we saw was never the biography of a group of heroes, but your Spirit using people willing to deny themselves to carry your kingdom all the way to the ends of the earth. Thank you that on this road there were the wind and fire of Pentecost, Stephen’s martyrdom, Saul’s falling down and being won back, the wall torn down at Cornelius’s house, the hymns in the Philippian jail, every strange city from Ephesus to Lystra to Caesarea, and that night of storm on the Mediterranean. Not one thing was outside your control.
Lord, we confess that we often draw the border of the gospel where we feel safe, and treat hindrances as a reason to stop rather than a sign that you are about to open the next door. Remove from us the self that always wants to protect itself, so that we may stand before the Council like Peter, see heaven opened among the stones like Stephen, and, even in chains, call those who hurt us brothers like Paul. Let the Holy Spirit be our guide for life, the Bible our standard for life and Jesus our example for life; reign truly in each of our days, and may all the glory go to you alone.
Lord, this book was not finished, because your work is not finished. Chapter 29 is being written in us: in the sentence we are about to speak today, in the person we are willing to welcome, in every small decision to lay down self and let you be King. Accompany us, and accompany every family member who reads this book, that all our lives we may be overcomers, until we sit with Christ on his throne in your kingdom forever. We pray in the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ, Amen.
